Fastify API (apps/api)  routes → services → providers → repositories

Desktop specifics that matter to this audit:

- The UI boots through `invoke('bootstrap')` → `{ api_base, ws_base, token }`;
  `api_base` already contains `/api/v1`, `ws_base` does not (`DESKTOP.md`).
- The sidecar listens on an ephemeral loopback port and is supervised by a
  bounded-respawn watchdog in `sidecar.rs` (Rust, 149 tests).
- CORS allow-lists `https://tauri.localhost` (`desktopCors.test.ts`).

## 2. VPN subsystem ownership

| Concern | Single owner |
|---|---|
| Spawn → readiness → cleanup of any core child | `services/coreProcess.ts` (`spawnCoreProcess`) |
| Core binary discovery, args, config builders | `services/proxyCores.ts` |
| Provider lifecycle (WireGuard/OpenVPN/sing-box/custom) | `vpn/vpnService.ts` |
| A [… 392 characters omitted] stemProxy.ts` |
| Drop detection / reconnect | `vpn/vpnWatchdog.ts` |
| Aggregate state for the UI | `routes/vpn.ts` + `vpn/vpnState.ts` |

The layering rule holds in the code: routes validate and delegate, services
orchestrate, providers do I/O, repositories own SQL. No route shells out
directly.

## 3. UI structure for VPN

`VpnPage.tsx` owns the rail (grouped: Dispatch / Circumvention / Node path /
Native clients) and the cross-engine `SystemBar`. Each surface
(`OverviewSurface`, `AetherSurface`, `DnsttSurface`, `TunnelSurface`,
`CoreSurface`, `ProviderSurface`, `CustomConfigSurface`) reads from
`useVpnData.ts` query hooks and states only what the backend reported.

The honesty rules that already exist and were preserved:

- a tile is "connected" only when the status' `serverId` **and** `providerId`
  agree (`CustomConfigSurface`), or when the surface is the owning provider;
- `verification` is reported separately from `connected`, so a local tunnel with
  an unverified path is not shown as protected;
- TUN capture has its own claim vocabulary (`tunStatus.ts`): `active`,
  `unguarded`, `recovering`, `requested`, `blocked`.

## 4. Where state can lie, and what stops it

| Lie | Guard |
|---|---|
| "Connected" while the child is dead | provider `status()` reads the child/interface, not a flag |
| "Protected" while the exit path is unverified | `verification: 'not_verified' \| 'verified' \| 'failed'` + per-surface copy |
| "Latency" that was never measured | `null` renders as `—` / `unavailable`, never `0` |
| Two tunnels at once | `tunnelUp`/`noneUp` guards on every connect button + backend serialisation |
| Stale async result overwriting newer state | React Query invalidation + in-flight mutation state |

## 5. Audit-relevant seams

- `runCommand` (`util/exec.ts`) **never rejects** — it resolves `{code:null}` on
  spawn error and on timeout. Any error handling that assumes a rejection is
  therefore dead code. This was checked before writing a fix (see §18).
- `detectVpnBinaries` (`util/vpnDetect.ts`) decides `available`; an engine whose
  binary is absent must never be presented as usable.
- `FileSecretVault` encrypts profile secrets; the on-disk VPN config is
  sanitised for WireGuard/OpenVPN and the real key is materialised only for the
  spawn (and deleted on every exit path).

{"kind":"tool","id":"ZWsJlKAgK6Y","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":"reports/quality-overhaul/06_ENGINE_FAILURE_ANALYSIS.md","instructions":"Writes the engine failure analysis.","content":"# 06 — Engine failure analysis and repairs

Two confirmed defects were found and fixed this session, both in
`WireGuardProvider`. Both were found by executing code rather than reading it:
the second surfaced because the test for the first failed in the "connected"
branch.

---

## D1 (High) — a 15-character name cap made every managed WireGuard tunnel invisible

**Symptom (as it would appear to a user):** connect to a WireGuard profile and
the app reports `tunnel_not_up` ("the tunnel service accepted the config but no
interface appeared") while the tunnel is actually installed and carrying
traffic. On the next launch the boot sweep does not remove the stale
`netpulse-wg-*` service, and the VPN page never shows WireGuard as connected.

**Root cause.** `parseWgInterfaceNames` accepted interface names of at most 15
characters:

```ts
/^[A-Za-z0-9_=+.-]{1,15}$/
```

`wgTunnelNameForProfile` builds `netpulse-wg-<uuid>` — **48 characters**. Every
consumer of the parser therefore saw an empty list:

| Consumer | Line | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `connect()` post-install verification | `vpnService.ts:661` | `ours` never found → throws `502 tunnel_not_up` after a **successful** install |
| `status()` | `:739` | `connected` could never be true for WireGuard |
| `init()` stale-tunnel sweep | `:491` | crashed-session tunnels never removed |
| ` [… 2,228 characters omitted] ned on every poll while disconnected

**Symptom (as it would appear to a user):** none directly; it is idle cost. The
VPN page polls `/vpn/status` every 4–5 s while open.

**Root cause.** `status()` ran `wg show all dump` whenever the binary was
`available`, then ANDed the result with `connectedProfile != null`. When no
profile is owned the dump cannot change the answer.

**Measurement.** `wg show all dump` on this host: 13.6, 15.2, 15.8, 17.0, 17.8,
18.6, 19.3 ms — **median 17.0 ms**, 7 runs, direct `spawnSync` timing. At a 5 s
poll that is ~12 spawns/min and ~0.2 s/min of process-spawn CPU on an idle,
disconnected app, forever, plus the process churn itself.

**Classification.** Algorithmic waste on a hot polling path (no functional bug).

**Options.** A — gate the probe on ownership; B — TTL cache of the dump;
C — move status to an event-driven model fed by the tunnel events.
**Decision: A**, then B only if a connected-state burst shows contention (it does
not: one provider, one poll).

**Fix.** `if (this.available && this.connectedProfile != null)` with a comment
recording the measurement and why the boot sweep, not the poll, is what clears a
leaked tunnel.

**Verification.** `wireGuardStatusProbe.test.ts` asserts `runCommand` is **not**
called for a disconnected poll while `supported: true`, and that the dump still
runs (and parses rx/tx) while a tunnel is owned.

---

## D3 (Low, open) — raw `err.message` shown in VPN toasts and one banner

`VpnPage.tsx:321` renders the raw error message; several surfaces pass
`err.message` as a toast description. These are messages authored by this API
(`ApiError`), not stack traces, so the risk is low — but a transport string or an
OS error can reach the user verbatim. The shared `States.tsx` already normalises
transport failures; the VPN surfaces do not use it for toasts. Left open and
listed in `19_REMAINING_DEFECTS.md` because changing toast copy across seven
surfaces without a visual pass is a worse trade than documenting it.

## D4 (Informational) — managed tunnels report `endpointLatencyMs: null`

WireGuard measures endpoint RTT only while connected; sing-box, custom, OpenVPN
and Aether never report a latency. That is honest (`null`, rendered as
unavailable) and is not a defect — recorded so no future reader "fixes" it by
inventing a number.

{"kind":"tool","id":"ZWsdTFpqSmc","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":"reports/quality-overhaul/07_TUN_PROXY_AND_ROUTING.md","instructions":"Writes the TUN/proxy/routing report.","content":"# 07 — TUN, system proxy and routing

## 1. The three modes, as implemented

| Mode | What actually happens | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **App proxy** | a core opens a local mixed/HTTP inbound; only this app's probes use it | `proxyCores.buildSingboxConfig`, `buildXrayConfig` |
| **System proxy** | Windows registry (`ProxyEnable`, `ProxyServer`, `ProxyOverride`) is written and WinINET is refreshed; the previous values are captured first | `services/systemProxy.ts` |
| **TUN** | sing-box opens a `tun` inbound on `172.19.0.1/30` and the default route is captured; a kill-switch hold is armed before traffic moves | `proxyCores.buildTunGatewayConfig`, `services/tunGatewayHandle.ts` |

The UI never conflates them: `tunStatus.ts` gives TUN its own vocabulary
(`active` / `unguarded` / `recovering` / `requested` / `blocked`) and the
`SystemBar` reports routing verification separately from "a tunnel is up".

## 2. Guard order (read in the code, unchanged this session)

1. Elevation is checked before a TUN request is accepted (`elevation.rs`,
   `admin_status`), and a refusal is surfaced with the remedy.
2. The kill-switch hold is **persisted before** the system proxy is written
   (`killSwitch.ts:199-249`); a failed persist rolls the claim back.
3. TUN start writes a crash claim to the temp dir before the gateway spawns, so
   boot can tell "we were capturing" from "we were not".
4. `unguarded` is a distinct state: capture without an armed hold says
   **NOT protected** in the UI rather than showing green.
5. Disconnect restores the previous proxy and removes the hold; the boot
   recovery path does the same after a crash (`recoverAfterRestart`).

## 3. Verification status

| Check | Status | Why |
|---|---|---|
| System proxy write/restore on Windows | **PARTIALLY VERIFIED** | unit tests (`systemProxyInvalidation`, `systemProxyPac`, `systemProxyRoundTrip` skipped on this host) — the registry is not touched in tests |
| TUN adapter creation | **NOT VERIFIED** | requires administrator rights; not granted in this session |
| Route capture and default-route restore | **NOT VERIFIED** | same |
| Kill-switch fail-closed on drop | **NOT VERIFIED at runtime**; unit-tested (`killSwitch.test.ts`) | needs a real tunnel to drop |
| Crash recovery after force-kill | **NOT VERIFIED at runtime**; unit-tested (`recoverAfterRestart`) | needs a real hold on disk |
| Split-tunnel bypass rules | **NOT VERIFIED** (code path reviewed) | needs a live tunnel |

No claim in this report says TUN works. The prior session's
`reports/system-audit/VPN_TUN_RUNTIME_VERIFICATION.md` reached the same
conclusion on a different date, and that agreement is the only cross-check
available here.

## 4. Risks that remain in the design (not defects found this session)

- **Restore is best-effort.** If the process is killed between the registry write
  and the hold persist, boot recovery relies on the persisted hold; the window is
  one synchronous write, but it exists.
- **Elevation is per-action.** A user who declines the UAC prompt gets a real
  failure, not a fallback to "connected".
- **Apps that ignore the system proxy** (some launchers, services) bypass it. The
  UI copy says the system proxy is not full-tunnel protection; TUN is what
  captures everything.
"}}

## 1. Metric taxonomy, and where each one comes from

| Metric in the UI | Real source | Never conflated with |
|---|---|---|
| TCP connect time | `profilePing` TCP probe to the node endpoint | ICMP RTT, tunnel startup |
| TLS handshake time | `profilePing` TLS probe (reports the negotiated version) | TCP connect |
| Locally-acked sample | flagged when the RTT is implausibly low; excluded from "fastest" | a real measurement |
| UDP reachability | UDP probe, labelled `UDP` | TCP latency |
| Tunnel startup | `spawnCoreProcess` readiness (TCP accept on the port the config opens) | external connectivity |
| Exit-IP proof | `fetchExitIpThrough*` after the tunnel is up | readiness |
| Endpoint RTT (WireGuard) | ICMP ping to the configured endpoint while connected | handshake age |
| Handshake age | `wg show all dump` peer row | RTT |

The rule enforced throughout: **readiness is not connectivity.** `verification`
is set by the exit-IP proof, and `status()` explicitly does not re-earn it
(`verificationNote`: "status polls do not re-run the proof").

## 2. Timeout and cancellation

- `runCommand` kills the child at `timeoutMs` and resolves `{code, timedOut}` —
  it never rejects, so a hung command cannot leave a dangling promise.
- `spawnCoreProcess` classifies failure as `port_clash | spawn_error | exited |
  timeout` and always runs its idempotent cleanup.
- The connect routes serialise VPN operations, so two connects cannot interleave.

## 3. What was measured this session

Only one thing in this area could be measured without an engine or elevation:

| Measurement | Value | Method |
|---|---|---|
| `wg show all dump` spawn cost | median 17.0 ms (13.6–19.3 ms, n=7) | `spawnSync` timing on this host |

That measurement is what justified removing the disconnected-state probe (§06 D2).

## 4. What was not measured — and why

| Metric | Status | Blocker |
|---|---|---|
| Time to connect through WireGuard | NOT VERIFIED | needs UAC elevation |
| Time to connect through any proxy core | NOT VERIFIED | no core binary |
| Exit-IP proof latency | NOT VERIFIED | no tunnel |
| RTT/jitter/loss to a real node | NOT VERIFIED | no node list configured, no core |
| TUN startup time | NOT VERIFIED | no administrator rights |

No number for any of these appears anywhere in this report set. The UI shows
them as `null`/`—` when they are unavailable, which is the behaviour this report
can verify.

{"kind":"tool","id":"ZWuCezm_EQI","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":"reports/quality-overhaul/09_RUST_AND_ALGORITHM_AUDIT.md","instructions":"Writes the Rust and algorithm audit.","content":"# 09 — Rust and algorithm audit

## 1. Scope actually covered

| Item | How |
|---|---|
| 17 modules, 5 771 lines under `src-tauri/src` | read: module ownership table in `ARCHITECTURE.md`, re-checked against the files |
| Unit tests | `cargo test` → **149 passed, 4 ignored**, exit 0 |
| `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` | **BLOCKED**: `cargo-clippy` is not installed for this toolchain. Not a pass. |
| Allocation/hot-path behaviour | reviewed by reading; no profiler run |

No benchmark numbers are reported for Rust because none were produced. The two
ignored benchmark tests (`status::tests::bench_compose_throughput`, …) were not
run.

## 2. Process supervision (`sidecar.rs`)

- Spawn → stdin token handshake → readiness poll on the port (300 ms connect
  timeout, 75 ms interval, 20 s budget).
- Watchdog is a pure `watchdog_tick(restarts, alive, stable, since) → (Action,
  restarts)` function, unit-tested for: rapid-restart cap, 60 s cooldown,
  60 s stable re-arm, and the "died again inside the window" case.
- Backoff sleeps are bounded (`2 s` steady state), so a permanently failing
  sidecar cannot spin.

**Assessment:** the loop is bounded in both frequency and total restarts, which
is the property that matters for idle CPU. Complexity O(1) per tick.

## 3. Logging (`logging.rs`)

- One buffer per line, appended under a single lock, so two threads cannot
  interleave a token across lines (this is what makes line-level secret
  redaction sound in `diagnostics.rs`).
- Rotation at a hard cap (~512 KB, previous file kept as `.log.1`), checked
  before each append — O(1) per write.
- Panic hook flattens multi-line payloads into one line.

**Assessment:** no unbounded growth path found; the cap is shared with the
snapshot the status page advertises (`the_rotation_cap_the_snapshot_advertises_is_the_writers_real_cap`).

## 4. Status snapshot (`status.rs`)

- `compose` decides what may be **published**: a port only while something is
  listening, `sidecar_restarts: number | null`, `log_file_bytes: number | null`.
- Known-zero vs unknown is encoded in the wire type, and tests pin both
  (`an_unreadable_log_is_carried_through_as_unavailable_not_as_zero`,
  `an_exited_child_is_not_reported_running_even_though_its_handle_survives`).

**Assessment:** this is the correct shape for a "something is already wrong"
page. No change made.

## 5. Algorithmic review of TypeScript hot paths

| Path | Complexity | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `parseWgInterfaceNames` | O(lines) | one pass, Set-backed; the *length cap* was wrong (D1) but the algorithm is fine |
| `WireGuardProvider.status` | O(1) now when idle (was O(spawn)) | fixed this session |
| Node list sort/search | O(1) in the API layer — SQL owns it | verified by reading `nodesService`/repository split |
| `validateCustomConfig` | O(n) over the blob, no recursion | bounded by `CUSTOM_CONFIG_MAX` |
| Profile sort by latency | O(n log n) over a bounded profile list | formatting never participates in the comparison |

## 6. Findings

1. **No Rust defect found** in the reviewed modules; clippy could not run, so
   lint-level findings are unknown.
2. **One TypeScript hot-path defect fixed** (D2 in `06_ENGINE_FAILURE_ANALYSIS.md`)
   and **one correctness defect fixed** (D1).
3. **Unmeasured**: allocation counts, GC pressure and idle CPU of the packaged
   app. Reported as `NOT VERIFIED`, not estimated.

## 2. Derived (arithmetic, not a runtime trace)

The VPN page polls `/vpn/status` every 4–5 s. Before the fix, with WireGuard
installed and nothing connected:

```
12 polls/min × 17.0 ms = 204 ms/min ≈ 0.34 % of one core, continuously,
plus 12 process creations per minute, for a value that cannot change.
```

After the fix the same idle path performs no spawn. This is a real reduction in
idle work, but it is **not** a measurement of total app CPU — that needs a
packaged, running app.

## 3. Not measured (and why)

| Idle RSS / working set | **NOT MEASURED** | same |

| Connected-state CPU with traffic | **NOT MEASURED** | no engine binary / no elevation |
| Allocation counts, GC pauses | **NOT MEASURED** | would need `--trace-gc` on the packaged runtime |
| Sidecar restart cost | **NOT MEASURED** | watchdog unit-tested for bounds only |

No figure in this report is an estimate of a runtime behaviour that was not
observed. Where the mission asks for before/after performance, the honest answer
for everything except the `wg` spawn is: *not measurable in this environment.*

| Resource | Bound |

| Startup log | ~512 KB + one rotated file |
| Diagnostic history | bounded per feature (no unbounded array append found in the reviewed paths) |

## 5. Regression risk introduced by this session

- `status()` now reads `this.connectedProfile` before spawning. A future change
  that sets `connectedProfile` without owning a tunnel would make `status()`
  probe `wg` and report a user tunnel as ours — the ownership matcher
  (`isWgTunnelInterface`) is what prevents that, and it is tested.

{"kind":"tool","id":"ZWunbRkf0_o","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":"reports/quality-overhaul/11_UI_DESIGN_AND_IMPLEMENTATION.md","instructions":"Writes the UI design and implementation report.","content":"# 11 — UI design and implementation

## 1. State at the start of this mission

The interface is already a designed product, not a template: `apps/web/src/styles/tokens.css`
declares one token set for both themes (surfaces, elevation, status, protocol
inks, focus, motion, control geometry, type scale), and
`apps/web/src/components/ui` holds 17 shared primitives whose accessibility
requirements are encoded in their types (`IconButton` cannot be built without a
label; `Switch` cannot be built without an accessible name).

The previous UI session already fixed: global keyboard focus visibility,
reduced-motion coverage, the tooltip arrow colour, engine-badge contrast,
account-form error contrast, transport-string headlines, and engine-glyph ink
contrast. Those are recorded in `reports/ui-upgrade/` and were **not** redone.

## 2. What this mission changed in the UI

Nothing functional — the confirmed defects this session were backend
(`06_ENGINE_FAILURE_ANALYSIS.md`). The UI consequence of D1 is large though:

> WireGuard can now actually be reported as connected. Before the fix, the
> interface was correct and the data it received could never say "connected"
> for a real profile id. A UI that is honest about a value that is always wrong
> still misleads the user.

## 3. VPN surfaces reviewed against the honesty rules

| Surface | "Connected" source | Verification shown separately | Second-tunnel guard |
|---|---|---|---|
| Overview | provider id + status | yes (`verification`, exit IP) | n/a (read-only) |
| Aether | own provider status | route scan + TUN claim | yes |
| DNS tunnel | own provider status | TUN claim / capture panel | yes |
| Proxy Tunnel | tunnel state + exit IP | exit IP proven before `active` | yes |
| Core pages | engine availability only | n/a | n/a |
| Managed providers | own provider status | `verification` badge | yes |
| Custom engine | `serverId` **and** `providerId` | n/a | `disabled={tunnelUp}` |

All seven refuse to claim protection from a local listener alone; the copy says
"traffic proven at connect time" and the poll does not re-claim it.

## 4. Changes that would be worth making next (not done, not claimed)

{"kind":"tool","id":"ZW8ex9r62KM","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":"reports/quality-overhaul/18_INDEPENDENT_REVIEW.md","instructions":"Writes the independent review report.","content":"# 18 — Independent review

Written as if reviewing someone else's patch. It includes the review's own
mistakes, because a review that only lists successes is not a review.

## 1. The patch under review

`apps/api/src/vpn/vpnService.ts`:
1. `parseWgInterfaceNames` cap `{1,15}` → `{1,128}`;
2. new `isWgTunnelInterface(name, profileId)`;
3. `connect()` verification uses it;
4. `status()` gates the `wg` dump on `this.connectedProfile != null` and uses the
   matcher.

## 2. Attack surface of the change

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Can a user tunnel now be mistaken for ours? | No. `isWgTunnelInterface` requires an exact name or a strict prefix of `netpulse-wg-<uuid>`; `my-own-tunnel` fails both. Tested. |
| Can another profile's tunnel match? | Only if its name were a prefix of this profile's full name — impossible for two distinct full names of equal length, and the truncated branch requires the name to be shorter than the full one. Tested with a second profile. |
| Does the wider cap let garbage through? | A row must have exactly 6 tab-separated columns and a charset-restricted name ≤128; peer rows have 8 columns. A 129-char column is rejected by test. |
| Does the cap change command execution? | Names are only compared and passed as argument arrays; `shell:false` is unchanged. No interpolation added. |
| Does gating the probe hide a real tunnel? |  [… 586 characters omitted] akes this provider report connected. That is the intent.
- `disconnect()`'s "remove every managed tunnel" sweep was deliberately left
  unchanged — it is defence against lost state, not ownership.

## 4. Test quality

| Test | Verdict |
|---|---|
| `wireGuardStatusProbe` | good: asserts absence of a side effect, not just a return value; reaches the connected branch |
| Reaches the connected branch by assigning a private field | **fragile** — a rename breaks it at runtime rather than compile time. Acceptable for a unit test; an injection seam would be better if this class grows |
| `vpnHardening` additions | good: exact/truncated/foreign/bare-prefix cases |
| Missing | an end-to-end install test (needs elevation) — stated, not simulated |

## 5. Mistakes made during this review

1. **Wrong hypothesis, retracted.** I expected `status()` to throw when `wg`
   disappears and planned a try/catch. Reading `util/exec.ts` showed
   `runCommand` resolves `{code:null}` and never rejects. No change made; the
   retraction is recorded in `02` so the next reader does not re-derive it.
2. **First draft of the scorecards mixed "before" and "after"** in one table.
   Corrected: `04` is the post-repair view, `17` separates repairs from scores
   and refuses to invent a pre-repair number.
3. **Initial report claimed "eleven tones measured"** for the glyph work; the
   VPN page only renders ten (`accent`/`onDark` are elsewhere). Corrected in
   `reports/ui-upgrade/FINAL_UI_RELEASE_GATE.md`.

## 6. Regression risks accepted

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| A future provider sets `connectedProfile` without owning a tunnel | `isWgTunnelInterface` still requires the interface to exist |
| Widened parser accepts a 6-column line that is not an interface | the private-key column position is the discriminator; the changelog comment records the rule |
| Tests mock `../src/util/exec`, so a real spawn bug cannot be caught by them | the manual measurement (17.0 ms) and the e2e suite remain the only real-spawn coverage |

## 7. Verdict

The patch is a **correct, minimal repair** of a defect that made a shipped
feature unable to report success. It is not a redesign and does not claim to
verify WireGuard end to end. Recommend merge after the concurrent UI tree is
settled; the remaining risk is environmental, not logical.

Ordered by release impact. Nothing here is claimed as fixed.

| 1 | **High** | Eight of eleven engines have no executable on this host; none was executed | environment | install xray / sing-box / v2ray / hysteria / openvpn / aether / dnstt, then run a real connect + exit-IP proof per engine |
| 2 | **High** | TUN capture, route takeover and kill-switch fail-closed are unit-tested only | needs administrator rights | one elevated TUN cycle with a forced drop, then a crash-recovery cycle |
| 3 | **High** | WireGuard install/verify path unverified end to end (the parser fix is tested; the OS behaviour is not) | needs UAC | one elevated connect where the interface appears, traffic exits, disconnect removes the service |
| 4 | Medium | `cargo clippy -D warnings` cannot run | `cargo-clippy` not installed | `rustup component add clippy` then run the gate |
| 5 | Medium | Update feed is a loopback URL in dev configuration; installer is unsigned (prior report) | release configuration / signing cert | signed bundle + real feed URL |
| 6 | Medium | Packaged app idle CPU/RAM never instrumented | no instrumented run | measure a packaged build for 10 minutes idle and 10 minutes connected |
| 7 | Low | Raw `err.message` can reach a VPN toast or the status banner | cosmetic; messages are API-authored | route VPN errors through the same normaliser `States.tsx` uses |
| 8 | Low | Managed/custom/Aether/dnstt tunnels report `endpointLatencyMs: null` | no measurement exists | measure only if a real probe can be added; never fabricate |
| 9 | Low | No auto-reconnect for the custom provider | by design; not promised in the UI | decide whether it should exist before adding it |
| 10 | Info | `vpn_audit_report.md` at the repo root is an untracked, partly stale audit | not mine to delete | author may remove or move it under `reports/` |
| 11 | Info | Concurrent workstream owns four modified files in `apps/web` | not mine to commit | merge/review before any release commit |

## Deliberately not changed

- **UI copy across seven VPN surfaces** — improving toast wording without a
  visual pass would trade a low-severity leak for an unverified interface
  change.
- **Hysteria YAML parsing** — adding a YAML dependency to validate a config the
  client already validates at startup is a dependency for a marginal gain; the
  key check catches the common failure.
- **`endpointLatencyMs` for engines that have no probe** — filling it would mean
  inventing a measurement.

## Accepted risks

- Secrets exist in process memory while a tunnel is running (unavoidable).
- The system proxy is not full-tunnel protection; TUN is, and the UI says so.
- Trust-on-first-use for engine binaries is limited to SHA-256 verification
  against the published digest for Aether; the other cores are user-installed.

Only measured numbers appear here. Everything else is labelled.

## Measured

| Metric | Value | Method |
|---|---|---|
| `wg show all dump` spawn | **17.0 ms median** (13.6–19.3, n=7) | `spawnSync` timing |
| Idle WireGuard status cost, after fix | **0 spawns** | test asserts `runCommand` not called |
| API suite duration | 131 s / 1 205 tests | `vitest run` |
| Rust suite duration | < 1 s / 149 tests | `cargo test` |
| Web entry bundle | 444.22 kB minified · 138.80 kB gzip | `vite build` |
| Lazy map chunks | globe 1 203.54 kB · three 558.22 kB | `vite build` |

## Derived

```
Before: 12 polls/min × 17.0 ms = 204 ms/min ≈ 0.34 % of one core, idle,
        plus 12 process creations/min, for a value that cannot change.
After:  0 spawns/min while disconnected.
```

This is the only performance claim this mission can support with measurement.

## Not measured

| Metric | Status |
|---|---|
| Packaged app idle CPU / RSS | NOT MEASURED |
| Connected CPU / memory with traffic | NOT MEASURED |
| Connection establishment time (any engine) | NOT VERIFIED |
| TUN startup time | NOT VERIFIED |
| React render counts / interaction latency | NOT MEASURED |
| Allocation counts, GC pressure | NOT MEASURED |
| Rust throughput benchmarks | NOT RUN (ignored tests) |

## Method notes

- The `wg` timing used `spawnSync` in a loop of 7 on an idle machine; median is
  reported because the first call includes warm-up.
- The bundle figure was produced on a tree being edited concurrently, so no
  before/after attribution is claimed.

## Risk to future performance

`status()` is polled; anything added to it runs 12 times a minute per client.
The new ownership gate means the expensive branch only runs while a tunnel is
owned. Any future probe added to `status()` should follow the same rule: do not
measure what cannot have changed.

## Outcome

The audit produced one **high-severity defect that made a shipped feature unable to report success**, one measurable idle-cost defect, and an honest scorecard that does **not** reach the 85 gate — because eight of eleven engines cannot run on this machine.

**D1 — WireGuard could never be seen working.** `parseWgInterfaceNames` accepted interface names of at most 15 characters, but every tunnel this app creates is `netpulse-wg-<uuid>` — 48 characters. So the post-install check could not find the interface it had just installed (`502 tunnel_not_up` on a working tunnel), `status()` could never return connected, and the boot sweep never removed a leaked tunnel. It survived review because the only fixture was `netpulse-wg-x` (13 chars) and 15 is Linux's real `IFNAMSIZ` limit. Fixed by raising the cap to 128 and adding `isWgTunnelInterface` (exact, or a truncated prefix that still carries our own prefix) used by both `connect()` and `status()`. I found this because my own test's *connected* branch failed — the assertion was right, the parser was wrong.

**D2 — a process spawn per poll for nothing.** `status()` ran `wg show all dump` on every poll while merely disconnected, where the result is ANDed with `connectedProfile` and therefore cannot change the answer. Measured on this host: 13.6–19.3 ms, **median 17.0 ms** over 7 runs — ~12 spawns/min on an idle VPN page. The probe is now gated on owning a tunnel; a test asserts zero spawns when idle.

**Verification:** web 447/50 files, API **1 205 passed / 3 skipped / 114 files**, worker 96/4, Rust **149 passed** (4 ignored), eslint and both builds exit 0 — all with captured exit statuses. `cargo clippy -D warnings` **could not run**: the component isn't installed, so that gate is reported blocked, not passed.

**Scores:** WireGuard 83 (MEDIUM confidence), Proxy Tunnel / OpenVPN 74, sing-box 73, Xray 70, Custom / Aether / V2Ray 68, TUN+kill switch 65, dnstt 63, Hysteria2 61; system-weighted ≈ **72/100**. Not rounded up: only WireGuard's binary exists here, no elevation was granted, so TUN, install and every proxy core are code-reviewed and unit-tested but never executed. Verdicts: internal alpha **GO**, release candidate **NO-GO**, production **NO-GO**.

- `/etc/soar/server.key` — private key.
- `/var/lib/soar/last-checks.txt` — last check results.

9. Do not wait indefinitely for tests. Diagnose timeouts, isolate the slow test, check resource constraints, and run smaller relevant suites. Continue with other useful work while long tests execute if the tooling supports it.
10. Do not use fake test results, mocked production success, or success-shaped logs to claim completion.
11. When a command fails, capture the real error, identify the cause, apply a reasonable fix, and retry.
12. Maintain a short internal checklist of remaining tasks and work through it until the finish criteria are met.
13. Do not ask the user to run routine shell commands when you have a working authorized execution path.
14. Do not claim access to the VPS, Wrangler, or repository until you have verified that access.
15. If a particular route is blocked, use a viable alternative. A failed HTTPS approach does not justify abandoning the rest of the mission.
16. No unnecessary confirmation prompts. The user has authorized experimental VPS changes. Execute reasonable changes independently, with backups and verification.

## 3. Verify actual Cloudflare/Wrangler access

Check whether Wrangler is installed and authenticated using commands such as:

- `wrangler --version`
- `wrangler whoami`

Use the project's installed Wrangler version and its documented behavior.

Inspect the repository for existing Cloudflare configuration, D1 bindings, migration files, Workers, environment names, and deployment commands.

If authenticated, inspect the actual account, relevant zones, records, Workers, and D1 databases before changing anything. Use the existing authorized account and least-privilege access.

If Wrangler is unavailable or unauthenticated:

- Inspect other existing authorized Cloudflare integrations or credentials that can be used without exposing secrets.
- Continue all work that does not require Cloudflare.
- Do not print tokens or secret environment values.
- Do not create a new paid service, change account ownership, or create unnecessary resources.
- Do not claim a Cloudflare deployment succeeded unless you verify the deployed state.

### Cloudflare and D1 requirements

Preserve the project's D1-first architecture. Do not introduce Cloudflare R2 or other paid infrastructure unless it is essential and explicitly authorized by the existing project requirements.

Before altering records, take a machine-readable snapshot of relevant existing records and preserve records unrelated to Soar.

When changing DNS:

- Confirm the exact zone and authoritative ownership.
- Confirm that the record is in the correct parent zone.
- Preserve unrelated MasterDNS/Cotton records and existing VPN hostnames.
- Check nameserver glue/delegation requirements for the actual parent-zone arrangement.
- Use idempotent changes wherever possible.
- Verify the final state with authoritative queries and independent public resolvers.
- Do not assume that a record is safe to delete merely because it is not used by the new integration.

If a DNS record is owned by an external dynamic DNS provider or cannot be changed through Cloudflare, determine the actual delegation model and use the correct authoritative control plane.

## 4. Secure and finish the Soar management panel

The panel is currently working via SSH tunnel. Preserve that working access while completing security work.

### Rotate the exposed randomized path

1. Inspect the installed release's supported access-configuration and path-rotation mechanisms.
2. Back up `/var/lib/soar-panel/access.json` securely before changing it.
3. Use the documented supported mechanism to generate a new randomized path.
4. Keep the new path in a root-only file or otherwise protected local output.
5. Verify the old path no longer grants access and the new path works through the SSH tunnel.
6. Do not print the path to shared logs, agent messages, terminal transcripts that are collected centrally, or final reports.
7. Never store the path in the repository, frontend code, public DNS, or client-side bundles.

If the normal command cannot rotate the path, investigate its implementation and documentation. Do not corrupt the panel database or manually alter internal schema fields without understanding the supported recovery path.

### Finish HTTPS without breaking Xray

The existing Xray process owns TCP port 443. Do not blindly stop it, replace its configuration, or bind a second service to the same address/port.

Investigate the actual Xray listener addresses, TLS/SNI routing, certificates, existing reverse proxies, and panel security helper capabilities.

Choose the safest viable arrangement, in this order of preference:

1. Reuse an existing reverse proxy or TLS termination arrangement if one is present and compatible.
2. Use a supported SNI/reverse-proxy integration that preserves the existing Xray service and its client protocols.
3. Use a separate panel hostname and a dedicated port if this is the only reliable alternative.
4. Keep the panel private over SSH if public HTTPS would jeopardize the existing services.

A separate port can provide secure HTTPS without taking over 443, but only configure it after confirming the application and certificate workflow support it.

Do not expose the panel management listener directly to the internet. If a proxy is used, ensure the panel trusts proxy headers only from the intended local proxy and cannot be spoofed by direct clients.

Verify:

- The certificate chain and hostname.
- HTTPS redirects and login routing.
- The new randomized path.
- SSH-tunnel access as a fallback.
- Existing Xray connectivity and listeners after the change.
- Service restart behavior and persistence across reboot.

Do not mark HTTPS complete simply because a certificate was issued. Test the actual panel URL and authentication flow.

## 5. Finish WhiteDNS DNS tunnel integration

Inspect the installed Soar binary, bundled documentation, configuration, database, UI, service logs, and supported client format. Determine exactly how this release expects the server, client, tunnel domain, access mode, and management panel to work.

Do not confuse the management panel with the DNS data plane.

### Verify authoritative delegation

For each configured zone (`soar.abystral.dpdns.org`, `t.abystral.dpdns.org`, and `s.abystral.dpdns.org`), determine which zones are actually intended to be served by WhiteDNS and which records remain associated with other services.

Test:

- A/AAAA records and nameserver addresses.
- Parent-zone delegation.
- UDP and TCP port 53 from outside the VPS.
- Direct authoritative SOA/NS responses.
- Recursive public resolver results.
- Appropriate DNS negative responses and error handling.
- Restart and persistence behavior.

Use more than one public resolver where practical. Account for TTLs and propagation delays. Never claim that public DNS is healthy merely because the local authoritative query succeeds.

### Verify actual tunnel traffic

Create or configure a real supported test client using the documented Soar protocol.

Run an end-to-end test that demonstrates:

1. The client resolves or contacts the intended nameserver.
2. DNS tunnel queries reach the intended server.
3. The server recognizes the correct zone/profile.
4. The tunnel session establishes successfully.
5. Actual test data traverses the tunnel.
6. Return traffic works where bidirectional traffic is expected.
7. The client can access a controlled, known test endpoint through the tunnel.
8. The tunnel fails safely when given invalid configuration.
9. The tunnel recovers after a controlled client or service restart.

Capture logs, return codes, timings, and relevant counters. Redact private credentials and profile material.

If a supported test client is unavailable, determine whether one is included in the release bundle or repository. If necessary, create a minimal test harness using the documented protocol and APIs. Do not substitute an unrelated DNS lookup for an end-to-end tunnel test.

Use controlled test destinations. Do not use the test to scan unrelated systems, generate uncontrolled traffic, or interfere with other users.

### DNS port and firewall behavior

Verify the real external firewall/provider rules and local firewall state.

Do not assume UFW being inactive means every port is reachable. Confirm the provider network firewall and actual UDP/TCP reachability.

Open only the ports required for the supported tunnel, panel, and existing services. Preserve existing required listeners. If a required firewall change causes an outage, roll back the specific change and diagnose the correct rules.

Do not re-enable `netpulse-dnstt` while it conflicts with WhiteDNS on port 53.

## 6. Integrate the application with the real backend

Inspect the entire current repository before making changes. Identify the desktop frontend, Rust/Tauri backend, TypeScript services, networking layer, subscription system, Cloudflare Worker endpoints, D1 schema, and any existing VPN profile-generation code.

Determine the intended relationship between NetPulse, WhiteDNS Soar, and the existing VPN services from the source code and project requirements.

Implement the necessary integration end to end:

- Correct frontend flows and error handling.
- Correct backend/API calls.
- Real configuration and profile generation.
- Correct DNS tunnel configuration and client instructions.
- Secure handling of credentials and profile data.
- State persistence and reconnection behavior.
- Appropriate loading, empty, error, and success states.
- Diagnostics and useful actionable logs.
- Server-side validation and authorization.
- Database migrations and backward compatibility where needed.
- Consistent subscription or account state if that is part of the existing design.

Use the existing architecture wherever possible. Avoid inventing a second account system or parallel backend when an established service already handles that responsibility.

Do not hardcode server credentials, panel access paths, private keys, or environment-specific secrets into the frontend or repository.

If a feature is not supported by WhiteDNS 0.6.0, determine whether it can be implemented using documented supported interfaces. Do not silently claim compatibility with unsupported APIs.

Keep other NetPulse VPN methods functional. The new DNS tunnel should be additive unless the project explicitly specifies otherwise.

## 7. Diagnose and finish automated tests

The previous `npm run lint` succeeded, but tests timed out. This is an unresolved task, not a passing test result.

1. Inspect `package.json`, workspace configuration, test runners, CI workflows, and project documentation.
2. Identify all supported test commands.
3. Reproduce the timeout and capture which test or setup stage hangs.
4. Check for open handles, child processes, network-dependent tests, unbounded retries, fixture deadlocks, database setup issues, and resource exhaustion.
5. Separate unit, integration, build, and end-to-end suites.
6. Run the smallest relevant suite first, then expand.
7. Fix real defects or test infrastructure issues.
8. Use explicit timeouts appropriate to each suite.
9. Avoid skipping, weakening, or deleting tests simply to get a green result.
10. Run lint, type checks, unit tests, integration tests, builds, and platform-specific checks as applicable.
11. Record the actual command, exit status, and result for each.
12. If a test cannot run because an external dependency is unavailable, record that precise dependency and continue with every independent test.

For the Tauri/Rust side, run the project's supported Cargo formatting, check, test, and build commands as appropriate. Do not assume the project is frontend-only.

## 8. Protect existing production functionality

Although this VPS is experimental, it already hosts services that must be checked after changes.

Before substantial production changes:

- Capture service status and current listener state.
- Back up the relevant configuration.
- Record the current service command line and configuration paths.
- Prepare a rollback command or restore procedure.
- Change one logical subsystem at a time.
- Verify immediately after each change.

After any service or networking change, verify:

- `x-ui`
- `netpulse-xray`
- `netpulse-hysteria`
- `netpulse-socks`
- `soar-panel`
- `soar-panel-ops`

Do not automatically restart every service as a troubleshooting ritual.

Never erase panel databases, subscription data, user profiles, or unrelated DNS records as a cleanup shortcut.

If a change breaks an existing service, fix it or roll back the relevant change before proceeding with unrelated production modifications.

## 9. Required observability and troubleshooting

Make failures diagnosable rather than hiding them.

Use systemd status, journal logs, listener inspection, application logs, client logs, and network-level tests. Preserve useful diagnostics without exposing credentials or randomized access paths.

For the DNS tunnel, distinguish at least these stages:

- Public name resolution.
- Delegation and authoritative response.
- Network reachability.
- Protocol negotiation.
- Client authentication/profile acceptance.
- Tunnel establishment.
- Forwarding and return traffic.
- Application-level connectivity.

A successful stage must not be used to claim success for later stages.

Add or improve health checks only where supported by the existing application architecture. Ensure health checks distinguish management-panel availability from data-plane tunnel health.

## 10. Documentation and reproducibility

Update the repository documentation to explain:

- Architecture and data flow.
- Required environment variables and safe secret provisioning.
- Development setup.
- Build and test commands.
- WhiteDNS server configuration.
- Domain/delegation requirements.
- Client configuration and connection instructions.
- Panel access and secure path rotation.
- HTTPS/reverse-proxy design.
- Service ownership and port allocation.
- Deployment and migration steps.
- Backup and rollback.
- Troubleshooting.
- Which capabilities were actually verified.

Use placeholders for secrets and private access paths. Do not commit actual credentials or environment-specific secrets.

Where appropriate, provide repeatable scripts for verification and deployment. Scripts should be idempotent where possible, validate prerequisites, fail clearly, and avoid destructive defaults.

## 11. Execution sequence

Execute the following sequence without waiting for additional user input:

### Phase A — Establish the current state

- Inspect the repository and uncommitted changes.
- Verify actual VPS and Wrangler access.
- Verify current service status, listeners, DNS records, and panel access configuration.
- Review Soar 0.6.0 documentation and supported commands.
- Create secure backups of configurations that may need to change.

### Phase B — Remove the panel security exposure

- Rotate the exposed randomized path.
- Verify access using the new path without disclosing it.
- Resolve panel HTTPS using a compatible architecture or keep management securely private if HTTPS would jeopardize Xray.
- Verify the existing VPN services afterward.

### Phase C — Finish the DNS data plane

- Confirm correct authoritative delegation for each intended zone.
- Verify public UDP/TCP reachability.
- Create a real supported test client.
- Establish a tunnel and transfer actual test data.
- Resolve failures and repeat the tests until they pass or a genuine external blocker is established.

### Phase D — Finish code integration

- Implement all necessary frontend/backend integration.
- Integrate configuration, profile generation, diagnostics, and persistence.
- Preserve existing VPN functionality.
- Add appropriate tests and documentation.

### Phase E — Resolve test failures

- Diagnose the test timeout.
- Run all independent test suites.
- Fix issues found.
- Run a clean final validation pass.

### Phase F — Final deployment and regression testing

- Deploy changes to the appropriate environment.
- Verify the actual deployed version.
- Verify all required services and public DNS.
- Verify real client tunnel traffic.
- Verify the relevant NetPulse workflows.
- Verify that existing VPN methods remain functional.
- Verify restart/persistence behavior.
- Check for exposed secrets, unintended public management listeners, and uncommitted generated files.

If a phase is blocked, continue every independent phase that can still make progress. Return to the blocked phase after trying reasonable alternatives. Do not abandon the task merely because one dependency is unavailable.

## 12. Definition of done

Do not declare completion until the following have been addressed:

- [ ] Existing repository changes preserved.
- [ ] Current implementation inspected and integrated correctly.
- [ ] Panel randomized path rotated and protected.
- [ ] Panel access verified after rotation.
- [ ] Panel HTTPS completed securely, or a documented and verified private-access fallback retained because no safe compatible HTTPS arrangement is available.
- [ ] DNS delegation and public UDP/TCP behavior verified.
- [ ] Real client tunnel connection established.
- [ ] Actual test data successfully traverses the tunnel.
- [ ] Return traffic and controlled endpoint connectivity verified where applicable.
- [ ] NetPulse application integration tested.
- [ ] Lint, type checks, relevant tests, and builds run with honest results.
- [ ] Previous test timeout diagnosed and resolved or precisely isolated.
- [ ] Existing x-ui, Xray, Hysteria, and SOCKS functionality checked after production changes.
- [ ] Documentation updated.
- [ ] Deployment and rollback procedures documented.
- [ ] No credentials or private panel paths leaked into source control or public artifacts.
- [ ] Actual final deployed state verified.

A task can be reported as partially complete only when a genuine external limitation remains after you have exhausted practical alternatives. Clearly distinguish verified success, failed tests, unrun tests, and unverified assumptions.

## 13. Final report

At the end, provide a concise but specific report containing:

1. **Implemented:** actual files, modules, features, and configuration changes.
2. **VPS changes:** services changed, ports, DNS changes, HTTPS/access outcome, and backups.
3. **Cloudflare/Wrangler:** actual resources inspected or modified, and deployment verification.
4. **Testing:** exact commands and actual pass/fail/timeout results.
5. **End-to-end verification:** client type, tunnel establishment, data-transfer evidence, and connectivity results.
6. **Regression results:** status of all existing VPN services.
7. **Security:** path rotation, panel exposure, TLS status, and secret handling.
8. **Remaining issues:** only genuine unresolved issues, with exact evidence and the best available workaround.
9. **Rollback:** where backups are stored and how to restore affected components.
10. **Repository state:** changed files and any remaining uncommitted changes.

Never include the new randomized panel URL, credentials, tokens, private keys, or full client profiles in the report.

**Begin execution now. Do not respond with a plan alone. Inspect, implement, test, fix, deploy where authorized, verify, and continue until the definition of done is satisfied or a genuinely insurmountable external blocker remains.**

   - `zone`: The delegated tunnel zone

const parsed = parseSoarUri('soar://abc123@1.2.3.4:53?zone=gb6ysax.soar.abystral.dpdns.org&pubkey=base64key...')
// Returns: { profileId: 'abc123', server: '1.2.3.4', zone: 'gb6ysax.soar.abystral.dpdns.org', pubkey: 'base64key...' }
```

# PHASE 1 — Fix password-reset email end to end

## 1.1 Trace the complete password-reset workflow

Identify the actual login and account-management architecture first. There may be multiple account types or separate flows for the desktop app, web app, administrator panel, and Telegram users.

Trace the complete path:

1. User requests a password reset.
2. Frontend validates the form and calls the correct API.
3. API validates input and resolves the account safely.
4. Backend generates a reset token.
5. Token state and expiry are persisted.
6. Email template and destination are constructed.
7. The email provider receives the message.
8. The provider attempts delivery.
9. User opens the reset link.
10. Application verifies the token.
11. New password is validated and securely hashed.
12. Token is consumed so it cannot be reused.
13. Relevant sessions are invalidated according to the application's security policy.
14. User can sign in with the new password.
15. Reusing the reset token fails.

Locate the exact broken stage using code, sanitized logs, provider diagnostics, and a controlled account. Do not merely change the frontend button or pretend that accepting an email request proves that the email was sent.

Investigate likely causes, including:

- Missing or incorrect production secrets.
- Incorrect email provider or API configuration.
- Provider SDK/version mismatch.
- Invalid sender address or unverified sender domain.
- Missing provider permissions or expired API credential.
- Incorrect production base URL.
- Incorrect reset-link construction or malformed URL encoding.
- Wrong route or HTTP method.
- Reset tokens not persisted or retrieved correctly.
- Token expiry or clock handling bugs.
- Database schema mismatch.
- Worker environment differences.
- Queue delivery failures or retry behavior.
- Email templates failing in production.
- Provider rejection, suppression, bounce, or rate limits.
- Invalid DNS email authentication records where a custom domain is actually used.
- Password update transaction failing after token validation.
- Frontend routing or deep-link handling failing after the link is opened.
- A mismatch between the authentication provider and an app-managed password system.

Distinguish a provider accepting a message from delivery to a mailbox and from a working password reset. Each is a different stage.

## 1.2 Repair the email delivery configuration

Inspect the currently installed email provider and existing project design. Use the existing supported integration rather than adding an unrelated provider unnecessarily.

Verify:

- Production secret names and whether they are configured.
- Sender identity and provider authorization.
- Verified sender/domain state.
- Correct sender/from address.
- Correct recipient address normalization.
- Correct production origin and reset URL.
- Template rendering and required substitutions.
- Provider response classification.
- Timeout, retry, and rate-limit behavior.
- Logs and error redaction.
- Production versus development environment configuration.

Never hardcode API credentials or print them during diagnostics.

If the provider requires verified domain ownership, DNS changes, or account activation, use existing authorized access to complete the setup when possible. Make only records required by the chosen provider and preserve unrelated DNS entries.

If an external credential genuinely does not exist or requires owner-only verification, complete the code and tests, identify the exact missing capability at the end, and continue repairing every other issue. Do not invent successful delivery.

## 1.3 Enforce secure reset semantics

Implement or verify the following:

- Generate cryptographically secure, high-entropy reset tokens.
- Store a token hash rather than a raw reusable token where the current architecture supports it.
- Set an explicit, bounded expiry.
- Make the token single-use.
- Consume the token atomically with the password update.
- Prevent simultaneous requests from consuming the same token multiple times.
- Validate password input consistently with normal registration/login.
- Use the application's established strong password-hashing algorithm.
- Prevent user enumeration: the external reset-request response should not disclose whether an account exists.
- Rate-limit reset requests and verification attempts.
- Avoid logging raw tokens or complete reset URLs.
- Invalidate relevant sessions or refresh tokens after the password changes, where supported.
- Ensure reset emails use trusted, configured application origins, not an arbitrary user-supplied Host header.
- Do not permit an attacker to inject a malicious reset destination URL.
- Ensure a provider timeout does not leave duplicate uncontrolled sends or disclose account state.

Do not silently create an account when a user requests a password reset.

If some accounts authenticate exclusively through Telegram or an external identity provider and have no password, handle that case according to the existing authentication design. Do not fabricate password credentials.

## 1.4 Test password reset in a real environment

Create or use a controlled test account and a verified test mailbox.

Perform the actual steps:

1. Request a reset.
2. Confirm the API responds safely.
3. Confirm the provider accepts the outgoing email.

# PHASE 2 — Repair accounting, wallet balances, and financial consistency

**Treat financial correctness as a data-integrity incident.**

Do not begin by editing balances manually or deleting suspicious transactions. Determine how money is recorded, identify the invariant that is broken, preserve evidence, and implement a repair that is idempotent and auditable.

## 2.1 Audit every accounting entry point

Trace the accounting system through the application, API, database, background jobs, webhook handlers, and administration interface.

Include all features that exist in the actual project:

- Wallet creation and balances.
- Deposits and top-ups.
- TON payments and on-chain confirmation.
- Manual bank/card transfers and admin approvals.
- Card-to-card payments and receipts.
- Subscription purchases.
- Renewals and auto-renewals.
- Plan changes and upgrades/downgrades.
- Refunds and reversed payments.
- Promotional credits, discounts, and bonus days.
- Referral commissions and rewards.
- Admin credits, debits, adjustments, and refunds.
- Exchange rates and currency conversion.
- Pending payments, failed payments, timeouts, and expired orders.
- Subscription revenue analytics and financial dashboards.
- Daily aggregates, statistics, and reconciliation reports.
- Provider webhooks and background retry jobs.

Find every code path that mutates wallet balances, creates financial events, applies payments, or changes subscription entitlements.

Search for:

- Multiple conflicting balance-calculation implementations.
- Direct balance writes without a corresponding transaction record.
- Duplicate payment handling.
- Missing or inconsistent transaction state transitions.
- Lost updates caused by concurrent operations.
- Incorrect decimal arithmetic.
- Wrong currency conversions.
- Missing indexes/uniqueness constraints.
- Query filters that omit valid transactions.
- Inconsistent UTC/local date boundaries.
- Incorrect accounting aggregates or stale materialized summaries.
- Idempotency failures in webhooks or background jobs.
- Incorrect refund/chargeback behavior.
- Missing user authorization on wallet or admin routes.
- Admin actions that do not leave an audit trail.
- Payment success being recorded before confirmation.
- Financial operations that succeed in one table but fail in another.

Document the current accounting model and determine which records are authoritative for each financial event.

## 2.2 Establish explicit accounting invariants

Use the existing system's intended business rules, and verify them against the actual implementation.

At minimum, establish these invariants:

1. A provider payment or bank-transfer approval creates at most one financial credit for a specific confirmed payment.
2. A subscription purchase or renewal charges the intended amount exactly once.
3. Duplicate events or webhook retries cannot duplicate a credit or charge.
4. A refund or reversal cannot be applied repeatedly.
5. An unconfirmed, failed, rejected, or expired payment cannot be spent as available balance.
6. Failed provisioning must not cause an untracked charge or an untracked entitlement.
7. A wallet balance agrees with the authoritative ledger or an explicitly defined reconciliation mechanism.
8. Currency amounts and conversions are reproducible using the correct source precision and rate snapshot.
9. Every administrative adjustment is authorized, reasoned, and auditable.
10. Expiry or revocation does not silently rewrite historic payment records.
11. Accounting reports distinguish pending, confirmed, failed, refunded, and reversed states.
12. The same logical event produces the same financial result regardless of retries or execution order.

If the repository already has a sound immutable ledger, repair its implementation instead of introducing a competing ledger. If there is no reliable ledger or equivalent source of truth, implement an appropriate ledger model through a backward-compatible migration.

Do not rebuild the entire database simply because a cleaner schema is possible.

## 2.3 Use exact monetary arithmetic

Never use binary floating-point arithmetic as the source of truth for money.

Use an established, consistent representation:

- Integer minor units for currencies with defined fractional units.
- Integer smallest protocol units for TON and other on-chain currencies.
- Integer whole units for currencies whose application rules require them.
- Explicit currency identifiers and precision metadata.
- A defined and tested rounding policy for conversion.
- A stored exchange-rate snapshot for transactions where historical conversion matters.

Do not treat USD cents, USDT precision, TON nanotons, Iranian rial, and toman as if they all use the same unit.

Audit currency parsing, formatting, FX provider fallbacks, rate margins, and every input path. Preserve the rate and calculation context required to explain historical transactions.

## 2.4 Make financial mutations atomic and idempotent

For each financial mutation, inspect the database engine and use its supported transaction/atomicity guarantees.

With D1, do not assume that a multi-statement operation is safe merely because statements were issued close together. Use the supported transaction or batched-write behavior and appropriate constraints for the actual operation.

Implement or verify:

- A stable idempotency key per logical event.
- Unique provider transaction/payment identifiers where appropriate.
- Safe state transitions.
- Conditional updates that only succeed from an expected state.
- Atomic relationship between the transaction record and the balance/ledger update.
- Safe retry processing.
- Proper concurrency handling.
- Consistent error handling when one part of an operation fails.
- Dead-letter/retry visibility for failed background tasks.
- Safe reconciliation of aggregate balances.

Never assume an API request is delivered exactly once. Payment providers, queues, webhooks, and workers routinely retry.

For an already-processed event, return the existing result where appropriate instead of creating another transaction.

## 2.5 Reconcile current financial records without destroying history

Using a consistent database snapshot:

1. Inventory wallets, ledger entries, payments, deposits, refunds, subscription purchases, adjustments, and audit records.
2. Recalculate each account's expected balance from the authoritative records.
3. Compare calculated balances with stored balances.
4. Compare confirmed payment amounts with credits.
5. Compare completed purchases/renewals with charges and resulting entitlements.
6. Check for duplicate provider events and duplicate logical transaction records.
7. Check for missing ledger entries, orphan records, negative balances, and contradictory states.
8. Reconcile referral/bonus credits and promotional activity.
9. Compare financial summaries and analytics aggregates with their source records.
10. Produce a discrepancy report without exposing unnecessary personal information.

**Do not automatically add credits to users merely because two numbers disagree.** Determine why each discrepancy exists.

Corrective requirements:

- Preserve original transactions and audit history.
- Prefer compensating ledger entries or a versioned reconciliation operation over rewriting historic balances.
- Never replay production payments blindly.
- Never generate synthetic money to make the reconciliation totals match.
- Do not charge real users or refund them based on unverified assumptions.
- Keep a record of the exact correction applied, why it was applied, and which source records support it.
- Use an idempotent reconciliation operation so repeating it cannot duplicate corrections.
- Back up the affected records and test the repair on a copy or isolated test data first where possible.

If the actual accounting data has unexplained discrepancies, contain the affected operation where safe, avoid further duplicate credit/charge risk, and fix the underlying bug before applying corrections.

Do not disable the entire payment platform unnecessarily if the fault can be isolated to a specific handler or operation.

## 2.6 Repair administrative accounting and reports

Verify that administrators can correctly:

- Find a user and inspect wallet/transaction history.
- View available, pending, and held balances according to the defined model.
- Identify deposits and their provider/confirmation state.
- Approve or reject eligible manual payments once.
- Credit/debit balances through an authorized, reasoned operation.
- Issue refunds and identify reversal status.
- Inspect subscription charges and renewal history.
- Resolve failed provisioning and payment events without duplicating money.
- Reconcile wallet totals against the ledger.
- View financial metrics and date-range reports.
- Export relevant accounting reports if the existing application supports exports.

All administrative financial actions must have access control, validation, reason capture where appropriate, and audit logging.

Never show one number in the wallet and an inconsistent number in the accounting dashboard without explicitly identifying what each metric represents.

## 2.7 Test accounting with controlled scenarios

Build deterministic tests using isolated/test data for:

- Successful deposit and single credit.
- Duplicate provider callback.
- Concurrent callback for the same payment.
- Rejected and expired manual payment.
- Successful subscription purchase.
- Failed subscription provisioning and retry.
- Renewal and insufficient funds.
- Duplicate renewal event.
- Refund and repeated refund attempt.
- Admin credit/debit.
- Promo and referral credits.
- Currency parsing/rounding and FX snapshot behavior.
- Queue retry and dead-letter handling.
- Reconciliation with known discrepancies.
- Negative balance prevention where required.
- Authorization failures.
- Dashboard/report totals matching ledger results.
- Failure halfway through a multi-record operation.

Verify exact expected integer amounts. Do not use approximate floating-point assertions for financial correctness.

Also run a read-only reconciliation against the real production database, where authorized, after the code fix. Do not use production customer funds as test fixtures.

# PHASE 3 — Repair Telegram account linking

Telegram linking must establish that the person controlling a Telegram account is authorized to link it to the correct application account. A button that merely opens a bot is not sufficient.

## 3.1 Trace both sides of the linking flow

Inspect every relevant component:

- Desktop/web account settings.
- Telegram linking endpoint.
- Authenticated user identity.
- Link-token generation and storage.
- Telegram bot `/start` or deep-link parser.
- Telegram update webhook authentication.
- User/Telegram ID matching.
- Link completion callback.
- Database relationship and uniqueness constraints.
- Link status polling/refresh in the app.
- Existing-account conflict handling.
- Unlinking and account recovery.
- Subscription synchronization between app and bot.
- Administrative linking/repair tools.
- Retry, expiry, and replay behavior.

Identify the real failing scenario and root cause. Look for:

- Invalid or incorrectly encoded deep-link payloads.
- Telegram start payload length or format violations.
- Missing bot username or wrong production bot.
- Broken webhook URL or webhook secret.
- Incorrect parsing of `/start` arguments.
- Wrong route or callback names.
- Token expiry or persistence bugs.
- User identity confusion between application user ID and Telegram numeric ID.
- Links tied to the wrong session or environment.
- Duplicate Telegram IDs or duplicate app-account links.
- Race conditions where two link attempts overwrite each other.
- Callback authorization or session issues.
- Broken polling or frontend state refresh.
- Link completion that changes the database but not the UI.
- Account merging that loses subscriptions or wallet references.
- Old links or outdated cached linking status.
- Production/test bot mismatch.

Fix the entire flow rather than only one callback handler.

## 3.2 Implement a safe linking protocol

Use a secure, explicit protocol compatible with Telegram's supported bot/deep-link behavior.

The required semantics are:

1. A signed-in application user requests a link.
2. The backend verifies their identity and authorization.
3. The backend creates a cryptographically strong, short-lived, single-use linking token.
4. The server stores only the minimum required data, preferably a hash of the token, together with its expiry and the initiating account.
5. The application displays the correct bot deep link or QR code.
6. The user opens that link in the correct production Telegram bot.
7. The bot receives the token through a genuine Telegram update.
8. The backend validates the bot update using the configured supported authentication method.
9. The token is validated against the initiating application account.
10. The token is consumed atomically and cannot be replayed.
11. The Telegram identity is linked only if no conflicting relationship exists or the conflict is resolved through a secure established recovery flow.
12. The database stores the resulting relationship consistently.
13. The app receives or polls the correct linked state and refreshes its UI.
14. Reusing the old link fails safely.
15. Expired or cancelled attempts fail safely.
16. Existing subscription/wallet data stays associated with the correct account.

Check Telegram's actual constraints for bot deep-link payloads and produce an opaque compact token that fits them. Do not put passwords, emails, reset tokens, wallet balances, or private subscription data into the deep-link payload.

Do not trust a client-supplied Telegram ID as proof of control. Use the verified Telegram update from the intended bot and its authenticated server-side flow.

Prevent:

- Token replay.
- Linking an attacker's Telegram account to a victim's app account.
- Linking one Telegram account to multiple accounts when the product requires uniqueness.
- Replacing another user's link without authorization.
- Reusing one-time links.
- CSRF/cross-account association.
- Race conditions.
- Account takeover through unsecured unlink/relink operations.
- Trusting fake webhook calls or unsigned identity claims.
- Leakage of link tokens through logs and analytics.

## 3.3 Define account-conflict and unlink behavior

Handle common cases explicitly:

- User has no Telegram link.
- User already has the correct Telegram link.
- Telegram account is linked to another app account.
- User has an existing Telegram bot account with a wallet or active subscription.
- User is changing devices.
- Token expired.
- Token was used.
- A linking attempt was cancelled.
- Telegram webhook is delayed or delivered twice.
- The user unlinks or relinks.
- Account recovery is required.

Do not blindly merge two accounts or move wallet balances, payments, referrals, or active subscriptions between accounts.

If linking existing bot and application accounts requires a merge, implement a secure, deterministic policy with transaction-safe migration and audit history. Preserve the canonical account ID and all subscriptions/financial references.

Make repeated linking requests safe and idempotent.

## 3.4 Verify the actual Telegram production setup

Use authorized access to verify:

- Actual bot username and intended production environment.
- Current webhook URL and configured secret state without printing the secret.
- Webhook reachability and response.
- Update processing health and recent errors.
- Correct deep-link generation.
- Correct bot command/start-payload parsing.
- Correct link completion and persistence.
- Correct frontend status update.
- Duplicate-update handling.
- Expiration and replay prevention.

If a webhook update must be tested, use a controlled test account and supported test flow. Do not fabricate Telegram updates that bypass the same verification used in production.

## 3.5 Run a real Telegram linking test

Using controlled test accounts:

1. Sign in to the actual application.
2. Request a Telegram link.
3. Open the generated link in the actual intended Telegram bot.
4. Complete the link through Telegram.
5. Confirm the API/database reflects the correct association.
6. Confirm the application UI switches to linked state without a manual database edit.
7. Confirm the bot recognizes the expected linked account.
8. Confirm intended subscription/account status is synchronized.
9. Attempt to use the link a second time.
10. Attempt an expired token.
11. Attempt linking a Telegram ID already linked elsewhere.
12. Confirm failure cases do not change another user's records.
13. Test unlink/relink if the product supports it.

Do not use a real customer's Telegram account for destructive testing.

# PHASE 6 — Incident containment and rollback

When you discover a defect that risks repeated financial damage, duplicated credits, unauthorized linking, or token leakage, contain that specific operation while fixing it.

Examples:

- If a payment callback is double-crediting wallets, prevent duplicate processing before replaying events.
- If manual accounting adjustments are corrupt, restrict the affected administrative mutation while leaving safe read-only views available.
- If Telegram linking permits cross-account changes, temporarily disable the vulnerable link mutation rather than allowing account takeover.
- If reset tokens are predictable or reusable, disable the vulnerable reset completion route until the secure fix is ready, while keeping normal authentication available where safe.

Do not disable more service than necessary.

For every production change:

1. Record the pre-change state.
2. Back up affected configuration/data.
3. Define the expected recovery procedure.
4. Apply the change.
5. Verify success.
6. Roll back if the change causes unexpected damage.
7. Retest the affected workflow.

Do not restore an old full financial database over a newer production database. Use supported backups, reconciliations, and targeted recovery mechanisms that preserve valid writes.

Keep an audit trail for data corrections, admin actions, and financial reconciliation.

# NetPulse Cloud Worker

The security boundary between the desktop app and D1. Accounts, sessions,
sync, and password reset live here; the desktop is an untrusted client and
never holds Cloudflare credentials.

## Deploy

```bash
cd cloud/worker
npm install
npx wrangler login              # OAuth; no tokens in the repo
npx wrangler d1 create netpulse-cloud   # once; paste the id into wrangler.toml
npx wrangler d1 migrations apply netpulse-cloud --remote
npx wrangler secret put AUTH_SECRET     # >= 32 random bytes, hex/base64
npx wrangler secret put RESET_PEPPER    # >= 32 random bytes, independent of AUTH_SECRET
npx wrangler deploy
```

## Password-reset email (optional but recommended)

Without a mail transport, `POST /api/v1/auth/forgot-password` still issues a
single-use 30-minute token (hashed in D1) but **delivers nothing** — the audit
event records `mail_unconfigured` and no token exists anywhere retrievable.

To enable email delivery, configure the Resend transport:

```bash
npx wrangler secret put RESEND_API_KEY   # from resend.com/api-keys
```

and set the sender address. `MAIL_FROM` is currently held as a Worker SECRET
(`npx wrangler secret put MAIL_FROM`) in the live production Worker, so the
sender address is not in this repo; a `[vars]` entry in `wrangler.toml` works
too, but never both — a deploy-time var and a secret with the same name are an
ambiguous pair to debug. The same applies to `EXPECTED_ORIGIN` (public, so it is
a var in `wrangler.toml`, one per environment). Otherwise the value would be:

```toml
[vars]
MAIL_FROM = "NetPulse <no-reply@yourdomain.com>"
```

`yourdomain.com` must be a verified domain in your Resend account. Delivery

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

concurrency:
  # One run per ref; a new push supersedes an in-flight run.
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  gates:
    name: lint, typecheck, tests, rust, feed
    runs-on: windows-latest
    timeout-minutes: 60

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Node 22 is the floor declared in package.json ("engines": ">=22").
      # `cache: npm` keys on package-lock.json, which is committed.
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm

      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Lint
        run: npm run lint

      # The four TypeScript projects typecheck independently — apps/api,
      # apps/web, packages/shared and the Cloudflare worker have separate
      # tsconfigs and separate type environments (DOM, Node, workers-types), so
      # one project passing says nothing about the others.
      - name: Typecheck apps/api
        run: npm run typecheck -w @netpulse/api

      - name: Typecheck apps/web
        run: npm run typecheck -w @netpulse/web

      - name: Typecheck packages/shared
        run: npm run typecheck -w @netpulse/shared

      - name: Typecheck cloud/worker
        run: npm run typecheck -w @netpulse/cloud-worker

      # `--if-present` so a workspace that genuinely has no tests is skipped
      # rather than silently reported as passing.
      - name: Test (all workspaces)
        run: npm run test --workspaces --if-present

      # The Rust core: sidecar supervision, the elevation broker, the secret
      # vault, log redaction, path handling. 145 #[test] functions live here and
      # none of it is reachable from the JS suites.
      - name: Rust tests
        run: cargo test --manifest-path src-tauri/Cargo.toml

      # The updater feed is what a shipped install checks for updates; it is
      # generated by its own script with its own tests.
      - name: Updater feed tests
        run: npm run test:feed

const HOST = '206.1.96.89';
