+/*
+ * ============================== motion system ============================
+ * The shell's movement, in one place. Every rule here is opt-in by class, so
+ * a page that does not use it is unaffected, and all of it collapses to no
+ * movement under `prefers-reduced-motion` (bottom of this section).
+ */
+
+/*
+ * Page enter. The routed page rises 10px and fades, over 380ms. It is an
+ * ENTER-only animation (there is no exit presence): a page that animates out
+ * delays the next one, which is the opposite of feeling fluid.
+ *
+ * Deliberately no `filter` and no `will-change`: either one turns this element
+ * into a containing block for `position: fixed` descendants, so a modal or a
+ * floating panel inside a page would be positioned against the page box instead
+ * of the window. The same reason it is `translate3d(...)` and then `none` — a
+ * completed transform must not linger.
+ */
+@keyframes page-in {
+  from { opacity: 0; transform: translate3d(0, 10px, 0) scale(0.998); }
+  55% { opacity: 1; }
+  to { opacity: 1; transform: none; }
+}
+.page-enter {
+  animation: page-in var(--dur-slow) var(--ease-fluid) both;
+}
+
+/*
+ * Indeterminate route bar. Rendered only while a lazy page chunk is in flight
+ * (the Suspense fallback), so its life is exactly the wait: it grows to 72%
+ * quickly and creeps from there, which is the honest shape of "still loading"
+ * without pretending to know a percentage.
+ */
+@keyframes route-progress {
+  from { transform: scaleX(0.02); opacity: 0.9; }
+  40% { transform: scaleX(0.55); }
+  70% { transform: scaleX(0.72); }
+  to { transform: scaleX(0.86); opacity: 0.65; }
+}
+.route-progress {
+  position: fixed;
+  inset-inline: 0;
+  top: 0;
+  z-index: 60;
+  height: 2px;
+  transform-origin: 0 50%;
+  background: linear-gradient(90deg, var(--color-accent), var(--color-accent-strong));
+  box-shadow: 0 0 12px color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-accent) 60%, transparent);
+  animation: route-progress 2.4s var(--ease-fluid) both;
+  pointer-events: none;
+}
+
+/*
+ * The sidebar's active-row highlight exists as ONE element that travels,
+ * instead of a background painted on whichever link happens to be current.
+ * That is the difference between a menu that highlights and a menu that has
+ * a cursor. Position/size are set inline by `SidebarContent`; this rule owns
+ * only the look and the travel.
+ */
+.nav-pill {
+  position: absolute;
+  inset-inline: 0;
+  top: 0;
+  border-radius: 0.5rem;
+  pointer-events: none;
+  opacity: 0;
+  background: linear-gradient(
+    90deg,
+    var(--color-accent-soft),
+    color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-accent) 5%, transparent) 72%,
+    transparent
+  );
+  box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-accent) 20%, transparent);
+  will-change: transform, height;
+}
+
+/* The 2px rail is the "you are here" marker; the glow is what makes it read
+   as lit rather than drawn. */
+.nav-pill::before {
+  content: '';
+  position: absolute;
+  left: 0;
+  top: 22%;
+  bottom: 22%;
+  width: 2px;
+  border-radius: 2px;
+  background: var(--color-accent);
+  box-shadow: 0 0 10px color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-accent) 70%, transparent);
+}
+
+.nav-pill[data-visible='true'] {
+  opacity: 1;
+}
+
+/*
+ * The travel is enabled only once the pill has been measured in a laid-out
+ * sidebar (`data-ready`). Two things depend on that:
+ *
+ *   - on mount, so the pill does not fly in from y=0 before it has a place;
+ *   - while the sidebar is `display: none` (below `lg`), because a transition
+ *     started inside a non-rendered subtree never advances in Chromium: the
+ *     element keeps the value it had when it was hidden. That was observed

+ * `height` is deliberately NOT transitioned. It is layout, not movement: it

+.nav-pill[data-ready='true'] {
+  transition:

+
+/*
+ * Command palette. The backdrop fades; the panel rises and settles with the
+ * spring curve. Kept out of the JS so opening it costs no layout read.

+@keyframes palette-backdrop-in {
+  from { opacity: 0; }

+@keyframes palette-panel-in {

+.palette-backdrop-in {
+  animation: palette-backdrop-in var(--dur-quick) linear both;
+}
+.palette-panel-in {
+  animation: palette-panel-in var(--dur-base) var(--ease-spring) both;
+}
+
+/*
+ * Toasts arrive from the right edge they are anchored to, which is the
+ * direction they will leave in — a toast that fades up from below reads as

+@keyframes toast-in {

+  to { opacity: 1; transform: none; }
+}
+.toast-in {
+  animation: toast-in var(--dur-base) var(--ease-fluid) both;
+}
+
+/*
+ * The active nav row no longer paints its own background — the travelling
+ * pill does. Only the ink changes here.
+ */
+.nav-row {

+  z-index: 1;
+}

+@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
+  .page-enter,
+  .palette-panel-in,
+  .palette-backdrop-in,
+  .toast-in {

+  }
+  .route-progress {
+    animation: none;
+    transform: scaleX(0.5);
+  }
+  .nav-pill {
+    transition: none;
+  }
+}

export function sweepStaleCoreDirs(maxAgeMs = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000): { removed: number; failed: number } {
  const dir = os.tmpdir();
  let entries: string[];
  try {
    entries = fs.readdirSync(dir);
  } catch {
    return { removed: 0, failed: 0 };
  }
  const cutoff = Date.now() - maxAgeMs;
  let removed = 0;
  let failed = 0;
  for (const name of entries) {
    if (!CORE_TMP_PREFIXES.some((prefix) => name.startsWith(prefix))) continue;
    const target = path.join(dir, name);
    try {
      const stat = fs.statSync(target);
      if (!stat.isDirectory() || stat.mtimeMs > cutoff) continue;
      fs.rmSync(target, { recursive: true, force: true });
      removed += 1;
    } catch {
      failed += 1;
    }
  }

 * Engine start-to-ready benchmark.
 *
 * Measures the exact production gate a probe, a tunnel hop and a TUN gateway
 * all wait on: `spawnCoreProcess` resolving when the core's inbound accepts
 * TCP. A real core binary is not required — the child is a stub that binds the
 * reserved port after a fixed delay, so the number isolates OUR startup latency
 * (poll cadence, port check, readiness probe) from the binary's own boot time.
 *
 *   npx tsx scripts/bench-engine-start.ts            # default run
 *   RUNS=25 STUB_DELAY_MS=40 npx tsx scripts/bench-engine-start.ts
 *
 * Reported per run, in ms:
 *   ready  spawn → inbound accepts (the gate every caller blocks on)
 *   start  reserve port + write config + spawn → inbound accepts
 *
 * The stub's own delay is subtracted nowhere: it is part of both sides of a
 * before/after comparison, and keeping it in makes the reported number the
 * honest wall-clock wait a caller experiences.
 */
import fs from 'node:fs';
import os from 'node:os';
import path from 'node:path';

import { findEngineBinary } from '../apps/api/src/services/proxyCores.ts';
import { reservePort, spawnCoreProcess } from '../apps/api/src/services/coreProcess.ts';

const RUNS = Number(process.env['RUNS'] ?? 15);
/** How long the stub takes to bind, i.e. a fast core. */
const STUB_DELAY_MS = Number(process.env['STUB_DELAY_MS'] ?? 15);

const STUB = `
import net from 'node:net';
const port = Number(process.argv[2]);
const delay = Number(process.argv[3] ?? 0);
const server = net.createServer((socket) => socket.destroy());
setTimeout(() => server.listen(port, '127.0.0.1'), delay);
`;

function percentile(values: number[], p: number): number {
  const sorted = [...values].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const idx = Math.min(sorted.length - 1, Math.max(0, Math.round((p / 100) * (sorted.length - 1))));
  return sorted[idx]!;
}

function summary(values: number[]): string {
  const min = Math.min(...values);
  const p50 = percentile(values, 50);
  const p90 = percentile(values, 90);
  const max = Math.max(...values);
  const mean = values.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / values.length;
  return `min ${min.toFixed(0)}  p50 ${p50.toFixed(0)}  mean ${mean.toFixed(0)}  p90 ${p90.toFixed(0)}  max ${max.toFixed(0)}`;
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const workDir = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'netpulse-bench-'));
  const stubPath = path.join(workDir, 'stub-core.mjs');
  fs.writeFileSync(stubPath, STUB);

  const ready: number[] = [];
  const start: number[] = [];

  try {
    for (let i = 0; i < RUNS; i += 1) {
      // ---- the gate on its own: spawn → ready ----
      const portA = await reservePort();
      const configDirA = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'netpulse-bench-cfg-'));
      fs.writeFileSync(path.join(configDirA, 'core.json'), '{"inbounds":[]}');

      let t0 = performance.now();
      const runA = await spawnCoreProcess({
        bin: process.execPath,
        args: [stubPath, String(portA), String(STUB_DELAY_MS)],
        readyPort: portA,
        readyTimeoutMs: 5_000,
        tempDir: configDirA,
        label: 'core',
      });
      const readyMs = performance.now() - t0;
      if (!runA.ok) throw new Error(`ready run failed: ${runA.failure} ${runA.error}`);
      runA.process.cleanup();
      ready.push(readyMs);

      // ---- the whole startCore-shaped cost: reserve + write + spawn → ready ----
      t0 = performance.now();
      const portB = await reservePort();
      const configDirB = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'netpulse-bench-cfg-'));
      fs.writeFileSync(
        path.join(configDirB, 'core.json'),
        JSON.stringify({ inbounds: [{ port: portB }], outbounds: [] }),
      );
      const runB = await spawnCoreProcess({
        bin: process.execPath,
        args: [stubPath, String(portB), String(STUB_DELAY_MS)],
        readyPort: portB,
        readyTimeoutMs: 5_000,
        tempDir: configDirB,
        label: 'core',
      });
      const startMs = performance.now() - t0;
      if (!runB.ok) throw new Error(`start run failed: ${runB.failure} ${runB.error}`);
      runB.process.cleanup();
      start.push(startMs);
    }

    // Binary discovery runs on every engine status / probe call; time it so a
    // cache is only added if it is actually worth anything.
    const lookups: number[] = [];
    for (let i = 0; i < 20; i += 1) {
      const t = performance.now();
      findEngineBinary('xray');
      lookups.push(performance.now() - t);
    }

    console.log(`\nengine start benchmark · runs ${RUNS} · stub binds after ${STUB_DELAY_MS}ms · ${process.platform}\n`);
    console.log(`ready (spawn → inbound accepts)   ${summary(ready)}`);
    console.log(`start (port+config+spawn → ready) ${summary(start)}`);
    console.log(`findEngineBinary('xray')          ${summary(lookups)}`);
  } finally {
    try {
      fs.rmSync(workDir, { recursive: true, force: true });
    } catch {
      /* best effort */
    }
  }
}

void main();
"}}

   * the loop the moment the address changes, so the common case costs one

   *

   * (4 attempts, 200ms apart ≈ 600ms plus the probes' own time), so a tunnel
   * that genuinely does not route is still called out at the same point rather
   * than much later — this changes when we LOOK, not what counts as a failure.

  const VERIFY_ATTEMPTS = 4;
  const VERIFY_RETRY_MS = 200;
  let after: string | null = null;
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < VERIFY_ATTEMPTS; attempt += 1) {

    // change, so there is nothing to wait for in that case either — the caller

+/**
+ * Engine start-to-ready benchmark.
+ *
+ * Measures the exact production gate a probe, a tunnel hop and a TUN gateway
+ * all wait on: `spawnCoreProcess` resolving when the core's inbound accepts
+ * TCP. A real core binary is not required — the child is a stub that binds the
+ * reserved port after a fixed delay, so the numbers separate OUR startup
+ * latency (readiness cadence) from the child process's own boot time.
+ *
+ *   npx tsx scripts/bench-engine-start.ts            # default run
+ *   RUNS=25 STUB_DELAY_MS=40 npx tsx scripts/bench-engine-start.ts
+ *   CORE_MODULE=./baseline-core-process.ts npx tsx scripts/bench-engine-start.ts
+ *
+ * `CORE_MODULE` points the run at another copy of `coreProcess.ts`, which is
+ * how a before/after is produced from one harness: write the previous version
+ * anywhere importable, point CORE_MODULE at it, and compare the two tables.
+ *
+ * Reported per run, in ms, plus the summary table:
+ *   ready     spawn → inbound accepts (the gate every caller blocks on)
+ *   start     reserve port + write config + spawn → inbound accepts
+ *   boot      spawn → the child actually started listening (NOT ours)
+ *   overhead  listening → we noticed (this is the part the poll cadence owns)
+ *
+ * `overhead` is the number that matters for a before/after: it isolates the
+ * readiness probe from process startup, which no change in this repo controls.
+ * A fixed 300ms tick scored ~230-300ms here; the widening schedule scores one
+ * interval at most.
+ */
+import fs from 'node:fs';
+import os from 'node:os';
+import path from 'node:path';
+
+import { findEngineBinary } from '../apps/api/src/services/proxyCores.ts';
+
+type CoreModule = typeof import('../apps/api/src/services/coreProcess.ts');
+
+const RUNS = Number(process.env['RUNS'] ?? 15);
+/** How long the stub takes to bind, i.e. a fast core. */
+const STUB_DELAY_MS = Number(process.env['STUB_DELAY_MS'] ?? 15);
+
+const STUB = `
+import fs from 'node:fs';
+import net from 'node:net';
+const port = Number(process.argv[2]);
+const delay = Number(process.argv[3] ?? 0);
+const marker = process.argv[4];
+const server = net.createServer((socket) => socket.destroy());
+setTimeout(() => server.listen(port, '127.0.0.1', () => {
+  fs.writeFileSync(marker, String(Date.now()));
+}), delay);
+`;
+
+/** When the stub reports it is listening (its clock == ours). */
+async function readBindTime(markerPath: string): Promise<number | null> {
+  const deadline = Date.now() + 2_000;
+  while (Date.now() < deadline) {
+    try {
+      const value = Number(fs.readFileSync(markerPath, 'utf8'));
+      if (Number.isFinite(value) && value > 0) return value;
+    } catch {
+      /* not written yet */
+    }
+    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 2));
+  }
+  return null;
+}
+
+function percentile(values: number[], p: number): number {
+  const sorted = [...values].sort((a, b) => a - b);
+  const idx = Math.min(sorted.length - 1, Math.max(0, Math.round((p / 100) * (sorted.length - 1))));
+  return sorted[idx]!;
+}
+
+function summary(values: number[]): string {
+  const min = Math.min(...values);
+  const p50 = percentile(values, 50);
+  const p90 = percentile(values, 90);
+  const max = Math.max(...values);
+  const mean = values.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / values.length;
+  return `min ${min.toFixed(0)}  p50 ${p50.toFixed(0)}  mean ${mean.toFixed(0)}  p90 ${p90.toFixed(0)}  max ${max.toFixed(0)}`;
+}
+
+async function main(): Promise<void> {
+  // Loaded inside main, not at module scope: the root package is CommonJS, and
+  // a top-level await here fails to transform.
+  const core: CoreModule = await import(
+    process.env['CORE_MODULE'] ?? '../apps/api/src/services/coreProcess.ts'
+  );
+  const { reservePort, spawnCoreProcess } = core;
+
+  const workDir = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'netpulse-bench-'));
+  const stubPath = path.join(workDir, 'stub-core.mjs');
+  fs.writeFileSync(stubPath, STUB);
+
+  const ready: number[] = [];
+  const start: number[] = [];
+  const boot: number[] = [];
+  const overhead: number[] = [];
+
+  try {
+    for (let i = 0; i < RUNS; i += 1) {
+      // ---- the gate on its own: spawn → ready ----
+      const portA = await reservePort();
+      const configDirA = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'netpulse-bench-cfg-'));
+      fs.writeFileSync(path.join(configDirA, 'core.json'), '{"inbounds":[]}');
+      const markerA = path.join(workDir, `bind-a-${i}.txt`);
+
+      const t0 = Date.now();
+      const runA = await spawnCoreProcess({
+        bin: process.execPath,
+        args: [stubPath, String(portA), String(STUB_DELAY_MS), markerA],
+        readyPort: portA,
+        readyTimeoutMs: 5_000,
+        tempDir: configDirA,
+        label: 'core',
+      });
+      const detectedA = Date.now();
+      if (!runA.ok) throw new Error(`ready run failed: ${runA.failure} ${runA.error}`);
+      runA.process.cleanup();
+      ready.push(detectedA - t0);
+
+      const bindA = await readBindTime(markerA);
+      if (bindA != null) {
+        boot.push(bindA - t0);
+        // Negative only when the child's marker write landed after our connect
+        // succeeded — that is a detection at zero overhead, not a clock skew.
+        overhead.push(Math.max(0, detectedA - bindA));
+      }
+
+      // ---- the whole startCore-shaped cost: reserve + write + spawn → ready ----
+      const startAt = Date.now();
+      const portB = await reservePort();
+      const configDirB = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'netpulse-bench-cfg-'));
+      fs.writeFileSync(
+        path.join(configDirB, 'core.json'),
+        JSON.stringify({ inbounds: [{ port: portB }], outbounds: [] }),
+      );
+      const markerB = path.join(workDir, `bind-b-${i}.txt`);
+      const runB = await spawnCoreProcess({
+        bin: process.execPath,
+        args: [stubPath, String(portB), String(STUB_DELAY_MS), markerB],
+        readyPort: portB,
+        readyTimeoutMs: 5_000,
+        tempDir: configDirB,
+        label: 'core',
+      });
+      const startMs = Date.now() - startAt;
+      if (!runB.ok) throw new Error(`start run failed: ${runB.failure} ${runB.error}`);
+      runB.process.cleanup();
+      start.push(startMs);
+    }
+
+    // Binary discovery runs on every engine status / probe call; time it so a
+    // cache is only added if it is actually worth anything.
+    const lookups: number[] = [];
+    for (let i = 0; i < 20; i += 1) {
+      const t = performance.now();
+      findEngineBinary('xray');
+      lookups.push(performance.now() - t);
+    }
+
+    console.log(`\nengine start benchmark · runs ${RUNS} · stub binds after ${STUB_DELAY_MS}ms · ${process.platform}\n`);
+    console.log(`ready     (spawn → inbound answers)        ${summary(ready)}`);
+    console.log(`start     (port+config+spawn → answers)    ${summary(start)}`);
+    if (boot.length > 0) {
+      console.log(`boot      (child process boots)            ${summary(boot)}`);
+      console.log(`overhead  (listening → we notice it)       ${summary(overhead)}`);
+    }
+    console.log(`findEngineBinary('xray')                   ${summary(lookups)}`);
+  } finally {
+    try {
+      fs.rmSync(workDir, { recursive: true, force: true });
+    } catch {
+      /* best effort */
+    }
+  }
+}
+
+void main();

description = "NetPulse — VPN & Network Intelligence Platform (desktop)"
authors = ["NetPulse"]
edition = "2021"
rust-version = "1.77"

# NetPulse desktop core.
#
# The Rust layer owns everything OS-sensitive:
#   - sidecar lifecycle (supervised Node/TypeScript backend on a private loopback port)
#   - ephemeral daemon token generation (never persisted to disk)
#   - single-instance enforcement
#   - system tray
#   - native application-data paths
#   - capability reporting
#
# The React frontend talks to the sidecar over loopback HTTP/WS with the
# ephemeral token; the token is delivered to the webview only through typed
# Tauri IPC (bootstrap command), never through disk or a public channel.

[build-dependencies]
tauri-build = { version = "2", features = [] }

[dependencies]
tauri = { version = "2", features = ["tray-icon"] }
tauri-plugin-single-instance = "2"
tauri-plugin-dialog = "2"
tauri-plugin-process = "2"
tauri-plugin-updater = "2"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1"
# url: parsing the updater's configured endpoints to decide loopback proxy bypass.
url = "2"
rand = "0.8"
# Elevation broker: descriptor integrity (SHA-256 of the staged tunnel config)
# and loopback-only HTTP to the sidecar for the pending-op handshake.
sha2 = "0.10"
reqwest = { version = "0.12", default-features = false, features = ["json", "blocking"] }


[features]
# this feature is used for production builds or when `devPath` points to the
# filesystem and the built-in dev server is disabled.
custom-protocol = ["tauri/custom-protocol"]

[profile.release]
codegen-units = 1
lto = true
opt-level = "s"
panic = "abort"
strip = true

  stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe'],

driver.stderr.on('data', (d) => process.stdout.write(`[driver:err] ${d}`));

async function req(method, path, body) {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}${path}`, {
    method,
    headers: body ? { 'content-type': 'application/json' } : {},
    body: body ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined,
  });

  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${method} ${path} -> ${res.status}: ${JSON.stringify(json).slice(0, 400)}`);
  return json;
}

//! The navigation backstop, exercised through a real webview.
//!
//! `navigation::classify` is unit-tested as a pure function, but the thing that
//! makes it a backstop is the *wiring* in `window::create_main_window`: the
//! builder's `on_navigation` / `on_new_window` closures, and the fact that they
//! run before the platform webview acts. A unit test cannot see that — Tauri's
//! mock runtime never navigates, and by design it has no engine to refuse.
//!
//! So this test drives the shipped binary itself through `tauri-driver`,
//! Tauri's WebDriver harness, which puts a real WebView2 (or WebKitGTK) window
//! under WebDriver control. It then does the two things the in-page guard
//! cannot see — assigns `location.href` and calls `window.open` — and asserts
//! the window stayed on the app document.
//!

//!   - `#[ignore]` keeps `cargo test` (and every developer's quick loop) from
//!     launching a window; CI runs it explicitly with `-- --ignored`.
//!   - It needs a built app binary, `tauri-driver`, and the platform's native
//!     driver (`msedgedriver` on Windows). Missing pieces fail with a message
//!     naming the env var, never a silent pass.
//!   - There is no dependency on the UI's copy: the assertions are about URL

//!     boundary rather than any particular page.

//! Run locally, Windows:
//!   cargo build --bin netpulse-desktop
//!   set NAV_WEBVIEW_APP=...
//!   set MSEDGEDRIVER=...
//!   cargo test --test navigation_webview -- --ignored --nocapture

fn wait_for<T>(what: &str, timeout: Duration, mut f: impl FnMut() -> Option<T>) -> T {
    let deadline = Instant::now() + timeout;
    loop {
        if let Some(v) = f() { return v; }
        if Instant::now() >= deadline { panic!("timed out waiting for {what}"); }
        std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(100));
    }
}

///
/// Dropping it kills the child, so a failed assertion cannot leave a WebDriver
/// and an app window behind for the next run (or for the user).
struct Driver {
    child: Child,
    base: String,
    log_path: PathBuf,
}

impl Driver {
    fn start() -> Self {
        let bin = std::env::var("TAURI_DRIVER").unwrap_or_else(|_| "tauri-driver".to_string());

        let native_port = free_port();
        let log_path = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("netpulse-webdriver-{}.log", std::process::id()));

        let mut cmd = Command::new(&bin);

            .arg(port.to_string())
            .arg("--native-port")
            .arg(native_port.to_string())
            .stdin(Stdio::null());

            cmd.arg("--native-driver").arg(native);

        // the app's log for the duration of the run — the first place to look
        // when the window never reaches the app document.
        let log = File::create(&log_path).unwrap_or_else(|e| panic!("create {}: {e}", log_path.display()));

            panic!(
                "could not start `{bin}`: {e}\n\

            )
        });

    }

    fn wait_ready(&self, client: &Client) {
        let deadline = Instant::now() + DRIVER_READY;
        loop {
            if let Ok(res) = client.get(format!("{}/status", self.base)).send() {
                if let Ok(json) = res.json::<Value>() {
                    if json["value"]["ready"].as_bool() == Some(true) {
                        return;
                    }
                }
            }
            if Instant::now() >= deadline {
                panic!(
                    "tauri-driver did not become ready at {}\n{}",
                    self.base,
                    self.log_tail()
                );
            }
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(200));
        }
    }

    /// The last few kilobytes of the driver/app log, for a failure message.
    fn log_tail(&self) -> String {
        let mut text = String::new();
        if let Ok(mut file) = File::open(&self.log_path) {
            let _ = file.read_to_string(&mut text);
        }
        let start = text.len().saturating_sub(4_000);
        format!("--- {} ---\n{}", self.log_path.display(), &text[start..])
    }
}

impl Drop for Driver {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        let _ = self.child.kill();
        let _ = self.child.wait();
        // A passing run has no reason to keep its driver log; a failing one is
        // the only copy of what the app said, so keep it and point at it.
        if std::thread::panicking() {
            eprintln!("{}", self.log_tail());
        } else {
            let _ = std::fs::remove_file(&self.log_path);
        }
    }
}

/// Deletes the WebDriver session however the test ends.
struct Session {
    base: String,
    id: String,
}

impl Drop for Session {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        let _ = Client::new()
            .request(Method::DELETE, format!("{}/session/{}", self.base, self.id))
            .send();
    }
}

/// One WebDriver request, with the `value` unwrapped and errors made readable.
fn call(client: &Client, method: Method, url: &str, body: Option<Value>) -> Value {
    let mut request = client.request(method.clone(), url);
    if let Some(body) = body {
        request = request.json(&body);
    }
    let response = request.send().unwrap_or_else(|e| panic!("{method} {url}: {e}"));
    let status = response.status();
    let json: Value = response.json().unwrap_or(Value::Null);
    if !status.is_success() {
        let message = json["value"]["message"].as_str().unwrap_or("(no message)");
        panic!("{method} {url} failed ({status}): {message}");
    }
    json["value"].clone()
}

fn execute(client: &Client, session: &Session, script: &str) {
    call(
        client,
        Method::POST,
        &format!("{}/session/{}/execute/sync", session.base, session.id),
        Some(json!({ "script": script, "args": [] })),
    );
}

fn current_url(client: &Client, session: &Session) -> String {
    call(client, Method::GET, &format!("{}/session/{}/url", session.base, session.id), None)
        .as_str()
        .unwrap_or_default()
        .to_string()
}

/// them from Tauri's custom protocol; a `tauri dev` build loads the Vite
/// server instead. Which one is in use is a build detail — both are the app.
fn is_app_document(url: &str) -> bool {
    url.contains("tauri.localhost") || url.contains("localhost:5173") || url.contains("127.0.0.1:5173")
}

fn wait_for<T>(what: &str, timeout: Duration, mut poll: impl FnMut() -> Option<T>, log: impl Fn() -> String) -> T {
    let deadline = Instant::now() + timeout;
    loop {
        if let Some(value) = poll() {
            return value;
        }
        if Instant::now() >= deadline {
            panic!("timed out waiting for {what}\n{}", log());
        }
        sleep(Duration::from_millis(150));
    }
}

Bulk node testing now batches: a group of nodes shares one core process instead of paying a full start per node.

**What changed**

- [coreProcess.ts](apps/api/src/services/coreProcess.ts) — `spawnCoreProcess` takes `extraReadyPorts`; the readiness gate now requires *every* inbound in the batch to answer (one loopback connect each, own timeout), and the port-clash precheck covers all reserved ports.
- [proxyCores.ts](apps/api/src/services/proxyCores.ts) — `buildXrayMultiConfig` / `buildSingboxMultiConfig` emit one outbound **and** one loopback inbound per node with routing rules pinning inbound *i* → outbound *i*, so a probe on port *i* provably exits through node *i*; `startMultiCore` reserves the batch's ports, does one spawn, one readiness wait, one teardown, and retries once on a port clash. Hysteria is refused (its config holds a single server) rather than silently testing one node N times.
- [proxyEngineRunner.ts](apps/api/src/services/proxyEngineRunner.ts) — `proxyProbeManyWithEngine`: preflight per node costs nothing, nodes are grouped by the engine that can actually dial them, packed 8 per core with 2 cores in flight, probed concurrently through their own ports; unstarted nodes stay `null` (cancelled, not failed), and nodes no shared core can dial fall back to the single-node path.
- [nodeTestProbes.ts](apps/api/src/services/nodeTestProbes.ts) — `proxyProbeMany` wraps that with per-node vaulted secrets and streaming callbacks.
- [nodesService.ts](apps/api/src/services/nodesService.ts) — `testNodes()` opens test rows per group start (so a cancelled scan leaves no `running` rows), finalizes each result and updates node stats; tcp/tls/icmp keep the bounded worker pool since they spawn nothing.
- [routes/nodes.ts](apps/api/src/routes/nodes.ts) — both bulk callers, `POST /nodes/test-batch` and the scanner's `deep-test`, go through `testNodes`; response shape and error masking are unchanged.

**Verification**

`tsc -p apps/api` clean, eslint clean on every touched file, and the full API suite passes: 97 files / 1049 tests (including 25 new tests in [bulkCoreConfig.test.ts](apps/api/test/bulkCoreConfig.test.ts) and [bulkProbeRunner.test.ts](apps/api/test/bulkProbeRunner.test.ts) covering the batched configs, tag/credential wiring, spawn counting, cancellation and row lifecycle).

Measured with [bench-engine-start.ts](scripts/bench-engine-start.ts) (8 nodes, stub cores that bind every inbound, same boot cost on both sides, so the delta is spawn/readiness/teardown only):

| path | p50 | processes |
|---|---|---|
| per-node, sequential | 741 ms | 8 |
| per-node, 8 concurrent (old runner) | 176–208 ms | 8 |
| one batched core | **119 ms** | **1** |

**Limitation:** no xray/sing-box binaries are installed in this environment, so the end-to-end run against real cores (and real proxy latency numbers) wasn't executed here — the unit tests exercise the runner against mocked cores and the bench isolates the startup cost.

The saving scales worst at one or two nodes (a batch of 1 is the old path) and pays off from three nodes up.

{"kind":"tool","id":"dlGYMGIesIA","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":"apps/web/src/lib/quickConnect.ts","instructions":"Add the pure filtering, navigation and display helpers for the quick-connect overlay.","content":"/**
 * Quick-connect picker logic.
 *
 * Pure, React-free rules for the keyboard overlay, so the overlay itself only
 * renders: which nodes a query matches, how the active row moves, and which
 * text a row shows. Keeping them here means the keyboard behaviour is testable
 * without a DOM, and the candidate shape is documented in one place.
 */

/**
 * The subset of a node DTO the picker needs.
 *
 * No host/port: the server never sends a node's dial endpoint to the browser,
 * and the overlay only ever posts the id back.
 */
export interface QuickNode {
  id: string;
  /** Server-built display name; always non-empty. */
  label: string;
  protocol: string;
  country: string | null;
  city: string | null;
  remark: string | null;
  medianProxyMs: number | null;
  status: string;
}

/** Everything a token may match, lower-cased and joined once. */
export function quickNodeHaystack(node: QuickNode): string {
  return [node.label, node.protocol, node.country, node.city, node.remark]
    .filter((v): v is string => typeof v === 'string' && v.length > 0)
    .join(' ')
    .toLowerCase();
}

/**
 * Filter by every whitespace-separated token, in the order the server returned
 * (already fastest-tested first).
 *
 * The whole query as one substring would make "japan tokyo" match nothing even
 * though both words are on screen; token AND is what a user typing two words
 * expects. An empty query keeps the list — opening the overlay should show
 * candidates, not a blank panel.
 */
export function filterQuickNodes(nodes: readonly QuickNode[], query: string): QuickNode[] {
  const tokens = query.trim().toLowerCase().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
  if (tokens.length === 0) return [...nodes];
  return nodes.filter((node) => {
    const haystack = quickNodeHaystack(node);
    return tokens.every((token) => haystack.includes(token));
  });
}

/**
 * Move the active row by `delta`, wrapping at both ends.
 *
 * Wrapping matters here because the overlay opens with the first row selected:
 * ArrowUp from the top should reach the last candidate (the slowest one, still
 * possibly the right choice), not stall.
 */
export function stepActive(index: number, length: number, delta: number): number {
  if (length <= 0) return 0;
  const next = (index + delta) % length;
  return next < 0 ? next + length : next;
}

/** The one-line meta a row shows next to its name: place, then measured latency. */
export function quickNodeMeta(node: QuickNode): string {
  const where = [node.city, node.country].filter((v): v is string => Boolean(v)).join(', ');
  const latency = node.medianProxyMs != null ? `${Math.round(node.medianProxyMs)} ms` : 'unmeasured';
  return [where || 'location unknown', latency].join(' · ');
}

A keyboard-driven quick-connect overlay is live: **Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+K** opens it, arrows move, Enter connects to the highlighted node, Esc closes — and the page you were on never changes.

**How it behaves**

- Lists only what the backend would accept: the same tested-healthy candidate query the Proxy Tunnel card uses (`sortField=proxyLatency`, `maxLatency=5000`), so a node without a recent successful proxy test never appears as pickable.
- Search is token-AND over name, protocol, country, city and remark — "japan vless" narrows instead of matching nothing.
- ↑/↓ wrap at both ends, the list scrolls the selection into view, and `aria-activedescendant` follows it.
- Enter posts `{ nodeId, systemProxy: true }` to `/vpn/tunnel/start`. The toast is built from the tunnel the server stored, so "Tunnel verified · Exit …" only appears once an exit IP was observed; the overlay closes only for `state: 'active'`.
- A 4xx keeps the dialog open with the server's own reason and focus still in the field, so Enter retries on another node. A live tunnel shows a status strip (name, exit IP, state) with a Disconnect button.
- Choosing a different node while connected switches the tunnel — the server tears the previous one down as part of start.

**Files**

- [QuickConnectOverlay.tsx](apps/web/src/components/QuickConnectOverlay.tsx) — the dialog: candidates, status strip, keyboard handling, focus management.
- [quickConnect.ts](apps/web/src/lib/quickConnect.ts) — pure filtering, wrap-around selection, row text, and the one owner of the shortcut decision.
- [AppShell.tsx](apps/web/src/app/AppShell.tsx) — mounts the overlay, one keydown handler for both shortcuts, and a topbar **Connect** button (`Ctrl ⇧ K`).
- [CommandPalette.tsx](apps/web/src/components/CommandPalette.tsx) — "Quick connect to a node" entry that swaps the palette for the overlay.
- [quickConnect.test.ts](apps/web/test/quickConnect.test.ts) — 17 tests.

**Verification**

`tsc -p apps/web` and eslint clean; web suite 48 files / 423 tests pass (17 new); production build succeeds.

Exercise in the real app (dev server + API, with the node/tunnel responses stubbed in-page since the local database has no tested nodes): Ctrl+Shift+K opens the overlay and Ctrl+K still opens the palette — no cross-trigger; typing `tokyo` narrowed 4 → 2 with the footer reading "2 of 4 tested nodes"; ArrowDown moved to the second row and Enter sent `{"nodeId":"node:tokyo2","systemProxy":true}`, closed the dialog, left `location.pathname` at `/`, and showed "Tunnel verified — Exit 203.0.113.9 (JP) via xray"; ArrowUp from the top wrapped to the last row; Disconnect posted to `/vpn/tunnel/stop` and cleared the strip; a forced 400 kept the dialog open with the server's message; Esc closed it; the topbar button and the palette entry both open it.

Two fixes came out of that run: the search input is no longer disabled while connecting (disabling it dropped focus to `<body>`, so a failed attempt needed a mouse click before Enter worked again), and clicking a row or Disconnect no longer steals focus from the field. Ctrl+K is ignored while the overlay is open, so two dialogs can't stack.

**Limitations:** the overlay always connects in proxy mode (`systemProxy: true`) — TUN capture and nested two-hop chains still live on the VPN page. I started and then stopped my own API/web dev servers; the one already running on `:5173` was left untouched.

# 3. COORDINATION RULES FOR PARALLEL DEVELOPMENT

Concurrency must accelerate implementation without creating conflicting changes.

Establish a shared task ledger containing:

- Task ID.
- Owning agent.
- Dependencies.
- Priority.
- Current status.
- Files or components affected.
- Test requirements.
- Integration status.
- Acceptance evidence.
- Blockers.

Use a shared interface contract before implementing cross-component changes.

Examples:

- VPN configuration schema.
- Client/server protocol capabilities.
- Subscription entitlement schema.
- WHITEDNS configuration schema.
- Connection status and health API.
- Credential creation and revocation interfaces.
- Provisioning idempotency rules.
- Error and diagnostic formats.

### Repository isolation

Each agent must:

1. Inspect Git status before making changes.
2. Preserve existing user modifications.
3. Work in an isolated branch, worktree, patch, or equivalent supported workspace where practical.
4. Avoid editing files owned by another active agent without coordination.
5. Add tests for its changes.
6. Submit changes for integration review.
7. Resolve conflicts without discarding unrelated work.

The integration lead must run the combined tests after merging work from multiple agents.

If two proposed changes conflict, stop the conflicting integration and resolve the architecture before proceeding.

Do not claim concurrent execution unless agents really are running concurrently.

---

# 4. CREATE A RESEARCH-TO-PRODUCTION PIPELINE

Every documented technique and imported implementation must pass through this pipeline.

**Discover → Inspect → Verify → Prototype → Test → Compare → Review → Integrate → Deploy → Monitor.**

## Step 1 — Inventory available techniques

Extract the actual techniques discussed in the existing research files.

For each candidate record:

- Mechanism.
- Source and exact implementation location.
- License and redistribution requirements.
- Protocol and client compatibility.
- Required server changes.
- Required DNS or infrastructure support.
- Security implications.
- Expected improvement.
- Evidence quality.
- Test method.
- Current adoption status.

## Step 2 — Inspect the code

Read the relevant source code, configuration, upstream documentation, and release history.

Never adopt an undocumented third-party patch simply because it claims to bypass DPI.

Check maintenance status, dependency vulnerabilities, license compatibility, and whether the implementation is compatible with the existing application.

## Step 3 — Establish a baseline

Run the current VPN under known test conditions before changing it.

Record:

- Connection success rate.
- Establishment latency.
- Throughput.
- DNS success and failure rate.
- Reconnection behavior.
- Server and client resource consumption.
- Actual traffic forwarding.
- IPv4 and IPv6 leak-test results.
- Subscription enforcement.

## Step 4 — Implement one controlled change at a time

Introduce a candidate feature behind an explicit configuration option or feature flag where appropriate.

Do not combine several untested changes in a single production release. Make it possible to identify which modification improved or degraded behavior.

## Step 5 — Compare and decide

Use the same test environment, test destinations, client versions, and measurement process for baseline and candidate.

Record success rates and sample sizes. Repeat results to account for ordinary network variation.

Reject a candidate when it has no demonstrated benefit, introduces a security flaw, or increases failures beyond the defined acceptable limit.

## Step 6 — Integrate the winner

Only merge a technique when it has:

- Documented compatibility.
- Passing regression tests.
- A security review.
- A measured improvement or justified product benefit.
- A migration plan.
- A rollback method.
- Updated documentation.

**The goal is to deploy the most effective compatible combination—not to enable every technique indiscriminately.**

---

# 5. BUILD A MULTI-TRANSPORT, RECOVERABLE VPN

Research and implement a reliable connection architecture that can use the most appropriate supported transport for the user's environment.

Where feasible, support multiple independently verified transport options with a common configuration and entitlement model.

Investigate:

- Existing WireGuard or OpenVPN implementations.
- Xray-based options.
- Compatible VLESS transport configurations.
- AmneziaWG.
- Suitable QUIC-based transports.
- TLS-related deployment options.
- DNS-dependent connection and bootstrap improvements.
- Existing client transport capabilities.
- Other research-backed options discovered during the mission.

For every transport, define:

- Supported client versions.
- Server deployment requirements.
- Authentication and credential model.
- Configuration format.
- Connection and traffic health checks.
- Expected failure modes.
- Resource cost.
- Fallback behavior.
- Subscription and expiry enforcement.
- Security and privacy limitations.

Implement a connection manager that can choose among supported options according to verified configuration and observed health.

Provide appropriate:

- Connection timeouts.
- Backoff and retry limits.
- Reconnection behavior.
- Failure classification.
- Configuration versioning.
- Credential rotation and revocation.
- Safe fallback.
- Kill-switch or fail-closed behavior when supported by the platform and appropriate to the user's settings.
- Useful, privacy-preserving diagnostics.

Avoid retry storms and silent downgrade to an insecure transport. Never silently bypass subscription enforcement during fallback.

A failed connection must remain visibly failed. A transport must not be marked healthy until traffic can actually pass over the intended tunnel.

---

# 6. BUILD WHITEDNS INTO THE ACTUAL PRODUCT

WHITEDNS must be integrated with the actual VPN client, server configuration, and subscription system.

Use the existing research documents to identify the capabilities that can be implemented and proven.

Test:

- Resolver bootstrap.
- DNS resolution and response validation.
- Resolver selection and fallback.
- Behavior during network changes.
- DNS leaks when the VPN connects or disconnects.
- IPv4 and IPv6 resolution.
- Timeout and packet-loss recovery.
- Configuration integrity.
- Cache consistency.
- Correct handling of inconsistent or suspicious responses.
- Access-control and subscription integration.
- Actual client behavior over the VPN tunnel.

Do not implement arbitrary DNS overrides without validation. Do not make a resolver answer authoritative merely because it happens to produce a result that works.

If research suggests a genuinely new WHITEDNS method, implement it as an isolated candidate, document the hypothesis, compare it to the baseline, and merge it only after measurable improvement and security review.

WHITEDNS and the VPN must be tested together, not just in separate unit tests.

---

# 7. ADVERSARIAL TESTING OF THE FULL APPLICATION

Test the combined system as though you are trying to find every practical way that it can fail.

Use owned infrastructure, authorized VPS systems, controlled network emulation, staging, test accounts, and permitted endpoints.

### Network and DPI-resilience tests

Simulate relevant conditions such as:

- DNS failures.
- Inconsistent DNS responses.
- TCP resets.
- Connection timeouts.
- Packet loss.
- High latency.
- UDP or QUIC unavailability.
- Restricted ports.
- TLS negotiation failure.
- Server restart.
- VPN interruption.
- Temporary resolver or API outage.
- Configuration mismatch.
- Expired credentials.

Use authorized test networks and published measurements to validate hypotheses about real Iranian networks. Do not claim that lab simulation proves operation on all Iranian ISPs.

### Security tests

Test:

- Invalid or revoked VPN credentials.
- Expired subscriptions.
- Unauthorized access to another user's configurations.
- Invalid input and malformed configurations.
- API authentication and authorization.
- Rate limiting.
- Duplicate billing events.
- Forged or replayed provider notifications.
- Incomplete provisioning.
- DNS and routing leaks.
- Sensitive information in logs.
- Dependency vulnerabilities.
- Secrets accidentally included in client distributions.

### Controlled load tests

Gradually increase load against the configured staging systems and authorized test services.

Before each test, define traffic, duration, concurrency, resource thresholds, and automatic stop conditions.

Stop if CPU, memory, database connections, latency, or error rates reach predetermined limits or the system begins affecting unrelated workloads.

Do not run unbounded stress tests against production or third-party infrastructure.

---

# 8. END-TO-END PRODUCT INTEGRATION

The agents must coordinate to deliver one working product, not a collection of disconnected components.

The following user journey must work:

1. A user opens NetPulse.
2. The user registers or logs in.
3. The user selects a subscription.
4. The user initiates a purchase.
5. The backend verifies the actual payment result.
6. The accounting system records the correct transaction.
7. The subscription becomes active exactly once.
8. The server provisions the appropriate VPN access.
9. WHITEDNS entitlements and client configuration are assigned where included.
10. The client receives a valid configuration.
11. The client establishes a real VPN tunnel.
12. External test traffic passes through the tunnel.
13. DNS behaves as configured.
14. Usage, connection status, and subscription state stay consistent.
15. Renewal extends the correct entitlement.
16. Expiration or revocation removes access.
17. Failure recovery does not double-charge users or lose verified payments.

Use the payment provider's sandbox for automated purchase tests. Do not invent payment confirmations or use real customer charges to debug the system.

Ensure Telegram bot state, backend state, database state, billing state, VPN access, and WHITEDNS access all reconcile.

---

# 9. UI AND CONNECTION EXPERIENCE

Improve the actual app interface while preserving existing functionality.

Make VPN state accurate and understandable:

- Disconnected.
- Connecting.
- Connected and verified.
- Reconnecting.
- Degraded.
- Failed.
- Subscription expired.
- Access revoked.

The application must not report a successful connection without evidence from the real data path.

Add useful diagnostics for DNS failures, transport errors, invalid configurations, expired entitlements, and unavailable servers.

Keep sensitive tokens and subscription links protected.

Improve the onboarding and purchase flow, loading states, error recovery, server selection, subscription management, accessibility, responsiveness, and appropriate Persian RTL presentation.

Every major UI improvement must be backed by the relevant frontend or end-to-end tests.

---

# 10. CONTROLLED STAGING AND PRODUCTION DEPLOYMENT

Deployment is part of this mission, but an untested modification must not be pushed directly into production simply because an agent considers it finished.

The infrastructure agent and integration lead must coordinate.

For each release:

1. Confirm the target repository, service, and deployment environment.
2. Inspect current Git status and preserve existing user changes.
3. Build the application and required server components.
4. Run unit tests, integration tests, and relevant security checks.
5. Run the staging smoke tests.
6. Verify required backups and rollback procedures.
7. Deploy the validated change.
8. Verify the deployed revision and configuration.
9. Check service health and sanitized logs.
10. Perform end-to-end connectivity and regression tests.
11. Roll back if the deployment creates an unacceptable regression.

Do not share production credentials among research agents unnecessarily. Only the authorized deployment agent should perform coordinated production changes through the approved credential source.

Do not print secrets or private VPN configuration in logs.

If required access is unavailable, continue all independent tasks and report the exact blocker. Never fabricate a successful deployment.

---

# 11. PROVE THAT THE VPN REALLY WORKS

The final verification must use a real supported client and the actual deployed VPN server.

The test must establish all of the following:

- The client accepts a valid configuration.
- The connection is genuinely established.
- Encrypted tunnel traffic passes to external destinations.
- The observed public egress IP matches the intended VPN path.
- DNS behavior is checked under the intended configuration.
- IPv4 and IPv6 leakage are investigated.
- Traffic counters change consistently.
- Disconnect and reconnect work.
- The client can recover from a temporary network interruption.
- Revoked credentials no longer grant access.
- An expired subscription loses the expected entitlements.
- Invalid configurations fail clearly and safely.
- The application reports accurate connection state.
- WHITEDNS works through the intended end-to-end path.

Capture sanitized logs, measurements, commands, and results.

If testing is performed only from a VPS or laboratory, state that clearly. Do not claim successful bypass on a particular Iranian provider unless it has actually been tested from that network.

---

# 12. CONTINUOUS MISSION AND SELF-IMPROVEMENT

Keep this mission active through Hermes' supported persistent execution, scheduling, or resumption facilities.

At each cycle:

1. Read the latest research documents.
2. Review previous experimental findings.
3. Refresh the task ledger.
4. Check for relevant upstream changes and security updates.
5. Select the highest-priority unfinished item.
6. Execute, test, and document the change.
7. Integrate completed work.
8. Deploy only through the approved release process.
9. Verify the actual result.
10. Continue to the next item.

Update the living research documents whenever an experiment produces a meaningful finding. Research documentation must evolve from the implementation and measurements instead of remaining disconnected from code.

When a candidate technique fails, document the reason so future agents do not waste time repeating the same approach.

After all acceptance criteria pass, switch to maintenance mode with bounded health checks, regression testing, dependency review, and performance monitoring.

Never create unlimited retry loops, unbounded background jobs, or uncontrolled resource consumption. If a session or process terminates, resume through the supported execution mechanism rather than claiming to operate after shutdown.

---

# 13. FINAL ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

The mission is not complete merely because the agents have written code or generated research documents.

The integration lead must collect evidence that:

- The research documents have been read and applied.
- The source and license requirements have been reviewed.
- The selected techniques are implemented in the real NetPulse codebase.
- Relevant tests pass.
- The VPN connects through a real supported client.
- Traffic passes through the intended tunnel.
- DNS behavior and leakage have been evaluated.
- WHITEDNS is integrated and verified.
- Subscription and accounting flows work end to end.
- UI connection status reflects real behavior.
- Security and resilience tests have been performed.
- Production deployment is verified where access permits.
- Rollback instructions exist.
- Known limitations and unverified network conditions are documented.

Use four statuses for every major requirement:

- `PASS` — verified with reproducible evidence.
- `FAIL` — tested and unsuccessful.
- `BLOCKED` — an exact external dependency or permission is missing.
- `NOT TESTED` — no valid evidence exists.

Do not mark blocked or untested items as passed.

The final report must summarize the actual changes, tests, measured results, deployment version, remaining risks, and next engineering priorities.

---

# START IMMEDIATELY

Do not return only a plan.

First, discover the actual projects and existing DPI research documentation. Then start the specialist workstreams, assign independent tasks, establish shared interfaces, and begin implementing the highest-priority improvements in parallel.

The lead agent must continuously integrate the results, resolve conflicts, build the application, run the end-to-end tests, and deploy verified changes through the approved process.

**Build a genuinely better VPN—not just a VPN with more configuration options. The benchmark is reliable, secure, measurable, maintainable connectivity under difficult network conditions, with an application users can trust.**

import { z } from 'zod';

import type { FastifyInstance } from 'fastify';

import type { AppContext } from './context';

const TunnelTestRequestSchema = z.object({
  zone: z.string().trim().min(1).max(253).optional(),
  server: z.string().trim().min(1).max(64).optional(),
  pubkey: z.string().trim().min(1).max(160).optional(),
  url: z.string().url().optional(),
  timeoutMs: z.coerce.number().int().min(1000).max(120_000).optional(),
});

export function registerWhitednsRoutes(app: FastifyInstance, ctx: AppContext): void {
  // Current WhiteDNS tunnel configuration (secrets are never returned).
  app.get('/api/v1/whitedns/config', async () => {
    return ctx.services.whitedns.config();
  });

  // Run the WhiteDNS Soar tunnel diagnostic. Falls back to the configured
  // zone/server/pubkey when the request omits them.
  app.post(
    '/api/v1/whitedns/tunnel-test',
    { config: { rateLimit: { max: 6, timeWindow: '1 minute' } } },
    async (req) => {
      const parsed = TunnelTestRequestSchema.safeParse(req.body ?? {});
      if (!parsed.success) throw parsed.error;
      const configured = ctx.services.whitedns.config();
      const zone = parsed.data.zone ?? configured.zone;
      const server = parsed.data.server ?? configured.server;
      if (!zone || !server) {
        return {
          ok: false,
          stage: 'error',
          stages: [],
          checkedAt: Date.now(),
          tookMs: 0,
          error: 'WhiteDNS zone and server are not configured',
        };
      }
      return ctx.services.whitedns.test({
        zone: zone!,
        server: server!,
        pubkey: parsed.data.pubkey ?? undefined,
        url: parsed.data.url ?? 'https://example.com/',
        timeoutMs: parsed.data.timeoutMs ?? 60_000,
      });
    },
  );
}

Progress note:
A keyboard-driven quick-connect overlay is live: **Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+K** opens it, arrows move, Enter connects to the highlighted node, Esc closes — and the page you were on never changes.

**How it behaves**

- Lists only what the backend would accept: the same tested-healthy candidate query the Proxy Tunnel card uses (`sortField=proxyLatency`, `maxLatency=5000`), so a node without a recent successful proxy test never appears as pickable.

/**

 * Two structural decisions own this file:
 *
 *  1. The rail is the navigation. Engines are grouped by HOW they reach the
 *     internet (circumvention binary / public-node cores / native clients)
 *     instead of being one flat strip of eight identical tabs, and each rail
 *     item carries the live state of its own engine. Opening an engine is
 *     therefore possible from anywhere on the page, not only from the Overview.
 *  2. The system bar is the only cross-engine surface. "What is up right now"
 *     and "what is blocking" exist in exactly one place, so no engine surface
 *     has to repeat it and none of them can disagree with each other.
 */

interface RailItem {
  id: VpnSurfaceId;
  label: string;
  icon: LucideIcon;
  glyph: string;
  dot: { tone: 'ok' | 'warn' | 'danger' | 'idle'; pulse?: boolean };
  state: string;
}

interface RailGroup {
  heading: string;
  items: RailItem[];
}

/** Everything the rail and the system bar need, resolved once. */
function useVpnShellState() {
  const statusQuery = useVpnStatus();
  const killSwitchQuery = useKillSwitch();
  const enginesQuery = useProxyEngines();
  const providersQuery = useVpnProviders();
  const aetherQuery = useAetherEngine();
  const tunnelQuery = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['tunnel', 'status'],
    queryFn: () => api.get<{ tunnel: ProxyTunnelStatus }>('/vpn/tunnel/status'),
    refetchInterval: 5_000,
  });

  return {
    statusQuery,
    status: statusQuery.data,
    killSwitch: killSwitchQuery.data?.killSwitch,
    engines: enginesQuery.data?.engines ?? [],
    preferred: enginesQuery.data?.preferred ?? 'auto',
    effective: enginesQuery.data?.effective ?? null,
    providers: providersQuery.data?.providers ?? [],
    aether: aetherQuery.data,
    tunnel: tunnelQuery.data?.tunnel,
  };
}

/** The cross-engine bar: one bordered strip, hairline-separated segments. */
function SystemBar({
  status,
  tunnel,
  killSwitchBlocking,
  blockingReason,
}: {
  status: VpnStatus | undefined;
  tunnel: ProxyTunnelStatus | undefined;
  killSwitchBlocking: boolean;
  blockingReason: string | null | undefined;
}) {
  const connected = status?.connected === true;
  const tunnelActive = tunnel?.state === 'active';
  const provider = status?.providerId ? (PROVIDER_LABEL[status.providerId] ?? status.providerId) : null;

  const tone = killSwitchBlocking ? 'danger' : connected || tunnelActive ? 'ok' : 'idle';
  const headline = killSwitchBlocking
    ? 'Kill switch engaged — traffic is blocked'
    : connected
      ? `Tunnel up via ${provider ?? 'a provider'}`
      : tunnelActive
        ? 'Proxy tunnel active'
        : 'No tunnel is up';

  const segments: Array<{ label: string; value: ReactNode; tone?: 'ok' | 'warn' | 'danger' }> = [];

  if (connected) {
    segments.push({ label: 'Profile', value: status?.serverName ?? '—' });
    segments.push({ label: 'Protocol', value: status?.protocol ?? '—' });
    if (status?.verifiedPublicIp) segments.push({ label: 'Exit', value: <span className="metric-num">{status.verifiedPublicIp}</span>, tone: 'ok' });
    if (status?.since != null) segments.push({ label: 'Up since', value: new Date(status.since).toLocaleTimeString() });
    if (status?.verification === 'failed') segments.push({ label: 'Routing', value: 'not through the tunnel', tone: 'danger' });
  }

  if (tunnelActive) {
    segments.push({ label: 'Node', value: tunnel?.nodeName ?? tunnel?.nodeId ?? '—' });
    segments.push({ label: 'Exit', value: <span className="metric-num">{tunnel?.exitIp ?? 'unverified'}</span> });
    if (tunnel?.engine) segments.push({ label: 'Core', value: tunnel.engine });
    if (tunnel?.chain) {
      segments.push({
        label: 'Chain',
        value: tunnel.chain.exitDiffers ? 'nested · exit differs' : 'nested · exit identical',
        tone: tunnel.chain.exitDiffers ? 'ok' : 'warn',
      });
    }
  }

  if (!connected && !tunnelActive) {
    segments.push({ label: 'Mode', value: 'nothing is carrying traffic' });
  }

  return (
    <div className="mb-5 flex flex-wrap items-center gap-x-6 gap-y-2 rounded-xl border border-line bg-surface px-4 py-3">
      <span className="flex items-center gap-2.5">
        <StatusDot tone={tone} pulse={tunnel?.state === 'starting' || tunnel?.state === 'stopping'} />
        <span className="text-sm text-text">{headline}</span>
      </span>

# PROJECT OVERDRIVE: NETPULSE SUPER VPN
## Persistent Multi-Agent Research, Engineering, Integration & Deployment Mission

**Mission ID:** `NETPULSE_OVERDRIVE_PARALLEL`

**Mission priority:** Highest engineering priority.

**Role:** Operate as a principal VPN architect, censorship-resistance research team, network protocol engineering team, security laboratory, application development team, and production reliability team working together.

**Final objective:** Transform the existing NetPulse application into a highly reliable, secure, censorship-resistant VPN product, using the living research documentation, verified techniques from relevant open-source projects, the actual NetPulse codebase, WHITEDNS, the existing VPS infrastructure, and rigorous real-world connectivity testing.

**Operating model:** Concurrent workstreams coordinated by one lead agent. Persistent progress through supported Hermes continuation mechanisms. Evidence-driven implementation. Continuous integration and regression testing. Staged deployment and verified recovery.

**Do not merely research. Do not merely write plans. BUILD THE PRODUCT.**

**Every relevant research finding must become one of three things:**

1. A tested implementation improvement.

3. A documented reason not to adopt the technique.

Do not allow research to accumulate indefinitely without engineering progress.
