# 2. RUN CONCURRENT SPECIALIST AGENTS

Use actual supported Hermes subagents or independent execution contexts to make progress in parallel. If the installed runtime does not support parallel agents, implement the same workstreams using its supported execution model and be honest about the limitation.

The lead agent owns architecture, integration, prioritization, task allocation, and final acceptance. Specialist agents must not independently overwrite shared production configuration or deploy conflicting changes.

## Agent A — Chief Architect and Integration Lead

Responsibilities:

- Map the complete NetPulse ecosystem.
- Read the evolving DPI research documents.
- Maintain the technical architecture and task ledger.
- Assign work to specialist agents.
- Establish interfaces between the client, API, VPN server, DNS system, Telegram bot, and subscriptions.
- Resolve conflicts and dependencies.
- Review every proposed implementation before integration.
- Keep the project in a buildable state.
- Coordinate releases and rollback.
- Verify actual end-to-end functionality.

This agent must continuously look for integration defects between components that work independently but fail when combined.

## Agent B — DPI and Censorship-Resistance Research Engineer

Responsibilities:

- Maintain and update the Iran-specific censorship threat model.
- Read papers, repositories, protocol specifications, issues, commits, and implementation examples.
- Investigate SNI, TLS metadata, ECH support, client fingerprints, DNS interference, transport classification, and protocol compatibility.
- Evaluate techniques from PattNG and comparable projects.
- Design reproducible experiments and test competing hypotheses.
- Identify limitations of existing NetPulse transport configurations.
- Propose, implement, and measure improvements.

Do not treat an Internet hostname as a magic solution. Every proposed SNI, TLS, transport, or DNS method must be compatible with the real client and server configuration and supported by evidence.

## Agent C — VPN Protocol and Server Engineer

Responsibilities:

- Inspect the actual VPN server and client architecture.
- Audit existing protocol configuration and provisioning.
- Evaluate established, maintained transport implementations against the threat model.
- Implement and configure the best-supported candidates.
- Integrate connection setup, authentication, routing, traffic forwarding, reconnection, and credential revocation.
- Test deployment, performance, reliability, and resource consumption.
- Ensure every server-side change is compatible with the actual shipped client.

Investigate WireGuard, OpenVPN, Xray-based transports, supported VLESS transports, AmneziaWG, QUIC-based transports, and other appropriate candidates. Adopt only those that make sense for the actual product.

Do not install every protocol simply to maximize feature count.

## Agent D — WHITEDNS and DNS Reliability Engineer

Responsibilities:

- Find the actual WHITEDNS repository and understand its existing behavior.
- Read the live DNS research documents and experimental findings.
- Evaluate resolver selection, DNS censorship behavior, bootstrap failures, inconsistent answers, encrypted DNS, fallback behavior, and leak prevention.
- Design and implement the appropriate DNS architecture.
- Integrate DNS settings into VPN configurations.
- Test DNS behavior both independently and over a real VPN connection.
- Make DNS policy, access, and subscription entitlement consistent.

WHITEDNS must become a tested system component, not a disconnected proof of concept.

Do not assume that DNS circumvention automatically defeats IP filtering or that encrypted DNS hides all connection metadata.

## Agent E — NetPulse Client and UI Engineer

Responsibilities:

- Find the actual frontend and supported client applications.
- Integrate the selected VPN capabilities into the real user interface.
- Improve onboarding, server selection, connection state, diagnostics, configuration delivery, and subscription screens.
- Make connection state reflect actual data-plane functionality.
- Integrate WHITEDNS configuration and status.
- Preserve supported platform behavior.
- Improve accessibility, error handling, responsiveness, and Persian right-to-left layout where applicable.
- Add tests for critical flows.

The UI must not display “Connected” simply because a socket has opened or the backend returned success. Require real evidence of a working tunnel.

## Agent F — Telegram, Accounting, and Subscription Engineer

Responsibilities:

- Inspect the Telegram bot, API, database, billing logic, and entitlement system.
- Verify purchase, payment confirmation, provisioning, renewal, expiration, cancellation, and refunds where supported.
- Establish one authoritative source of truth for payment and subscription state.
- Prevent duplicate webhook processing, duplicate provisioning, and entitlement inconsistencies.
- Integrate VPN and WHITEDNS access with the actual subscription.
- Test that inactive, expired, revoked, or unpaid subscriptions cannot use protected resources.

Use sandbox payments and test accounts for test automation. Do not charge real users to debug a payment flow.

## Agent G — Security, QA, and Adversarial Test Engineer

Responsibilities:

- Audit authentication, authorization, secret handling, transport security, dependency vulnerabilities, routing, DNS leaks, and configuration distribution.
- Design adversarial tests against the actual application.
- Build regression and integration tests.
- Simulate network disruption and service failures within controlled environments.
- Perform bounded load and resilience tests.
- Investigate discrepancies between application status and actual network behavior.
- Verify access revocation and recovery from failure.
- Produce reproducible evidence.

Test aggressively within the authorized environment, but stop when predefined resource or service-health limits are reached.

## Agent H — Build, Deployment, and Infrastructure Engineer

Responsibilities:

- Establish the real VPS and deployment architecture.
- Check service configuration, logs, firewall rules, DNS, certificates, databases, and deployment versions.
- Prepare isolated staging infrastructure where available.
- Automate repeatable builds, deployments, health checks, and smoke tests.
- Maintain backups and rollback procedures.
- Verify that a deployment actually activated the intended version.
- Detect regressions after release.
- Keep production and staging configuration separated.

Use only authorized access paths and existing credential sources. Never expose SSH keys, tokens, API keys, VPN private keys, or passwords in reports or source code.

---

# 3. COORDINATION RULES FOR PARALLEL DEVELOPMENT

Concurrency must accelerate implementation without creating conflicting changes.

Establish a shared task ledger containing:

- Task ID.
- Owning agent.
- Dependencies.
- Priority.
- Current status.
- Files or components affected.
- Test requirements.
- Integration status.
- Acceptance evidence.
- Blockers.

Use a shared interface contract before implementing cross-component changes.

Examples:

- VPN configuration schema.
- Client/server protocol capabilities.
- Subscription entitlement schema.
- WHITEDNS configuration schema.
- Connection status and health API.
- Credential creation and revocation interfaces.
- Provisioning idempotency rules.
- Error and diagnostic formats.

### Repository isolation

Each agent must:

1. Inspect Git status before making changes.
2. Preserve existing user modifications.
3. Work in an isolated branch, worktree, patch, or equivalent supported workspace where practical.
4. Avoid editing files owned by another active agent without coordination.
5. Add tests for its changes.
6. Submit changes for integration review.
7. Resolve conflicts without discarding unrelated work.

The integration lead must run the combined tests after merging work from multiple agents.

If two proposed changes conflict, stop the conflicting integration and resolve the architecture before proceeding.

Do not claim concurrent execution unless agents really are running concurrently.

---

# 4. CREATE A RESEARCH-TO-PRODUCTION PIPELINE

Every documented technique and imported implementation must pass through this pipeline.

**Discover → Inspect → Verify → Prototype → Test → Compare → Review → Integrate → Deploy → Monitor.**

## Step 1 — Inventory available techniques

Extract the actual techniques discussed in the existing research files.

For each candidate record:

- Mechanism.
- Source and exact implementation location.
- License and redistribution requirements.
- Protocol and client compatibility.
- Required server changes.
- Required DNS or infrastructure support.
- Security implications.
- Expected improvement.
- Evidence quality.
- Test method.
- Current adoption status.

## Step 2 — Inspect the code

Read the relevant source code, configuration, upstream documentation, and release history.

Never adopt an undocumented third-party patch simply because it claims to bypass DPI.

Check maintenance status, dependency vulnerabilities, license compatibility, and whether the implementation is compatible with the existing application.

## Step 3 — Establish a baseline

Run the current VPN under known test conditions before changing it.

Record:

- Connection success rate.
- Establishment latency.
- Throughput.
- DNS success and failure rate.
- Reconnection behavior.
- Server and client resource consumption.
- Actual traffic forwarding.
- IPv4 and IPv6 leak-test results.
- Subscription enforcement.

## Step 4 — Implement one controlled change at a time

Introduce a candidate feature behind an explicit configuration option or feature flag where appropriate.

Do not combine several untested changes in a single production release. Make it possible to identify which modification improved or degraded behavior.

## Step 5 — Compare and decide

Use the same test environment, test destinations, client versions, and measurement process for baseline and candidate.

Record success rates and sample sizes. Repeat results to account for ordinary network variation.

Reject a candidate when it has no demonstrated benefit, introduces a security flaw, or increases failures beyond the defined acceptable limit.

## Step 6 — Integrate the winner

Only merge a technique when it has:

- Documented compatibility.
- Passing regression tests.
- A security review.
- A measured improvement or justified product benefit.
- A migration plan.
- A rollback method.
- Updated documentation.

**The goal is to deploy the most effective compatible combination—not to enable every technique indiscriminately.**

---

# 5. BUILD A MULTI-TRANSPORT, RECOVERABLE VPN

Research and implement a reliable connection architecture that can use the most appropriate supported transport for the user's environment.

Where feasible, support multiple independently verified transport options with a common configuration and entitlement model.

Investigate:

- Existing WireGuard or OpenVPN implementations.
- Xray-based options.
- Compatible VLESS transport configurations.
- AmneziaWG.
- Suitable QUIC-based transports.
- TLS-related deployment options.
- DNS-dependent connection and bootstrap improvements.
- Existing client transport capabilities.
- Other research-backed options discovered during the mission.

For every transport, define:

- Supported client versions.
- Server deployment requirements.
- Authentication and credential model.
- Configuration format.
- Connection and traffic health checks.
- Expected failure modes.
- Resource cost.
- Fallback behavior.
- Subscription and expiry enforcement.
- Security and privacy limitations.

Implement a connection manager that can choose among supported options according to verified configuration and observed health.

Provide appropriate:

- Connection timeouts.
- Backoff and retry limits.
- Reconnection behavior.
- Failure classification.
- Configuration versioning.
- Credential rotation and revocation.
- Safe fallback.
- Kill-switch or fail-closed behavior when supported by the platform and appropriate to the user's settings.
- Useful, privacy-preserving diagnostics.

Avoid retry storms and silent downgrade to an insecure transport. Never silently bypass subscription enforcement during fallback.

A failed connection must remain visibly failed. A transport must not be marked healthy until traffic can actually pass over the intended tunnel.

---

# 6. BUILD WHITEDNS INTO THE ACTUAL PRODUCT

WHITEDNS must be integrated with the actual VPN client, server configuration, and subscription system.

Use the existing research documents to identify the capabilities that can be implemented and proven.

Test:

- Resolver bootstrap.
- DNS resolution and response validation.
- Resolver selection and fallback.
- Behavior during network changes.
- DNS leaks when the VPN connects or disconnects.
- IPv4 and IPv6 resolution.
- Timeout and packet-loss recovery.
- Configuration integrity.
- Cache consistency.
- Correct handling of inconsistent or suspicious responses.
- Access-control and subscription integration.
- Actual client behavior over the VPN tunnel.

Do not implement arbitrary DNS overrides without validation. Do not make a resolver answer authoritative merely because it happens to produce a result that works.

If research suggests a genuinely new WHITEDNS method, implement it as an isolated candidate, document the hypothesis, compare it to the baseline, and merge it only after measurable improvement and security review.

WHITEDNS and the VPN must be tested together, not just in separate unit tests.

---

# 7. ADVERSARIAL TESTING OF THE FULL APPLICATION

Test the combined system as though you are trying to find every practical way that it can fail.

Use owned infrastructure, authorized VPS systems, controlled network emulation, staging, test accounts, and permitted endpoints.

### Network and DPI-resilience tests

Simulate relevant conditions such as:

- DNS failures.
- Inconsistent DNS responses.
- TCP resets.
- Connection timeouts.
- Packet loss.
- High latency.
- UDP or QUIC unavailability.
- Restricted ports.
- TLS negotiation failure.
- Server restart.
- VPN interruption.
- Temporary resolver or API outage.
- Configuration mismatch.
- Expired credentials.

Use authorized test networks and published measurements to validate hypotheses about real Iranian networks. Do not claim that lab simulation proves operation on all Iranian ISPs.

### Security tests

Test:

- Invalid or revoked VPN credentials.
- Expired subscriptions.
- Unauthorized access to another user's configurations.
- Invalid input and malformed configurations.
- API authentication and authorization.
- Rate limiting.
- Duplicate billing events.
- Forged or replayed provider notifications.
- Incomplete provisioning.
- DNS and routing leaks.
- Sensitive information in logs.
- Dependency vulnerabilities.
- Secrets accidentally included in client distributions.

### Controlled load tests

Gradually increase load against the configured staging systems and authorized test services.

Before each test, define traffic, duration, concurrency, resource thresholds, and automatic stop conditions.

Stop if CPU, memory, database connections, latency, or error rates reach predetermined limits or the system begins affecting unrelated workloads.

Do not run unbounded stress tests against production or third-party infrastructure.

---

# 8. END-TO-END PRODUCT INTEGRATION

The agents must coordinate to deliver one working product, not a collection of disconnected components.

The following user journey must work:

1. A user opens NetPulse.
2. The user registers or logs in.
3. The user selects a subscription.
4. The user initiates a purchase.
5. The backend verifies the actual payment result.
6. The accounting system records the correct transaction.
7. The subscription becomes active exactly once.
8. The server provisions the appropriate VPN access.
9. WHITEDNS entitlements and client configuration are assigned where included.
10. The client receives a valid configuration.
11. The client establishes a real VPN tunnel.
12. External test traffic passes through the tunnel.
13. DNS behaves as configured.
14. Usage, connection status, and subscription state stay consistent.
15. Renewal extends the correct entitlement.
16. Expiration or revocation removes access.
17. Failure recovery does not double-charge users or lose verified payments.

Use the payment provider's sandbox for automated purchase tests. Do not invent payment confirmations or use real customer charges to debug the system.

Ensure Telegram bot state, backend state, database state, billing state, VPN access, and WHITEDNS access all reconcile.

---

# 9. UI AND CONNECTION EXPERIENCE

Improve the actual app interface while preserving existing functionality.

Make VPN state accurate and understandable:

- Disconnected.
- Connecting.
- Connected and verified.
- Reconnecting.
- Degraded.
- Failed.
- Subscription expired.
- Access revoked.

The application must not report a successful connection without evidence from the real data path.

Add useful diagnostics for DNS failures, transport errors, invalid configurations, expired entitlements, and unavailable servers.

Keep sensitive tokens and subscription links protected.

Improve the onboarding and purchase flow, loading states, error recovery, server selection, subscription management, accessibility, responsiveness, and appropriate Persian RTL presentation.

Every major UI improvement must be backed by the relevant frontend or end-to-end tests.

---

# 10. CONTROLLED STAGING AND PRODUCTION DEPLOYMENT

Deployment is part of this mission, but an untested modification must not be pushed directly into production simply because an agent considers it finished.

The infrastructure agent and integration lead must coordinate.

For each release:

1. Confirm the target repository, service, and deployment environment.
2. Inspect current Git status and preserve existing user changes.
3. Build the application and required server components.
4. Run unit tests, integration tests, and relevant security checks.
5. Run the staging smoke tests.
6. Verify required backups and rollback procedures.
7. Deploy the validated change.
8. Verify the deployed revision and configuration.
9. Check service health and sanitized logs.
10. Perform end-to-end connectivity and regression tests.
11. Roll back if the deployment creates an unacceptable regression.

Do not share production credentials among research agents unnecessarily. Only the authorized deployment agent should perform coordinated production changes through the approved credential source.

Do not print secrets or private VPN configuration in logs.

If required access is unavailable, continue all independent tasks and report the exact blocker. Never fabricate a successful deployment.

---

# 11. PROVE THAT THE VPN REALLY WORKS

The final verification must use a real supported client and the actual deployed VPN server.

The test must establish all of the following:

- The client accepts a valid configuration.
- The connection is genuinely established.
- Encrypted tunnel traffic passes to external destinations.
- The observed public egress IP matches the intended VPN path.
- DNS behavior is checked under the intended configuration.
- IPv4 and IPv6 leakage are investigated.
- Traffic counters change consistently.
- Disconnect and reconnect work.
- The client can recover from a temporary network interruption.
- Revoked credentials no longer grant access.
- An expired subscription loses the expected entitlements.
- Invalid configurations fail clearly and safely.
- The application reports accurate connection state.
- WHITEDNS works through the intended end-to-end path.

Capture sanitized logs, measurements, commands, and results.

If testing is performed only from a VPS or laboratory, state that clearly. Do not claim successful bypass on a particular Iranian provider unless it has actually been tested from that network.

---

# 12. CONTINUOUS MISSION AND SELF-IMPROVEMENT

Keep this mission active through Hermes' supported persistent execution, scheduling, or resumption facilities.

At each cycle:

1. Read the latest research documents.
2. Review previous experimental findings.
3. Refresh the task ledger.
4. Check for relevant upstream changes and security updates.
5. Select the highest-priority unfinished item.
6. Execute, test, and document the change.
7. Integrate completed work.
8. Deploy only through the approved release process.
9. Verify the actual result.
10. Continue to the next item.

Update the living research documents whenever an experiment produces a meaningful finding. Research documentation must evolve from the implementation and measurements instead of remaining disconnected from code.

When a candidate technique fails, document the reason so future agents do not waste time repeating the same approach.

After all acceptance criteria pass, switch to maintenance mode with bounded health checks, regression testing, dependency review, and performance monitoring.

Never create unlimited retry loops, unbounded background jobs, or uncontrolled resource consumption. If a session or process terminates, resume through the supported execution mechanism rather than claiming to operate after shutdown.

---

# 13. FINAL ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA

The mission is not complete merely because the agents have written code or generated research documents.

The integration lead must collect evidence that:

- The research documents have been read and applied.
- The source and license requirements have been reviewed.
- The selected techniques are implemented in the real NetPulse codebase.
- Relevant tests pass.
- The VPN connects through a real supported client.
- Traffic passes through the intended tunnel.
- DNS behavior and leakage have been evaluated.
- WHITEDNS is integrated and verified.
- Subscription and accounting flows work end to end.
- UI connection status reflects real behavior.
- Security and resilience tests have been performed.
- Production deployment is verified where access permits.
- Rollback instructions exist.
- Known limitations and unverified network conditions are documented.

Use four statuses for every major requirement:

- `PASS` — verified with reproducible evidence.
- `FAIL` — tested and unsuccessful.
- `BLOCKED` — an exact external dependency or permission is missing.
- `NOT TESTED` — no valid evidence exists.

Do not mark blocked or untested items as passed.

The final report must summarize the actual changes, tests, measured results, deployment version, remaining risks, and next engineering priorities.

---

# START IMMEDIATELY

Do not return only a plan.

First, discover the actual projects and existing DPI research documentation. Then start the specialist workstreams, assign independent tasks, establish shared interfaces, and begin implementing the highest-priority improvements in parallel.

The lead agent must continuously integrate the results, resolve conflicts, build the application, run the end-to-end tests, and deploy verified changes through the approved process.

**Build a genuinely better VPN—not just a VPN with more configuration options. The benchmark is reliable, secure, measurable, maintainable connectivity under difficult network conditions, with an application users can trust.**

rotated config is the host rewriting its server configs from the published set.
`cloud/worker/README.md` claims:

> expiry/revocation/refund → the identity disappears from the config on the next
> pass (≤ 1 min) and the next handshake is refused, even if the config was
> already copied elsewhere

Half of that is trivially true (the Worker stops listing the secret). The half
that matters was untested: does the reconciler *replace* the client lists, or
would a rotated identity linger in the server config?

## 2. Method

`scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-removal.py` (new, in-repo) runs the real
reconciler, unmodified, in its `--print` mode ("show what would be applied,
touch nothing") against a sandbox:

Done. The one command is `npm run e2e:navigation`, backed by [verify-navigation-webview.mjs](scripts/verify-navigation-webview.mjs).

**What it does**, in order, with one PASS/FAIL line per step: checks `cargo` and `tauri-driver`, resolves a native driver (on Windows it reads the installed WebView2 runtime's version and downloads that exact `msedgedriver` into `node_modules/.cache/netpulse/` when none is on `PATH`; Linux uses `WebKitWebDriver`; macOS fails with a clear message because tauri-driver can't drive a macOS webview), serves the dev origin, runs `cargo build`, then runs the `#[ignore]`d test with `MSEDGEDRIVER`/`NAV_WEBVIEW_APP` set, and exits non-zero on the first failure.

It encodes the three traps that made this test look broken when run by hand — and that I hit myself earlier in this thread:

- the driver must match the **runtime**, not the installed Edge browser (a mismatch fails every session with "only supports Microsoft Edge version N");
- a debug binary resolves its window to `build.devUrl`, not to the compiled `frontendDist`, so something has to serve `http://localhost:5173`;
- vite's default `localhost` can bind the **IPv6 loopback only**, in which case the webview sits on `chrome-error://chromewebdata/` while WebDriver still reports the app URL. The script binds `127.0.0.1` explicitly, with `--strictPort` so a taken port fails loudly instead of silently moving to 5174.

**Verified**, by running it four ways:

| Run | Result |
|---|---|
| `npm run e2e:navigation`, nothing on 5173 | exit 0 — driver downloaded and cached, server started, `cargo build`, test `1 passed ... finished in 6.85s`, server stopped |
| with my own dev server already on 5173 | exit 0, `PASS dev origin already served — http://127.0.0.1:5173 (left running)`, and HTTP 200 afterwards — it never kills a server it did not start |
| `--no-build` | exit 0 (skips the build, still checks the binary exists) |
| `--app <missing>` | exit 1 with `FAIL app binary` |

After each run the port is free and no `node`/app/driver process is left behind; `Ctrl-C` stops only its own server. Flags: `--no-build`, `--keep-server`, `--driver`, `--app`, `--port`. It's registered in [package.json](package.json) next to the other `e2e:*` scripts, and CI is untouched — the `webview-navigation` job still does its own equivalent steps with `msedgedriver-tool`.

**One honest wart.** Passing a copied env object to `spawnSync` for the test step made rustup's `cargo` shim fail on this machine ("could not choose a version of cargo to run ... no default is configured") even though the copy carried `RUSTUP_HOME` and `CARGO_HOME` — I checked that directly. The same command with the inherited env runs, so the script sets the two variables on `process.env` instead and does not pass an env object. That is a workaround for something I measured but did not fully explain, and it's noted as such in the code so it isn't mistaken for a load-bearing design choice. Also worth knowing: the Windows path is the one I verified here; the Linux branch (`WebKitWebDriver`) is written from the driver name but untested in this environment.

The test's own header and the [proof report](reports/ui-upgrade/NAVIGATION_HANDOFF_WEBVIEW_PROOF_2026-10-26.md) now lead with the one command, with the manual steps kept underneath for debugging the chain itself. I also removed the hand-downloaded `msedgedriver` scratch directory, since the script's cache supersedes it.

Two natural next steps if you want them: the same real-webview harness could cover the in-page guard's anchor-click path (`externalNavigation.ts`), which today only has JS-level tests, and this could be added to the local pre-release gate so a backstop regression fails before a release rather than in CI afterwards.

+#!/usr/bin/env node
+/**
+ * One command that builds the desktop app and runs the real-webview navigation
+ * backstop test (`src-tauri/tests/navigation_webview.rs`).
+ *
+ * Run: npm run e2e:navigation      (or: node scripts/verify-navigation-webview.mjs)
+ *
+ * **Why a script instead of a note in the test header.** Three things make that
+ * test annoying to run by hand, and each of them fails in a way that looks like
+ * the backstop is broken:
+ *
+ *   - the native driver must match the installed WebView2 RUNTIME, not the
+ *     installed Edge browser — a mismatch fails every session with "only
+ *     supports Microsoft Edge version N" (so this resolves the runtime's
+ *     version and, on Windows, downloads that exact msedgedriver when one is
+ *     not already on PATH);
+ *   - a DEBUG binary resolves its window to `build.devUrl`, not to the compiled
+ *     `frontendDist`, so something has to serve `http://localhost:5173` or the
+ *     window shows the engine's error page;
+ *   - vite's default `localhost` can bind the IPv6 loopback only. Measured: the
+ *     webview then sat on `chrome-error://chromewebdata/` while WebDriver still
+ *     reported the app URL, so the test failed for a reason unrelated to
+ *     navigation. This binds IPv4 loopback explicitly and waits for HTTP 200.
+ *
+ * It starts that server itself — and stops only a server it started (one already
+ * answering is reused and left alone) — then runs `cargo build` followed by the
+ * `#[ignore]`d test, and exits non-zero on the first failure.
+ *
+ * Nothing here is needed by CI: `.github/workflows/ci.yml` does the same steps
+ * in its `webview-navigation` job, where msedgedriver comes from
+ * `msedgedriver-tool` and the log is the Actions log.
+ *
+ * Flags:
+ *   --no-build        skip `cargo build` (reuse the binary already there)
+ *   --keep-server     leave the dev server running afterwards
+ *   --driver <path>   use this native driver instead of resolving one
+ *   --app <path>      drive this binary instead of target/debug/netpulse-desktop
+ *   --port <n>        dev origin port (default 5173, matching tauri.conf.json)
+ */
+import { spawn, spawnSync } from 'node:child_process';
+import fs from 'node:fs';
+import os from 'node:os';
+import path from 'node:path';
+import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
+
+const root = path.resolve(path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), '..');
+const argv = process.argv.slice(2);
+const has = (name) => argv.includes(name);
+const opt = (name, fallback) => {
+  const i = argv.indexOf(name);
+  return i >= 0 && argv[i + 1] ? argv[i + 1] : fallback;
+};
+
+const PORT = Number(opt('--port', '5173'));
+const ORIGIN = `http://127.0.0.1:${PORT}`;
+const MANIFEST = path.join('src-tauri', 'Cargo.toml');
+const BIN_NAME = process.platform === 'win32' ? 'netpulse-desktop.exe' : 'netpulse-desktop';
+const APP = path.resolve(opt('--app', path.join(root, 'src-tauri', 'target', 'debug', BIN_NAME)));
+
+let failures = 0;
+const step = (ok, name, detail = '') => {
+  console.log(`${ok ? 'PASS' : 'FAIL'}  ${name}${detail ? ` — ${detail}` : ''}`);
+  if (!ok) failures += 1;
+  return ok;
+};
+const note = (msg) => console.log(`      ${msg}`);
+
+/* ------------------------------- tool lookup ------------------------------ */
+
+function onPath(candidates) {
+  const dirs = (process.env.PATH || '').split(path.delimiter).filter(Boolean);
+  for (const name of candidates) {
+    for (const dir of dirs) {
+      const full = path.join(dir, name);
+      if (fs.existsSync(full)) return full;
+    }
+  }
+  return null;
+}
+
+function resolveTool({ envVar, candidates }) {
+  const pointed = envVar ? process.env[envVar] : undefined;
+  if (pointed && fs.existsSync(pointed)) return pointed;
+  return onPath(candidates);
+}
+
+/** The installed WebView2 runtime's version, which is what the driver must match. */
+function webview2Version() {
+  const base = 'C:/Program Files (x86)/Microsoft/EdgeWebView/Application';
+  try {
+    const versions = fs
+      .readdirSync(base)
+      .filter((v) => /^\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/.test(v))
+      .sort((a, b) => {
+        const left = a.split('.').map(Number);
+        const right = b.split('.').map(Number);
+        for (let i = 0; i < 4; i += 1) if (left[i] !== right[i]) return left[i] - right[i];
+        return 0;
+      });
+    return versions.at(-1) ?? null;
+  } catch {
+    return null;
+  }
+}
+
+/** Where a downloaded driver is kept: inside node_modules (already ignored), else temp. */
+function driverCacheDir(version) {
+  const base = fs.existsSync(path.join(root, 'node_modules'))
+    ? path.join(root, 'node_modules', '.cache', 'netpulse')
+    : path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'netpulse-cache');
+  return path.join(base, 'msedgedriver', version);
+}
+
+async function downloadMsedgedriver(version) {
+  const dir = driverCacheDir(version);
+  const exe = path.join(dir, 'msedgedriver.exe');
+  if (fs.existsSync(exe)) return exe;
+
+  const url = `https://msedgedriver.microsoft.com/${version}/edgedriver_win64.zip`;
+  note(`downloading ${url}`);
+  const res = await fetch(url);
+  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`driver download failed: HTTP ${res.status} from ${url}`);
+  fs.mkdirSync(dir, { recursive: true });
+  const zip = path.join(dir, 'edgedriver.zip');
+  fs.writeFileSync(zip, Buffer.from(await res.arrayBuffer()));
+
+  // bsdtar (Windows 10+, macOS, Linux) reads zip; PowerShell is the fallback.
+  let unpacked =
+    spawnSync('tar', ['-xf', zip, '-C', dir], { stdio: 'ignore' }).status === 0;
+  if (!unpacked) {
+    unpacked =
+      spawnSync(
+        'powershell.exe',
+        ['-NoProfile', '-Command', `Expand-Archive -LiteralPath '${zip}' -DestinationPath '${dir}' -Force`],
+        { stdio: 'ignore' },
+      ).status === 0;
+  }
+  if (!unpacked || !fs.existsSync(exe)) throw new Error(`could not unpack ${zip}`);
+  fs.rmSync(zip, { force: true });
+  return exe;
+}
+
+async function resolveNativeDriver() {
+  const given = opt('--driver', null);
+  if (given) return path.resolve(given);
+
+  if (process.platform === 'darwin') {
+    throw new Error(
+      'tauri-driver cannot drive a macOS webview: this test runs on Windows (WebView2) or Linux (WebKitGTK)',
+    );
+  }
+  if (process.platform !== 'win32') {
+    const webkit = resolveTool({ envVar: 'WEBKIT_WEBDRIVER', candidates: ['WebKitWebDriver'] });
+    if (!webkit) throw new Error('install WebKitWebDriver (`apt install webkit2gtk-driver`) or set WEBKIT_WEBDRIVER');
+    return webkit;
+  }
+
+  const installed = resolveTool({ envVar: 'MSEDGEDRIVER', candidates: ['msedgedriver.exe', 'msedgedriver'] });
+  if (installed) return installed;
+
+  const version = webview2Version();
+  if (!version) {
+    throw new Error(
+      'no msedgedriver on PATH and no WebView2 runtime version to match; install the WebView2 runtime or set MSEDGEDRIVER',
+    );
+  }
+  return downloadMsedgedriver(version);
+}
+
+/* ------------------------------- dev server ------------------------------- */
+
+/** The dev origin's HTTP status, or null when nothing answers there. */
+async function originStatus() {
+  try {
+    const res = await fetch(`${ORIGIN}/`, { redirect: 'manual', signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2_000) });
+    return res.status;
+  } catch {
+    return null;
+  }
+}
+
+function startDevServer() {
+  // Run vite's entry directly: one child, no npm wrapper, and therefore a PID
+  // that actually owns the listener when it comes time to stop it.
+  const viteBin = path.join(root, 'node_modules', 'vite', 'bin', 'vite.js');
+  const viteArgs = ['--host', '127.0.0.1', '--port', String(PORT), '--strictPort'];
+  const useViteDirectly = fs.existsSync(viteBin);
+
+  const child = useViteDirectly
+    ? spawn(process.execPath, [viteBin, ...viteArgs], {
+        cwd: path.join(root, 'apps', 'web'),
+        stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe'],
+        detached: process.platform !== 'win32',
+      })
+    : spawn(process.platform === 'win32' ? 'npm.cmd' : 'npm', ['run', 'dev', '-w', '@netpulse/web', '--', ...viteArgs], {
+        cwd: root,
+        stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe'],
+        shell: process.platform === 'win32',
+        detached: process.platform !== 'win32',
+      });
+
+  let log = '';
+  const collect = (buf) => {
+    log += buf.toString();
+    if (log.length > 20_000) log = log.slice(-20_000);
+  };
+  child.stdout.on('data', collect);
+  child.stderr.on('data', collect);
+  return { child, output: () => log };
+}
+
+function stopDevServer(server) {
+  const child = server?.child;
+  if (!child || child.exitCode !== null || child.killed) return;
+  if (process.platform === 'win32') {
+    spawnSync('taskkill', ['/PID', String(child.pid), '/T', '/F'], { stdio: 'ignore' });
+    return;
+  }
+  try {
+    process.kill(-child.pid, 'SIGTERM');
+  } catch {
+    child.kill('SIGTERM');
+  }
+}
+
+/* --------------------------------- runner -------------------------------- */
+
+function cargo(args, env) {
+  return spawnSync('cargo', args, { cwd: root, stdio: 'inherit', env: env ?? process.env });
+}
+
+/// The dev server this run started, so a Ctrl-C cannot leave a listener behind.
+let activeServer = null;
+
+async function main() {
+  console.log('Navigation backstop (real webview) — build, serve, drive\n');
+
+  // 1. Toolchain.
+  step(cargo(['--version']).status === 0, 'cargo on PATH');
+  const tauriDriver = resolveTool({ envVar: 'TAURI_DRIVER', candidates: ['tauri-driver.exe', 'tauri-driver'] });
+  step(
+    Boolean(tauriDriver),
+    'tauri-driver on PATH',
+    tauriDriver ? tauriDriver : 'install it with `cargo install tauri-driver --locked`',
+  );
+
+  let nativeDriver = null;
+  try {
+    nativeDriver = await resolveNativeDriver();
+    step(true, 'native webdriver resolved', nativeDriver);
+  } catch (err) {
+    step(false, 'native webdriver resolved', err.message);
+  }
+  if (failures) return 1;
+
+  if (!has('--no-build')) {
+    const built = cargo(['build', '--manifest-path', MANIFEST]);
+    if (!step(built.status === 0, 'cargo build', built.status === 0 ? '' : `exit ${built.status}`)) return 1;
+  }
+  if (!step(fs.existsSync(APP), 'app binary', APP)) {
+    note('build it first, or pass --no-build only when it really is already built');
+    return 1;
+  }
+
+  // 2. The document the window will load.
+  let server = null;
+  let startedHere = false;
+  const existing = await originStatus();
+  if (existing === 200) {
+    // Someone else's dev server: reuse it and leave it up. Only a server this
+    // script started is ever stopped.
+    step(true, 'dev origin already served', `${ORIGIN} (left running)`);
+  } else {
+    if (existing !== null) {
+      note(`something already answers ${ORIGIN} with HTTP ${existing}; trying our own server anyway`);
+    }
+    server = startDevServer();
+    activeServer = server;
+    startedHere = true;
+    let ready = false;
+    for (let i = 0; i < 45; i += 1) {
+      if ((await originStatus()) === 200) {
+        ready = true;
+        break;
+      }
+      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 1_000));
+    }
+    if (!step(ready, `dev origin served at ${ORIGIN}`, ready ? '' : 'it never answered HTTP 200')) {
+      note(server.output().trim() || '(the dev server wrote nothing)');
+      note(`a server that is already on port ${PORT} but does not serve the app (HTTP ${existing ?? 'no answer'}) will do this; stop it and retry`);
+      return 1;
+    }
+  }
+
+  try {
+    // 3. The test itself. `--ignored` is the only place it runs locally; it
+    //    fails rather than skips when a driver or the binary is missing.
+    // Set on `process.env` rather than passed as a copied env object: measured
+    // on this machine, handing `spawnSync` a spread copy made rustup's `cargo`
+    // shim fail with "could not choose a version of cargo to run ... no default
+    // is configured" even though the copy carried RUSTUP_HOME and CARGO_HOME,
+    // while the same command with the inherited env runs. The child sees these
+    // two either way; the difference is whose environment block is used.
+    process.env.MSEDGEDRIVER = nativeDriver;
+    process.env.NAV_WEBVIEW_APP = APP;
+    const tested = cargo(['test', '--manifest-path', MANIFEST, '--test', 'navigation_webview', '--', '--ignored', '--nocapture']);
+    step(tested.status === 0, 'navigation backstop (real webview)', tested.status === 0 ? '' : `exit ${tested.status}`);
+  } finally {
+    if (startedHere && !has('--keep-server')) {
+      stopDevServer(server);
+      activeServer = null;
+      console.log('      dev server stopped (it was started by this script)');
+    } else if (startedHere) {
+      console.log(`      dev server left running at ${ORIGIN} (--keep-server)`);
+    }
+  }
+
+  console.log(
+    `\n${failures === 0 ? 'PASS' : 'FAIL'}  ${failures === 0 ? 'the backstop held in a real webview' : `${failures} step(s) failed`}`,
+  );
+  return failures === 0 ? 0 : 1;
+}
+
+process.on('SIGINT', () => {
+  stopDevServer(activeServer);
+  process.exit(130);
+});
+
+main()
+  .then((code) => process.exit(code))
+  .catch((err) => {
+    console.error(`FAIL  ${err.message}`);
+    process.exit(1);
+  });

    const node = {

      protocol: row['protocol'],

}

import fs from 'node:fs';
import path from 'node:path';

import Database from 'better-sqlite3';

import { buildShareLink } from '../apps/api/src/services/nodeLinkExport.ts';
import { NodeSecretVault } from '../apps/api/src/services/nodeSecretVault.ts';

const LIMIT = Number(process.env['LIMIT'] ?? 12);

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const dataDir = path.resolve(process.env['APPDATA']!, 'app.netpulse.desktop');
  const sqlite = new Database(path.join(dataDir, 'netpulse.db'), { readonly: true, fileMustExist: true });
  const since = Date.now() - 14 * 86_400_000;
  const rows = sqlite
    .prepare(
      `SELECT id, protocol, host, port, transport, security, sni, alpn, path, host_header, service_name,
              flow, alter_id, allow_insecure, reality_public_key, reality_short_id, reality_server_name,
              encryption, remark, last_tls_ms, last_tcp_ms, last_seen
       FROM public_nodes
       WHERE last_tls_ms IS NOT NULL AND last_tls_ms < 500 AND last_seen > ?
         AND protocol IN ('vless','vmess','trojan','shadowsocks')
       ORDER BY (last_proxy_ms IS NOT NULL) DESC, last_tls_ms ASC
       LIMIT 400`,
    )
    .all(since) as Array<Record<string, unknown>>;
  sqlite.close();

  const vault = new NodeSecretVault(path.join(dataDir, 'secrets', 'vault'));
  const byProtocol = new Map<string, Array<Record<string, unknown>>>();
  for (const row of rows) {
    const list = byProtocol.get(String(row['protocol'])) ?? [];
    list.push(row);
    byProtocol.set(String(row['protocol']), list);
  }

  const links: string[] = [];
  const picked: Array<Record<string, unknown>> = [];
  while (links.length < LIMIT) {
    let progressed = false;
    for (const list of byProtocol.values()) {
      const row = list.shift();
      if (!row) continue;
      progressed = true;
      const secret = vault.get(String(row['id']));
      if (!secret) continue;
      const built = buildShareLink(
        {
          protocol: String(row['protocol']),
          host: String(row['host']),
          port: Number(row['port']),
          transport: String(row['transport']),
          security: String(row['security']),
          sni: row['sni'] as string | null,
          alpn: row['alpn'] ? JSON.parse(String(row['alpn'])) : [],
          path: row['path'] as string | null,
          hostHeader: row['host_header'] as string | null,
          serviceName: row['service_name'] as string | null,
          flow: row['flow'] as string | null,
          alterId: row['alter_id'] as number | null,
          allowInsecure: row['allow_insecure'] === 1,
          realityPublicKey: row['reality_public_key'] as string | null,
          realityShortId: row['reality_short_id'] as string | null,
          realityServerName: row['reality_server_name'] as string | null,
          encryption: row['encryption'] as string | null,
          remark: row['remark'] as string | null,
        },
        secret,
      );
      if (!built.ok) {
        process.stdout.write(`skip ${row['protocol']} ${row['host']}:${row['port']} — ${built.reason}\n`);
        continue;
      }
      links.push(built.link);
      picked.push(row);
      if (links.length >= LIMIT) break;
    }
    if (!progressed) break;
  }

  fs.mkdirSync('.tmp-bench', { recursive: true });
  fs.writeFileSync('.tmp-bench/live-nodes.txt', `${links.join('\n')}\n`);
  process.stdout.write(`wrote ${links.length} links (hosts only):\n`);
  for (const row of picked) {
    process.stdout.write(`  ${row['protocol']} ${row['host']}:${row['port']} tls=${row['last_tls_ms']}ms tcp=${row['last_tcp_ms']}ms\n`);
  }
}

void main();

import { spawn } from 'node:child_process';
import fs from 'node:fs';
import os from 'node:os';
import path from 'node:path';

import { reservePort } from '../apps/api/src/services/coreProcess.ts';
import { parseNodeUri } from '../apps/api/src/services/nodeParsers.ts';
import { buildXrayConfig, buildXrayMultiConfig, findEngineBinary } from '../apps/api/src/services/proxyCores.ts';

import type { ParsedNodeConfig } from '@netpulse/shared';

const bin = findEngineBinary('xray')!;

async function runCore(label: string, config: unknown, holdMs = 2500): Promise<{ started: boolean; code: number | null }> {
  const dir = fs.mkdtempSync(path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'debug-xray-'));
  const cfgPath = path.join(dir, 'core.json');
  fs.writeFileSync(cfgPath, JSON.stringify(config));
  const child = spawn(bin, ['run', '-c', cfgPath], { windowsHide: true, stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'pipe'] });
  let out = '';
  child.stdout?.on('data', (d: Buffer) => (out += d.toString()));
  child.stderr?.on('data', (d: Buffer) => (out += d.toString()));
  const exited = await new Promise<number | null>((resolve) => {
    const timer = setTimeout(() => resolve(null), holdMs);
    child.once('exit', (code) => {
      clearTimeout(timer);
      resolve(code);
    });
  });
  const started = exited === null;
  child.kill();
  await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 150));
  const reason = out
    .split(/\r?\n/)
    .map((l) => l.trim())
    .filter((l) => /failed|error|unknown|invalid|not specified|no such/i.test(l))
    .slice(-1)[0];
  process.stdout.write(`  ${started ? 'STARTED ' : `DIED(${exited})`} ${label}${started || !reason ? '' : `\n            ${reason.slice(0, 240)}`}\n`);
  fs.rmSync(dir, { recursive: true, force: true });
  return { started, code: exited };
}

**Date:** 2026-10-26
**Tool:** `npx tsx scripts/bench-bulk-probe.ts` (`npm run bench:bulk-probe`)
**Core:** xray `26.3.27` (installed) and xray `26.10.21` (fresh install, for the
download leg)
**Node source:** the installed app's own database + encrypted vault
(52,573 nodes) and a share-link file built from it

The benchmark times the two production paths — `proxyProbeWithEngine` (one core
spawned, readied, probed and torn down per node: what the pre-batching bulk
runner did for every node) against `proxyProbeManyWithEngine` (several nodes in
one core).

## What it measured

| Run | Nodes | per-node ×8 | batched | Spawns per-node vs batched |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| app DB sample | 12 | 13,412 ms | 12,107 ms | 12 vs 2 |
| share-link file (recently reached nodes) | 12 | 13,408 ms | 12,213 ms | 12 vs 2 |
| app DB sample (4) | 4 | 12,097 ms | 12,097 ms | 4 vs 2 |

**No sampled node carried traffic at the time of measurement** — every probe
ended in `probe timed out`, `read ECONNRESET`, or a TLS disconnect, on both
paths. Both columns are therefore dominated by the 12 s probe timeout, and the
wall-time advantage of the batched path is **not** demonstrated by these
numbers; the benchmark prints that caveat itself. What the numbers do show is
the spawn count: 12 core spawns + teardowns versus 2.

The mechanism the batched path exists to exploit is real and separately
measured (`scripts/bench-engine-start.ts`): a core spawn + readiness costs
~300 ms, which is charged once per group instead of once per node.

## Defect 1 — one node's config aborted a whole batch (CONFIRMED, fixed)

Measured, not inferred: a group of 8 real nodes whose configs the shared core
rejected **all 8** at startup (`xray (batch of 8) exited during startup (code
23)`), even though 7 of them started fine on their own. Reproduced by growing a
batch one node at a time — the 8th node is the one that poisons it, and that
node fails alone too:

```
-- each node on its own --
  STARTED  vless 27.50.48.8:443
  STARTED  vmess 185.143.233.213:80
  STARTED  trojan 77.239.98.141:8443
  STARTED  shadowsocks 77.83.246.74:443
  STARTED  vless 138.128.224.100:80
  STARTED  vmess 185.143.233.114:80
  STARTED  trojan 198.12.144.253:443
  DIED(23) vless 104.17.72.206:443          <-- the poison node
  STARTED  vmess 188.114.98.0:8080
  ...
-- the batch, growing one node at a time --
  STARTED  first 7: vless,vmess,trojan,shadowsocks,vless,vmess,trojan
  DIED(23) first 8: ... + the node above
```

With 5.4% of the stored nodes (2,856 of 52,573) holding no credential at all —
and a shared core refusing to start on a credential-less config — roughly a third
of 8-node groups were exposed to this.

**Fixed** in two layers:

- `proxyEngineRunner.ts` — a node with no credential is never placed in a shared
  core (its config cannot start one, so it would take its siblings with it); it
  takes the single-node path, where the failure stays its own.
- `proxyCores.ts` — `engineSupportsConfig` now refuses the v2ray family for a TLS
  node that sets `allowInsecure` (defect 2), so such a node is never handed to a
  core that cannot load it.

After the fix, the same 12-node list produced **per-node outcomes for all 12**
(`probe timed out` / `read ECONNRESET` / TLS disconnect) instead of 7 of them
inheriting one sibling's startup failure.

Tests: `apps/api/test/bulkProbeRunner.test.ts`,
`apps/api/test/proxyCores.test.ts` (75 tests across the three affected files,
plus the full `@netpulse/api` suite: 97 files / 1057 tests green).

## Defect 2 — `allowInsecure` is gone from xray (CONFIRMED, worked around)

The config builder emitted `tlsSettings.allowInsecure` for every TLS node. xray
26.3.27 refuses the **entire config file** when it is `true`:

```
Failed to start: main: failed to load config files: [...] > infra/conf: failed
to build outbound config with tag np-node > infra/conf: failed to build stream
settings for outbound detour > infra/conf: Failed to build TLS config. >
common/errors: The feature "allowInsecure" has been removed and migrated to
"pinnedPeerCertSha256". Please update your config(s) according to release note
and documentation.
```

1 node in 12 sampled real nodes hit this, and it was the node that poisoned its
batch. The same node's config **starts on sing-box** (`tls.insecure: true` is
still accepted there — verified by running it), so the node is now routed to
sing-box, and a machine without sing-box gets a specific reason instead of a bare
exit code.

**Not fixed, and worth deciding:** `allowInsecure: true` cannot be honoured by
the v2ray family any more. Pinning the peer certificate
(`pinnedPeerCertSha256`) is the supported replacement and would need the app to
fetch and hash the node's leaf certificate; until then such nodes depend on
sing-box being installed.

A freshly installed xray `26.10.21` (what `installEngine` fetches today,

The benchmark is built, run for real, and green; it earned its keep on the first run by finding two production defects.

## What I added

[scripts/bench-bulk-probe.ts](scripts/bench-bulk-probe.ts), plus `npm run bench:bulk-probe` in [package.json](package.json).

It times the two production paths, not stand-ins: `proxyProbeWithEngine` (one core spawned, readied, probed and torn down per node — what the pre-batching bulk runner did for every node) against `proxyProbeManyWithEngine` (several nodes in one shared core, what `POST /nodes/test-batch` reaches).

- **Core**: located the way the app locates it (`NETPULSE_CORES_DIR` → `<dataDir>/cores` → PATH), and when nothing is installed it fetches one with the app's own verified installer.
- **Node list**: by default the installed app's real SQLite database and real encrypted vault (read-only; the app is never booted, so no scheduler, source refresh or boot auto-connect runs as a side effect), or `NODES_FILE=<share links>` parsed by the app's own URI parsers — so you can benchmark nodes you know work, e.g. your own.
- **Report**: wall time per mode (median over `REPEAT`), spawn counts, per-node outcomes with the engine that measured each, a cross-mode agreement check, and a printed caveat when nothing carried traffic.

## What it measured (honest caveat first)

Against the app's 52,573-node database and a share-link list of nodes the app had recently reached, **no sampled node carried traffic** — every probe ended in `probe timed out`, `read ECONNRESET` or a TLS disconnect, on both paths. Both columns were therefore timeout-bound (12.4 s vs 12.1 s; ~12.1 s vs ~12.1 s on 4 and 2 nodes), so these numbers do **not** demonstrate the batched path's wall-time advantage; they quantify only the spawn count, 12 spawns + teardowns versus 2. The spawn cost the batched path amortizes was already measured separately by `bench:engine` (~300 ms per spawn + readiness).

## Two defects it exposed, and what I did

**1. One node's config aborted its entire batch.** A group of 8 real nodes all failed with `xray … exited during startup (code 23)` although 7 of them started fine alone — reproduced by growing the batch one node at a time, which isolates the poison node. With 2,856 of 52,573 stored nodes (5.4%) holding no credential, ~a third of 8-node groups were exposed. Fixed in [proxyEngineRunner.ts](apps/api/src/services/proxyEngineRunner.ts): a credential-less node is never placed in a shared core (it cannot start one, so it would take its siblings down); it takes the single-node path where the failure stays its own. Pinned by a new test in [bulkProbeRunner.test.ts](apps/api/test/bulkProbeRunner.test.ts).

**2. `allowInsecure` no longer exists in xray.** The builder emitted `tlsSettings.allowInsecure`; xray 26.3.27 refuses the *whole config file* when it is `true` (`The feature "allowInsecure" has been removed and migrated to "pinnedPeerCertSha256"`). One node in 12 real nodes hit this — and it was the node poisoning its batch. The same node's config starts on sing-box, so [proxyCores.ts](apps/api/src/services/proxyCores.ts) now refuses the v2ray family for that combination (in the existing "can this engine run this config" seam), routing it to sing-box, and reporting a specific reason when sing-box is absent. Pinned by a new test in [proxyCores.test.ts](apps/api/test/proxyCores.test.ts). After both fixes, the same 12-node list gave all 12 nodes their own outcome instead of 7 inheriting a sibling's failure.

Details, measurements and the reproduction are written up in [01_BULK_PROBE_FINDINGS.md](reports/engines/01_BULK_PROBE_FINDINGS.md).

## Checks actually run

- `npm run test -w @netpulse/api` → **97 files / 1057 tests pass** (after all three edits).
- Benchmark executed against the real database (isolated xray + real vault), against a share-link file, and with 2/4/12-node samples.
- Download leg verified for real: scratch cores + scratch data dir pulled xray **26.10.21** from the official release, `checksum verified: true`, installed and used.
- Cleanup: the local test server is stopped, and the temporary scripts and the credential-bearing `nodes.txt` are deleted (no secrets left behind).

**Not verified:** the wall-time speedup on nodes that actually carry traffic — I could not obtain a live node (the app's list has none working from this host, and a loopback test server is correctly refused by the import guard). Also unresolved: a freshly installed xray 26.10.21 rejected the same vless config the installed 26.3.27 loaded, on two synthetic links — the probe inbound is not the cause (both versions accept `http` and `socks`), and two synthetic links are not a faithful sample, so I recorded it as an open question rather than a claim. It matters because that is the version `installEngine` fetches today.

+# Bulk node-test benchmark — findings
+
+**Date:** 2026-10-26
+**Tool:** `npx tsx scripts/bench-bulk-probe.ts` (`npm run bench:bulk-probe`)
+**Core:** xray `26.3.27` (installed) and xray `26.10.21` (fresh install, for the
+download leg)
+**Node source:** the installed app's own database + encrypted vault
+(52,573 nodes) and a share-link file built from it
+
+The benchmark times the two production paths — `proxyProbeWithEngine` (one core
+spawned, readied, probed and torn down per node: what the pre-batching bulk
+runner did for every node) against `proxyProbeManyWithEngine` (several nodes in
+one core).
+
+## What it measured
+
+| Run | Nodes | per-node ×8 | batched | Spawns per-node vs batched |
+|---|---|---|---|---|
+| app DB sample | 12 | 13,412 ms | 12,107 ms | 12 vs 2 |
+| share-link file (recently reached nodes) | 12 | 13,408 ms | 12,213 ms | 12 vs 2 |
+| app DB sample (4) | 4 | 12,097 ms | 12,097 ms | 4 vs 2 |
+
+**No sampled node carried traffic at the time of measurement** — every probe
+ended in `probe timed out`, `read ECONNRESET`, or a TLS disconnect, on both
+paths. Both columns are therefore dominated by the 12 s probe timeout, and the
+wall-time advantage of the batched path is **not** demonstrated by these
+numbers; the benchmark prints that caveat itself. What the numbers do show is
+the spawn count: 12 core spawns + teardowns versus 2.
+
+The mechanism the batched path exists to exploit is real and separately
+measured (`scripts/bench-engine-start.ts`): a core spawn + readiness costs
+~300 ms, which is charged once per group instead of once per node.
+
+## Defect 1 — one node's config aborted a whole batch (CONFIRMED, fixed)
+
+Measured, not inferred: a group of 8 real nodes whose configs the shared core
+rejected **all 8** at startup (`xray (batch of 8) exited during startup (code
+23)`), even though 7 of them started fine on their own. Reproduced by growing a
+batch one node at a time — the 8th node is the one that poisons it, and that
+node fails alone too:
+
+```
+-- each node on its own --
+  STARTED  vless 27.50.48.8:443
+  STARTED  vmess 185.143.233.213:80
+  STARTED  trojan 77.239.98.141:8443
+  STARTED  shadowsocks 77.83.246.74:443
+  STARTED  vless 138.128.224.100:80
+  STARTED  vmess 185.143.233.114:80
+  STARTED  trojan 198.12.144.253:443
+  DIED(23) vless 104.17.72.206:443          <-- the poison node
+  STARTED  vmess 188.114.98.0:8080
+  ...
+-- the batch, growing one node at a time --
+  STARTED  first 7: vless,vmess,trojan,shadowsocks,vless,vmess,trojan
+  DIED(23) first 8: ... + the node above
+```
+
+With 5.4% of the stored nodes (2,856 of 52,573) holding no credential at all —
+and a shared core refusing to start on a credential-less config — roughly a third
+of 8-node groups were exposed to this.
+
+**Fixed** in two layers:
+
+- `proxyEngineRunner.ts` — a node with no credential is never placed in a shared
+  core (its config cannot start one, so it would take its siblings with it); it
+  takes the single-node path, where the failure stays its own.
+- `proxyCores.ts` — `engineSupportsConfig` now refuses the v2ray family for a TLS
+  node that sets `allowInsecure` (defect 2), so such a node is never handed to a
+  core that cannot load it.
+
+After the fix, the same 12-node list produced **per-node outcomes for all 12**
+(`probe timed out` / `read ECONNRESET` / TLS disconnect) instead of 7 of them
+inheriting one sibling's startup failure.
+
+Tests: `apps/api/test/bulkProbeRunner.test.ts`,
+`apps/api/test/proxyCores.test.ts` (75 tests across the three affected files,
+plus the full `@netpulse/api` suite: 97 files / 1057 tests green).
+
+## Defect 2 — `allowInsecure` is gone from xray (CONFIRMED, worked around)
+
+The config builder emitted `tlsSettings.allowInsecure` for every TLS node. xray
+26.3.27 refuses the **entire config file** when it is `true`:
+
+```
+Failed to start: main: failed to load config files: [...] > infra/conf: failed
+to build outbound config with tag np-node > infra/conf: failed to build stream
+settings for outbound detour > infra/conf: Failed to build TLS config. >
+common/errors: The feature "allowInsecure" has been removed and migrated to
+"pinnedPeerCertSha256". Please update your config(s) according to release note
+and documentation.
+```
+
+1 node in 12 sampled real nodes hit this, and it was the node that poisoned its
+batch. The same node's config **starts on sing-box** (`tls.insecure: true` is
+still accepted there — verified by running it), so the node is now routed to
+sing-box, and a machine without sing-box gets a specific reason instead of a bare
+exit code.
+
+**Not fixed, and worth deciding:** `allowInsecure: true` cannot be honoured by
+the v2ray family any more. Pinning the peer certificate
+(`pinnedPeerCertSha256`) is the supported replacement and would need the app to
+fetch and hash the node's leaf certificate; until then such nodes depend on
+sing-box being installed.
+
+## Unresolved observation
+
+A freshly installed xray `26.10.21` (what `installEngine` fetches today,
+checksum verified, 5.2 s) rejected at startup the same vless config that the
+installed `26.3.27` loaded, on two synthetic links. It is **not** the probe
+inbound: both versions accept `http` and `socks` inbounds. Two synthetic links
+are not a faithful node sample, so this is recorded as an open question, not a
+defect claim. Worth re-testing against real nodes with a fresh core, because a
+default engine install that rejects the app's own configs would break proxy
+testing and the local proxy tunnel outright.
+
+## Verification performed
+
+- `npm run test -w @netpulse/api` → 97 files, 1057 tests pass.
+- Benchmark run against the real 52,573-node database (isolated xray + real
+  vault) and against a share-link file.
+- Download leg: empty cores dir + scratch data dir → real release fetched,
+  `checksum verified: true`, installed, used (`Xray 26.10.21`).
+- A real xray server was started locally to sanity-check the probe inbound, then
+  stopped; nothing was left running and no temporary files remain.

# NETPULSE ADAPTIVE AI — AUTONOMOUS CONNECTIVITY INTELLIGENCE

**Mission ID:** `NETPULSE_ADAPTIVE_INTELLIGENCE`

**Priority:** Core product capability.

**Objective:** Build a lightweight, fast, continuously improving adaptive intelligence system inside NetPulse that learns from connection outcomes, selects suitable verified VPN and DNS strategies, discovers new approaches through ongoing research, and safely improves Internet connectivity under difficult network conditions, including censorship conditions relevant to Iran.

This mission extends the existing NetPulse DPI research and SUPER VPN development missions. It must use their research documents, implementation results, protocol comparisons, WHITEDNS research, and measured failures.

Do not stop at producing an architecture document. Inspect the real codebase, implement the system, add tests, integrate it with the real VPN, and verify actual connectivity.

## 1. Build three separate intelligence components

### A. Local adaptive connectivity engine

Implement this in the language and architecture best suited to the existing NetPulse client.

Requirements:

- Fast decisions suitable for an ordinary mobile or desktop device.
- Low CPU and memory consumption.
- No mandatory external AI API.
- Ability to operate using cached, previously verified profiles while offline.
- A defined interface to the real connection manager.
- Explicit decision explanations for diagnostics.
- Versioned policy and model updates.
- Safe fallback when the model is unavailable or uncertain.

Start with deterministic rules and a lightweight statistical or contextual-bandit policy. Introduce a small trained model only if experiments demonstrate an improvement over this baseline.

The engine may learn which approved connection strategies work best under observed network conditions. It must not invent arbitrary live configurations and immediately execute them.

### B. Research and discovery agent

Continuously investigate maintained protocol implementations, research publications, technical documentation, public censorship measurements, relevant GitHub repositories, and the existing NetPulse research corpus.

Prioritize:

- Iran-specific censorship research.
- PattNG and upstream V2RayNG.
- Xray-core and compatible transports.
- WHITEDNS and DNS-related research.
- OONI measurement data.
- Established censorship circumvention technologies.
- TLS metadata, SNI and ECH compatibility.
- DNS tampering, connection timeouts, transport failures and recovery.
- Research on automated circumvention and adaptive routing.
- Current security advisories, interoperability problems, and new implementation capabilities.

Use published sources and public APIs in accordance with their policies and rate limits.

For every new idea, record the source, evidence, compatibility requirements, license, security risks, expected benefit, test plan, and conclusion.

The research agent must be allowed to suggest new techniques and prototype new methods. It must not be allowed to bypass the validation and deployment controls in this mission.

### C. Verified profile and update service

Design a mechanism for distributing approved connection profiles and policy/model updates.

Requirements:

- Signed manifests and authenticated distribution.
- Versioning and expiry.
- Compatibility checks.
- Server and protocol identity validation.
- Integrity checks.
- Safe rollback.
- Revocation of compromised profiles.
- Clear separation between test and production profiles.
- No private credentials embedded in public manifests.
- No changes to active configurations merely because an Internet source has published a new configuration.

An update must be verifiably authentic before use. A valid signature establishes integrity and publisher authenticity; it does not automatically establish that a profile is safe or effective.

## 2. Design a useful learning system

Collect only the minimum observations required to improve connectivity.

Potential inputs include:

- Whether the network route is reachable.
- Whether DNS resolution succeeds.
- Whether the selected transport completes its handshake.
- Whether the tunnel actually forwards traffic.
- Connection establishment time.
- Latency, packet loss and throughput.
- Reconnection success.
- Relevant server and protocol compatibility.
- Coarse, user-approved network context.
- Whether the failure was DNS-related, transport-related, authentication-related, or an ordinary service outage.

Do not use user browsing history or unrelated content as training data. Do not send raw packet captures, credentials, subscription links, DNS query histories, or destination histories to an external AI model.

### Learning behavior

The engine should learn which approved strategy is most likely to work under the current observed conditions.

Use a controlled contextual-bandit model or another interpretable approach to estimate the success and cost of candidate strategies.

Include:

- Confidence estimates.
- Exploration limits.
- Conservative fallback.
- Minimum sample requirements.
- Protection against misleading observations.
- Decaying or segmented observations so old network conditions do not dominate new evidence.
- A mechanism to reset corrupted or outdated learning state.
- Explicit separation of model predictions from verified results.

A failed connection is not automatically evidence of DPI. Consider DNS failure, server outage, account expiry, routing problems, packet loss and incorrect configuration before attributing a failure to censorship.

When evidence is inconclusive, preserve the current safe configuration and perform only bounded, reversible attempts.

## 3. Implement adaptive connection management

Integrate the intelligence engine with the real NetPulse connection manager.

The engine may recommend switching between supported and verified options in the existing architecture, including appropriate VPN transports, DNS settings, servers, or authorized relay strategies.

It must not assume every transport works on every client or network.

Implement:

- A registry of compatible strategies.
- A health-check interface.
- A connection state machine.
- Bounded retries and backoff.
- Connection timeouts.
- Successful-tunnel verification.
- A recovery and fallback policy.
- Configuration compatibility checks.
- Credential and subscription validation.
- Safe handling of network changes.
- Diagnostic reason codes.
- A conservative mode when all tested options fail.

Test transport selection independently from actual tunnel operation.

Do not report a connection as successful until the intended traffic path has been verified. Do not silently switch to a direct, unprotected route if the user expects the VPN to protect all traffic.

## 4. Build a safe Internet research and configuration discovery workflow

The research agent may search public technical sources, official protocol documentation, maintained GitHub repositories, and approved public configuration services.

It must distinguish between:

1. Documentation and source code.
2. Configuration examples.
3. Public relay or bridge metadata from its legitimate publisher.
4. Provider-issued subscription profiles.
5. Arbitrary user-submitted configurations.
6. Unknown or potentially malicious endpoints.

Never blindly import and activate arbitrary configurations copied from websites, code comments, paste services, or untrusted repositories.

A configuration candidate must pass appropriate checks, including:

- Source provenance.
- Publisher authenticity where available.
- Protocol and client compatibility.
- TLS certificate and hostname handling.
- Endpoint and credential validation.
- License and usage requirements.
- Malware or suspicious configuration review.
- A controlled connection test.
- A check that traffic is sent only through the intended route.
- A check that credentials and subscription state are preserved.
- A rollback path.

Do not scrape leaked VPN credentials, stolen subscription URLs, private keys, or private provider configurations.

Do not use arbitrary third-party hostnames as SNI or relay endpoints without authorization and correct service compatibility. A hostname that resolves does not prove it supports the desired transport.

New configuration discovery must never bypass user subscription entitlements or expose an account's credentials to a third party.

## 5. Research and experiment on new connectivity methods

Maintain a backlog of hypotheses drawn from the research corpus.

For each proposed technique:

1. Identify an observed failure.
2. Locate relevant source material and prior art.
3. State the hypothesis and its assumptions.
4. Establish a baseline.
5. Implement an isolated prototype.
6. Run the same controlled test conditions against baseline and candidate.
7. Measure real traffic success, establishment time, stability, resource cost, and failure modes.
8. Investigate security and privacy implications.
9. Repeat promising measurements.
10. Accept, reject, or defer the technique with documented reasons.

Use owned servers, authorized staging infrastructure, controlled network emulation, and approved test endpoints.

Do not test by attacking censorship equipment, probing unrelated public infrastructure, or creating uncontrolled traffic.

Use real-world measurements only where authorized access is available. Clearly distinguish lab results from observations on actual Iranian access networks.

## 6. Use evidence-driven sources

Integrate the research registry and living DPI documentation created by the existing research missions.

Start with:

- PattNG: https://github.com/patterniha/PattNG
- V2RayNG: https://github.com/2dust/v2rayNG
- Xray-core: https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core
- OONI measurements: https://explorer.ooni.org/
- OONI measurement interpretation: https://ooni.org/support/interpreting-ooni-data/
- Tor circumvention and pluggable transports: https://support.torproject.org/tor-browser/circumvention/unblocking-tor/
- Current research on adaptive network path optimization and automated censorship-circumvention discovery.

Read source material and implementation details, not just search results or repository descriptions.

Do not assume every technique is relevant to NetPulse. Evaluate compatibility with the actual client, server, platform, and user's threat model.

## 7. Design the update process

The adaptive engine can learn locally from connectivity outcomes. Improved policies and experimental strategies may be developed separately by the research agent.

Define two separate update paths:

**Local adaptation:** Update bounded local success estimates and strategy preferences without downloading executable code or changing trust roots.

**Reviewed research updates:** Propose a new strategy or policy, test it in an isolated environment, obtain the required technical review, sign the release, stage it, and deploy only after acceptance tests pass.

The model must not gain unrestricted command execution, root access, unrestricted shell access, or the ability to deploy arbitrary code because it learned a new strategy.

Do not allow an AI-generated configuration, program, or policy to enter production merely because an LLM predicts that it will work.

## 8. Integrate privacy and security protections

- Store learning data locally where practical.
- Minimize network telemetry.
- Do not collect browsing contents.
- Avoid detailed persistent mappings between user identities and destinations.
- Protect client and server credentials.
- Never expose VPN private keys or subscription URLs in model prompts.
- Provide an option to clear local learning data.
- Document what observations leave the device.
- Make external model use optional.
- Restrict profile and model updates to authenticated, integrity-checked releases.
- Preserve the selected security and leak-protection settings during recovery.

## 9. Define the evaluation plan

Compare the adaptive engine against the existing non-adaptive implementation.

Measure:

- Initial connection success.
- Success after recovery attempts.
- Time to a genuinely working tunnel.
- Time spent retrying ineffective options.
- Median and p95 connection establishment time.
- Reconnection success.
- False positive connection states.
- DNS failure and leak-test outcomes.
- Resource consumption.
- Additional network traffic used for probing.
- Performance when no external AI service is available.
- The model's ability to avoid repeating known ineffective strategies.

Use repeatable, authorized test conditions and adequate sample sizes. Explain uncertainty and avoid overstating results.

The adaptive engine must be capable of outperforming the baseline without causing unacceptable resource consumption, privacy risks, security regressions or connection loops.

## 10. Implement the feature in the actual NetPulse project

Inspect the codebase first. Identify the true client platform, VPN core, connection manager, network APIs, supported configuration formats, build system, and testing framework.

Create a modular implementation suitable for the existing stack.

Add:

- A documented policy interface.
- A compatible strategy registry.
- Local learning state.
- Bounded adaptation rules.
- Research candidate schemas.
- Signed update validation.
- Automated tests.
- Simulated network failure tests.
- Integration tests.
- A small UI section explaining connection recovery and diagnostics.
- Metrics sufficient to evaluate performance without collecting unnecessary personal data.

Preserve existing user changes and keep the project buildable.

Do not claim the feature is integrated until the actual application calls it, the policy affects real connection decisions, and the end-to-end tests pass.

## 11. Autonomous execution

Use the supported Hermes persistence mechanism to continue working through implementation, testing, and integration.

Maintain a durable backlog and research journal.

When one dependency is unavailable, continue independent tasks instead of stopping the mission.

Do not claim that execution continues after the runtime has actually terminated.

Do not create unlimited retries, unbounded test loops, or uncontrolled network traffic.

Deploy through the established release process. Keep experimental behavior disabled by default until it passes its acceptance tests.

## 12. Acceptance criteria

The feature is complete only when:

- The actual NetPulse client uses the adaptive engine.
- The engine can select among multiple compatible, approved strategies.
- It uses observed outcomes to improve future decisions.
- It can function without an external LLM service.
- Failed connections are classified without automatically assuming DPI.
- A genuinely working tunnel is distinguished from a completed handshake.
- DNS and routing behavior are tested.
- Untrusted Internet configurations cannot activate automatically.
- Updates are authenticated, versioned and reversible.
- Subscription and credential controls remain intact.
- Privacy and resource consumption are measured.
- The adaptive policy beats or meaningfully improves upon the baseline under specified test conditions.
- The final report contains test evidence, limitations and deployment status.

Use `PASS`, `FAIL`, `BLOCKED` and `NOT TESTED` accurately. Do not equate a completed build with verified connectivity.

### Start now

Inspect the actual project and research documents. Build a baseline, define the interfaces, implement the smallest useful adaptive engine, and connect it to the real VPN manager. Continue iteratively toward verified functionality rather than stopping at a proposal.

The target is a fast, compact, privacy-preserving intelligence system that learns from experience, selects reliable strategies, discovers promising improvements, and improves NetPulse without sacrificing security or silently routing traffic outside the intended protection.

/**
 * Discovery profiles — how hard a "find me a working node" run searches.
 *
 * The trade-off is the one Aether exposes as scan modes: a run emits probe
 * traffic at whatever rate it probes, and on a censored or metered link that
 * traffic is itself a liability. So each profile states, honestly and up
 * front, both how deep it validates and roughly how many candidates it will
 * touch — a user can choose "fewest probes" or "prove it actually carries
 * traffic" instead of getting one hard-coded behaviour.
 *
 * Depth means exactly this:
 *   tcp   — the handshake connected
 *   tls   — TLS finished (the node speaks real TLS, not just a bare socket)
 *   proxy — a real request was carried through a local core, i.e. the node
 *           provably relays traffic
 */

export type ScanProfileId = 'turbo' | 'balanced' | 'thorough' | 'stealth' | 'ironclad';

/** How deeply each candidate is validated. */
export type ScanDepth = 'tcp' | 'tls' | 'proxy';

export interface ScanProfile {
  id: ScanProfileId;
  label: string;
  /** one-line trade-off statement, shown in the UI */
  summary: string;
  /** hard cap on candidates a single run may probe */
  candidateLimit: number;
  /** deepest validation applied to each candidate */
  depth: ScanDepth;
  /** per-candidate budget (ms) */
  timeoutMs: number;
  /** candidates probed concurrently */
  concurrency: number;
  /** confirm the winner by reading its exit IP through the tunnel */

}

 * installed version line — never a guess.
