export function engineVersionIsCurrent(installedLine: string | null, latestTag: string | null): boolean | null {
  if (!installedLine || !latestTag) return null;
  // "v1.14.0" → "1.14.0"; "app/v2.12.3" → "2.12.3"
  const want = latestTag.replace(/^[^0-9]*/i, '');
  if (want.length === 0) return null;
  // Match the version as a WHOLE token. A bare substring would call an
  // 11.4.0 install "current" for a v1.4.0 tag (the tag's digits appear
  // inside the longer number), hiding a real update — so the version
  // must be bounded by anything other than a digit or dot on both
  // sides. Deliberately conservative: null (unknown) unless that
  // number literally appears in the installed version line — never a
  // guess.
  const escaped = want.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&');
  return new RegExp(`(?:^|[^\\d.])${escaped}(?![\\d.])`).test(installedLine);
}

 *   1. NETPULSE_CORES_DIR (explicit override)
 *   2. <dataDir>/cores/ — the desktop app's per-user drop-in folder; users
 *      copy xray.exe / sing-box.exe there and the app finds them without
 *      touching PATH (existence check only — nothing is executed here)
 *   3. PATH

export function findEngineBinary(id: ProxyEngineId): string | null {
  const base = ENGINE_BINARY_BASE[id];
  const names = process.platform === 'win32' ? [`${base}.exe`] : [base];
  if (id === 'hysteria') {
    // Hysteria's own release filenames the executable after the platform, so a
    // manually dropped official build is recognised too (no copy step needed).
    names.push('hysteria-windows-amd64.exe', 'hysteria-windows-arm64.exe');
  }
  const dirs: string[] = [];
  if (process.env['NETPULSE_CORES_DIR']) dirs.push(process.env['NETPULSE_CORES_DIR']);
  if (process.env['NETPULSE_DATA_DIR']) dirs.push(path.join(process.env['NETPULSE_DATA_DIR'], 'cores'));
  dirs.push(...(process.env['PATH'] ?? '').split(path.delimiter).filter(Boolean));
  for (const dir of dirs) {
    for (const name of names) {

      try {

/**
 * Signature trust for adaptive policy updates.
 *
 * The same trust model as the release feed — an offline private key, a public key
 * pinned in the build, a key id, expiry and revocation — applied to raw Ed25519
 * detached signatures instead of minisign text.
 *
 * Why not reuse `scripts/lib/minisign.mjs`: that module is the *publishing* side
 * of the installer channel and lives outside this TypeScript project; the check
 * here has to run inside the sidecar bundle on the user's machine. What must not
 * drift is the trust model, not the file format, and the model is asserted by
 * tests that sign real payloads with a real key and tamper with them.
 *
 * A build with no configured key has NO trust anchor, and this module then
 * returns a verifier that refuses everything — the honest direction: an
 * unverifiable update is not an update.
 */

/** The 12-byte SPKI DER prefix that turns a raw 32-byte Ed25519 key into a key object. */
const ED25519_SPKI_PREFIX = Buffer.from('302a300506032b6570032100', 'hex');

export type SignatureVerifier = (message: string, signatureBase64: string) => boolean;

/** Base64 raw (32 bytes) or SPKI PEM → a Node KeyObject, or null when unusable. */
export function parseEd25519PublicKey(value: string): crypto.KeyObject | null {
  const trimmed = value.trim();
  if (trimmed.length === 0) return null;
  try {
    if (trimmed.includes('-----BEGIN')) {
      const key = crypto.createPublicKey(trimmed);
      return key.asymmetricKeyType === 'ed25519' ? key : null;
    }
    const raw = Buffer.from(trimmed, 'base64');
    if (raw.length !== 32) return null;
    return crypto.createPublicKey({ key: Buffer.concat([ED25519_SPKI_PREFIX, raw]), format: 'der', type: 'spki' });
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
}

/**
 * Build the verifier injected into the adaptive engine.
 *
 * Returns `null` when no usable key is configured, so the caller can report
 * "no trust anchor" rather than silently accepting anything.
 */
export function createEd25519Verifier(publicKey: string | undefined): SignatureVerifier | null {
  if (!publicKey) return null;
  const key = parseEd25519PublicKey(publicKey);
  if (!key) return null;

import { z } from 'zod';

import type { FastifyInstance } from 'fastify';

import type { AppContext } from './context';

const RunSchema = z.object({
  candidates: z
    .array(
      z.object({
        id: z.string().min(1).max(64),
        name: z.string().min(1).max(128),
        host: z.string().min(1).max(253),
        port: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(65535).optional(),
      }),
    )
    .max(32)
    .optional(),
  probes: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(10).optional(),
  withRoute: z.boolean().optional(),
});

export function registerOptimizerRoutes(app: FastifyInstance, ctx: AppContext): void {
  app.post(
    '/api/v1/optimizer/run',
    { config: { rateLimit: { max: 4, timeWindow: '1 minute' } } },
    async (req, reply) => {
      const parsed = RunSchema.safeParse(req.body ?? {});
      if (!parsed.success) throw parsed.error;
      const testId = crypto.randomUUID();
      void ctx.services.optimizer.run(parsed.data, testId).catch((err) => {
        // the service never rejects for network reasons (per-candidate failures
        // become honest nulls) — this is a programming/DB error; log it instead
        // of swallowing it silently
        ctx.log.error({ err, testId }, 'optimizer run failed');
      });
      return reply.status(202).send({ testId });
    },
  );
}

# NETPULSE ADAPTIVE AI — AUTONOMOUS CONNECTIVITY INTELLIGENCE

**Mission ID:** `NETPULSE_ADAPTIVE_INTELLIGENCE`

**Priority:** Core product capability.

**Objective:** Build a lightweight, fast, continuously improving adaptive intelligence system inside NetPulse that learns from connection outcomes, selects suitable verified VPN and DNS strategies, discovers new approaches through ongoing research, and safely improves Internet connectivity under difficult network conditions, including censorship conditions relevant to Iran.

This mission extends the existing NetPulse DPI research and SUPER VPN development missions. It must use their research documents, implementation results, protocol comparisons, WHITEDNS research, and measured failures.

Do not stop at producing an architecture document. Inspect the real codebase, implement the system, add tests, integrate it with the real VPN, and verify actual connectivity.

## 1. Build three separate intelligence components

### A. Local adaptive connectivity engine

Implement this in the language and architecture best suited to the existing NetPulse client.

Requirements:

- Fast decisions suitable for an ordinary mobile or desktop device.
- Low CPU and memory consumption.
- No mandatory external AI API.
- Ability to operate using cached, previously verified profiles while offline.
- A defined interface to the real connection manager.
- Explicit decision explanations for diagnostics.
- Versioned policy and model updates.
- Safe fallback when the model is unavailable or uncertain.

Start with deterministic rules and a lightweight statistical or contextual-bandit policy. Introduce a small trained model only if experiments demonstrate an improvement over this baseline.

The engine may learn which approved connection strategies work best under observed network conditions. It must not invent arbitrary live configurations and immediately execute them.

### B. Research and discovery agent

Continuously investigate maintained protocol implementations, research publications, technical documentation, public censorship measurements, relevant GitHub repositories, and the existing NetPulse research corpus.

Prioritize:

- Iran-specific censorship research.
- PattNG and upstream V2RayNG.
- Xray-core and compatible transports.
- WHITEDNS and DNS-related research.
- OONI measurement data.
- Established censorship circumvention technologies.
- TLS metadata, SNI and ECH compatibility.
- DNS tampering, connection timeouts, transport failures and recovery.
- Research on automated circumvention and adaptive routing.
- Current security advisories, interoperability problems, and new implementation capabilities.

Use published sources and public APIs in accordance with their policies and rate limits.

For every new idea, record the source, evidence, compatibility requirements, license, security risks, expected benefit, test plan, and conclusion.

The research agent must be allowed to suggest new techniques and prototype new methods. It must not be allowed to bypass the validation and deployment controls in this mission.

### C. Verified profile and update service

Design a mechanism for distributing approved connection profiles and policy/model updates.

Requirements:

- Signed manifests and authenticated distribution.
- Versioning and expiry.
- Compatibility checks.
- Server and protocol identity validation.
- Integrity checks.
- Safe rollback.
- Revocation of compromised profiles.
- Clear separation between test and production profiles.
- No private credentials embedded in public manifests.
- No changes to active configurations merely because an Internet source has published a new configuration.

An update must be verifiably authentic before use. A valid signature establishes integrity and publisher authenticity; it does not automatically establish that a profile is safe or effective.

## 2. Design a useful learning system

Collect only the minimum observations required to improve connectivity.

Potential inputs include:

- Whether the network route is reachable.
- Whether DNS resolution succeeds.
- Whether the selected transport completes its handshake.
- Whether the tunnel actually forwards traffic.
- Connection establishment time.
- Latency, packet loss and throughput.
- Reconnection success.
- Relevant server and protocol compatibility.
- Coarse, user-approved network context.
- Whether the failure was DNS-related, transport-related, authentication-related, or an ordinary service outage.

Do not use user browsing history or unrelated content as training data. Do not send raw packet captures, credentials, subscription links, DNS query histories, or destination histories to an external AI model.

### Learning behavior

The engine should learn which approved strategy is most likely to work under the current observed conditions.

Use a controlled contextual-bandit model or another interpretable approach to estimate the success and cost of candidate strategies.

Include:

- Confidence estimates.
- Exploration limits.
- Conservative fallback.
- Minimum sample requirements.
- Protection against misleading observations.
- Decaying or segmented observations so old network conditions do not dominate new evidence.
- A mechanism to reset corrupted or outdated learning state.
- Explicit separation of model predictions from verified results.

A failed connection is not automatically evidence of DPI. Consider DNS failure, server outage, account expiry, routing problems, packet loss and incorrect configuration before attributing a failure to censorship.

When evidence is inconclusive, preserve the current safe configuration and perform only bounded, reversible attempts.

## 3. Implement adaptive connection management

Integrate the intelligence engine with the real NetPulse connection manager.

The engine may recommend switching between supported and verified options in the existing architecture, including appropriate VPN transports, DNS settings, servers, or authorized relay strategies.

It must not assume every transport works on every client or network.

Implement:

- A registry of compatible strategies.
- A health-check interface.
- A connection state machine.
- Bounded retries and backoff.
- Connection timeouts.
- Successful-tunnel verification.
- A recovery and fallback policy.
- Configuration compatibility checks.
- Credential and subscription validation.
- Safe handling of network changes.
- Diagnostic reason codes.
- A conservative mode when all tested options fail.

Test transport selection independently from actual tunnel operation.

Do not report a connection as successful until the intended traffic path has been verified. Do not silently switch to a direct, unprotected route if the user expects the VPN to protect all traffic.

## 4. Build a safe Internet research and configuration discovery workflow

The research agent may search public technical sources, official protocol documentation, maintained GitHub repositories, and approved public configuration services.

It must distinguish between:

1. Documentation and source code.
2. Configuration examples.
3. Public relay or bridge metadata from its legitimate publisher.
4. Provider-issued subscription profiles.
5. Arbitrary user-submitted configurations.
6. Unknown or potentially malicious endpoints.

Never blindly import and activate arbitrary configurations copied from websites, code comments, paste services, or untrusted repositories.

A configuration candidate must pass appropriate checks, including:

- Source provenance.
- Publisher authenticity where available.
- Protocol and client compatibility.
- TLS certificate and hostname handling.
- Endpoint and credential validation.
- License and usage requirements.
- Malware or suspicious configuration review.
- A controlled connection test.
- A check that traffic is sent only through the intended route.
- A check that credentials and subscription state are preserved.
- A rollback path.

Do not scrape leaked VPN credentials, stolen subscription URLs, private keys, or private provider configurations.

Do not use arbitrary third-party hostnames as SNI or relay endpoints without authorization and correct service compatibility. A hostname that resolves does not prove it supports the desired transport.

New configuration discovery must never bypass user subscription entitlements or expose an account's credentials to a third party.

## 5. Research and experiment on new connectivity methods

Maintain a backlog of hypotheses drawn from the research corpus.

For each proposed technique:

1. Identify an observed failure.
2. Locate relevant source material and prior art.
3. State the hypothesis and its assumptions.
4. Establish a baseline.
5. Implement an isolated prototype.
6. Run the same controlled test conditions against baseline and candidate.
7. Measure real traffic success, establishment time, stability, resource cost, and failure modes.
8. Investigate security and privacy implications.
9. Repeat promising measurements.
10. Accept, reject, or defer the technique with documented reasons.

Use owned servers, authorized staging infrastructure, controlled network emulation, and approved test endpoints.

Do not test by attacking censorship equipment, probing unrelated public infrastructure, or creating uncontrolled traffic.

Use real-world measurements only where authorized access is available. Clearly distinguish lab results from observations on actual Iranian access networks.

## 6. Use evidence-driven sources

Integrate the research registry and living DPI documentation created by the existing research missions.

Start with:

- PattNG: https://github.com/patterniha/PattNG
- V2RayNG: https://github.com/2dust/v2rayNG
- Xray-core: https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core
- OONI measurements: https://explorer.ooni.org/
- OONI measurement interpretation: https://ooni.org/support/interpreting-ooni-data/
- Tor circumvention and pluggable transports: https://support.torproject.org/tor-browser/circumvention/unblocking-tor/
- Current research on adaptive network path optimization and automated censorship-circumvention discovery.

Read source material and implementation details, not just search results or repository descriptions.

Do not assume every technique is relevant to NetPulse. Evaluate compatibility with the actual client, server, platform, and user's threat model.

## 7. Design the update process

The adaptive engine can learn locally from connectivity outcomes. Improved policies and experimental strategies may be developed separately by the research agent.

Define two separate update paths:

**Local adaptation:** Update bounded local success estimates and strategy preferences without downloading executable code or changing trust roots.

**Reviewed research updates:** Propose a new strategy or policy, test it in an isolated environment, obtain the required technical review, sign the release, stage it, and deploy only after acceptance tests pass.

The model must not gain unrestricted command execution, root access, unrestricted shell access, or the ability to deploy arbitrary code because it learned a new strategy.

Do not allow an AI-generated configuration, program, or policy to enter production merely because an LLM predicts that it will work.

## 8. Integrate privacy and security protections

- Store learning data locally where practical.
- Minimize network telemetry.
- Do not collect browsing contents.
- Avoid detailed persistent mappings between user identities and destinations.
- Protect client and server credentials.
- Never expose VPN private keys or subscription URLs in model prompts.
- Provide an option to clear local learning data.
- Document what observations leave the device.
- Make external model use optional.
- Restrict profile and model updates to authenticated, integrity-checked releases.
- Preserve the selected security and leak-protection settings during recovery.

## 9. Define the evaluation plan

Compare the adaptive engine against the existing non-adaptive implementation.

Measure:

- Initial connection success.
- Success after recovery attempts.
- Time to a genuinely working tunnel.
- Time spent retrying ineffective options.
- Median and p95 connection establishment time.
- Reconnection success.
- False positive connection states.
- DNS failure and leak-test outcomes.
- Resource consumption.
- Additional network traffic used for probing.
- Performance when no external AI service is available.
- The model's ability to avoid repeating known ineffective strategies.

Use repeatable, authorized test conditions and adequate sample sizes. Explain uncertainty and avoid overstating results.

The adaptive engine must be capable of outperforming the baseline without causing unacceptable resource consumption, privacy risks, security regressions or connection loops.

## 10. Implement the feature in the actual NetPulse project

Inspect the codebase first. Identify the true client platform, VPN core, connection manager, network APIs, supported configuration formats, build system, and testing framework.

Create a modular implementation suitable for the existing stack.

Add:

- A documented policy interface.
- A compatible strategy registry.
- Local learning state.
- Bounded adaptation rules.
- Research candidate schemas.
- Signed update validation.
- Automated tests.
- Simulated network failure tests.
- Integration tests.
- A small UI section explaining connection recovery and diagnostics.
- Metrics sufficient to evaluate performance without collecting unnecessary personal data.

Preserve existing user changes and keep the project buildable.

Do not claim the feature is integrated until the actual application calls it, the policy affects real connection decisions, and the end-to-end tests pass.

## 11. Autonomous execution

Use the supported Hermes persistence mechanism to continue working through implementation, testing, and integration.

Maintain a durable backlog and research journal.

When one dependency is unavailable, continue independent tasks instead of stopping the mission.

Do not claim that execution continues after the runtime has actually terminated.

Do not create unlimited retries, unbounded test loops, or uncontrolled network traffic.

Deploy through the established release process. Keep experimental behavior disabled by default until it passes its acceptance tests.

## 12. Acceptance criteria

The feature is complete only when:

- The actual NetPulse client uses the adaptive engine.
- The engine can select among multiple compatible, approved strategies.
- It uses observed outcomes to improve future decisions.
- It can function without an external LLM service.
- Failed connections are classified without automatically assuming DPI.
- A genuinely working tunnel is distinguished from a completed handshake.
- DNS and routing behavior are tested.
- Untrusted Internet configurations cannot activate automatically.
- Updates are authenticated, versioned and reversible.
- Subscription and credential controls remain intact.
- Privacy and resource consumption are measured.
- The adaptive policy beats or meaningfully improves upon the baseline under specified test conditions.
- The final report contains test evidence, limitations and deployment status.

Use `PASS`, `FAIL`, `BLOCKED` and `NOT TESTED` accurately. Do not equate a completed build with verified connectivity.

### Start now

Inspect the actual project and research documents. Build a baseline, define the interfaces, implement the smallest useful adaptive engine, and connect it to the real VPN manager. Continue iteratively toward verified functionality rather than stopping at a proposal.

The target is a fast, compact, privacy-preserving intelligence system that learns from experience, selects reliable strategies, discovers promising improvements, and improves NetPulse without sacrificing security or silently routing traffic outside the intended protection.

access networks, or a controlled staging path where one transport is blocked
while another passes. The harness already supports it
(`NODES_FILE=<share links>`), so the experiment is a corpus, not a code change.

The live test is done, and it found something real. Running the app's own probe harness from the VPS host (`206.1.96.89`, node links in `/tmp/vps-corpus.txt`) across 15 nodes with the machine's real cores — 36 attempts, 8 s timeout, `https://httpbin.org/ip` through the tunnel:

- **xray: 0/15** carried traffic (every attempt "probe timed out")
- **sing-box: 0/12**
- **v2ray: 8/9** carried real traffic (1.3–7.0 s)

Replayed at the app's real 2-attempt budget, the fixed order reached a working core on **0/15** episodes; the adaptive order on **5/15 (33.3%)** — always on the first core it dialled, **0 losses**, mean attempts 1.6 → 1.27, wasted attempts 24 → 14.

That corpus also exposed a genuine defect, which is the more important finding: when every strategy with evidence was cooling off after consecutive failures, the policy kept ranking those known-broken cores first and burned both attempts on them. So I changed [policy.ts](packages/shared/src/adaptive/policy.ts) to a bounded **fallback** — when all trusted strategies are cooling, the first non-cooling approved strategy is dialled first. It is deliberately *not* gated on the exploration opt-in (this is recovery, not evidence gathering), it never invents a candidate, and it only reorders what the caller already approved. It is asserted end-to-end through `quickConnectCore` in [adaptiveConnect.test.ts](apps/api/test/adaptiveConnect.test.ts): the real connect path now dials an untried approved core once both learned ones are cooling.

Checks run: api `adaptiveConnect.test.ts` **6 passed** (3.45 s, including the new fallback test), `tsc --noEmit` in `apps/api` clean, eslint on the changed shared/api sources clean, and the saved evidence replays from [REPLAY_LIVE.json](reports/adaptive/REPLAY_LIVE.json) with identical numbers and no new traffic. [ADAPTIVE_EVIDENCE_2026-10-26.md](reports/adaptive/ADAPTIVE_EVIDENCE_2026-10-26.md) now carries the live-corpus section and criterion 12 reads **PASS on that corpus**; the [ledger](tmp/NETPULSE_TASK_LEDGER.md) was updated too.

What this is not: the replay is counterfactual over real measurements, the corpus is one staging host rather than subscribers' networks, two live repeats gave 6/15 and 5/15 (variance a replay can't show), and `xray`/`sing-box` failing there says nothing about those cores elsewhere. Nothing is deployed — the feature lives in the working tree.

The obvious next experiment is the same harness against a real Iranian vantage, since that's now a corpus rather than a code change.

Progress note:
The external-handoff proof is now data the test reads, not text it matches.

**The record.** `os_open::record_handoff` appends one JSON object per handoff to the file named by `NETPULSE_HANDOFF_RECORD`, written **after** the spawn attempt, so a row means the OS was really asked:

```json
{"at":1793101058095,"host":"example.com","ok":true,"source":"navigation","url":"https://example.com/"}
```

`source` is the layer that opened the URL — `command` (the page's guard → the `open_external` command), `navigation` (`on_navigation`), `new-window` (`on_new_window`). That field is what used to require asserting the *absence* of another layer's log line. The variable is unset in every normal run, deliberately: a durable journal of opened URLs is a browsing record this product does not keep, so the channel exists only for this test, which points the driver process (and through it the app) at a temp file and deletes it when the run passes. A missing or unwritable file is logged and never fails a handoff.

**The test** ([navigation_webview.rs](src-tauri/tests/navigation_webview.rs)) parses the record into rows and asserts on them: exactly one new `(url, source, ok)` row per handoff — `navigation`, `new-window`, `command` — and **no** row for the refused `http://` URL. The log is now diagnostics only; no log phrase remains in the file. The anchor step also waits for the guard to report itself installed (its disposer lives on the document under `Symbol.for('netpulse.external-navigation-guard')`) before clicking.

**Verified.** `npm run e2e:navigation` passes (1 test, 7.3–8.3 s across runs; the last, on the final file, 7.65 s). The record from a passing run, in step order: `navigation`, `new-window`, `command`, all `ok: true`. A mutation check keeps that honest: with `onActivate` in [externalNavigation.ts](apps/web/src/lib/externalNavigation.ts) made to `return` immediately — the guard still installs, so the precondition passes, but no click is intercepted — the test **fails in ~26 s** showing a third row with `source: navigation` for the click; the file was restored byte-identically and the run passed again. `cargo test` for the crate: **161 passed, 2 ignored**, no warnings. I also validated [ci.yml](.github/workflows/ci.yml) parses (`gates`, `webview-navigation`).

One honest bump: an earlier run (first after the binary rebuild) produced a `navigation` row for the anchor click — the signature of clicking before the reloaded bundle had installed the guard. It did not reproduce in nine passing runs, four of them instrumented to report the guard's presence and the click's `defaultPrevented`/`isTrusted` state (guard installed, click prevented in all four). The precondition above now turns that race into an explicit failure instead of a misattributed handoff.

+/**
+ * Lists the DISTINCT hosts (and ports) of a corpus file of share links, plus which
+ * of them are IP literals, so the raw-ISP-path bypass routes can be computed.
+ * Prints host:port only — never a credential, uuid or password.
+ */
+import fs from 'node:fs';
+import dns from 'node:dns/promises';
+
+const files = process.argv.slice(2);
+if (files.length === 0) {
+  console.error('usage: node tmp/rawpath-hosts.mjs <corpus.txt> [...]');
+  process.exit(2);
+}
+
+const isIpv4 = (h) => /^\d{1,3}(\.\d{1,3}){3}$/.test(h);
+const isIpv6 = (h) => h.includes(':');
+
+const distinct = new Map(); // host -> Set(port)
+for (const file of files) {
+  if (!fs.existsSync(file)) {
+    console.log(`${file}: MISSING`);
+    continue;
+  }
+  const lines = fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8').split(/\r?\n/).map((l) => l.trim()).filter((l) => l && !l.startsWith('#'));
+  console.log(`--- ${file} (${lines.length} entries)`);
+  for (const line of lines) {
+    const proto = line.split('://')[0] ?? '?';
+    const m = line.match(/@([^/?#]+)/);
+    if (!m) continue;
+    const [host, port = ''] = m[1].split(':');
+    if (!distinct.has(host)) distinct.set(host, new Set());
+    distinct.get(host).add(`${proto}:${port}`);
+  }
+}
+
+console.log('\n=== distinct hosts');
+for (const [host, kinds] of distinct) {
+  let resolved = '';
+  if (!isIpv4(host) && !isIpv6(host)) {
+    try {
+      const a = await dns.resolve4(host);
+      resolved += ` A=${a.join(',')}`;
+    } catch { resolved += ' A=none'; }
+    try {
+      const aaaa = await dns.resolve6(host);
+      resolved += ` AAAA=${aaaa.join(',')}`;
+    } catch { resolved += ' AAAA=none'; }
+  }
+  const kind = isIpv4(host) ? 'ipv4-literal' : isIpv6(host) ? 'ipv6-literal' : 'hostname';
+  console.log(`${host.padEnd(34)} ${kind.padEnd(13)} ${[...kinds].sort().join(' ')}${resolved}`);
+}

# NETPULSE ADAPTIVE AI — AUTONOMOUS CONNECTIVITY INTELLIGENCE

**Mission ID:** `NETPULSE_ADAPTIVE_INTELLIGENCE`

**Priority:** Core product capability.

**Objective:** Build a lightweight, fast, continuously improving adaptive intelligence system inside NetPulse that learns from connection outcomes, selects suitable verified VPN and DNS strategies, discovers new approaches through ongoing research, and safely improves Internet connectivity under difficult network conditions, including censorship conditions relevant to Iran.

This mission extends the existing NetPulse DPI research and SUPER VPN development missions. It must use their research documents, implementation results, protocol comparisons, WHITEDNS research, and measured failures.

Do not stop at producing an architecture document. Inspect the real codebase, implement the system, add tests, integrate it with the real VPN, and verify actual connectivity.

## 1. Build three separate intelligence components

### A. Local adaptive connectivity engine

Implement this in the language and architecture best suited to the existing NetPulse client.

Requirements:

- Fast decisions suitable for an ordinary mobile or desktop device.
- Low CPU and memory consumption.
- No mandatory external AI API.
- Ability to operate using cached, previously verified profiles while offline.
- A defined interface to the real connection manager.
- Explicit decision explanations for diagnostics.
- Versioned policy and model updates.
- Safe fallback when the model is unavailable or uncertain.

Start with deterministic rules and a lightweight statistical or contextual-bandit policy. Introduce a small trained model only if experiments demonstrate an improvement over this baseline.

The engine may learn which approved connection strategies work best under observed network conditions. It must not invent arbitrary live configurations and immediately execute them.

### B. Research and discovery agent

Continuously investigate maintained protocol implementations, research publications, technical documentation, public censorship measurements, relevant GitHub repositories, and the existing NetPulse research corpus.

Prioritize:

- Iran-specific censorship research.
- PattNG and upstream V2RayNG.
- Xray-core and compatible transports.
- WHITEDNS and DNS-related research.
- OONI measurement data.
- Established censorship circumvention technologies.
- TLS metadata, SNI and ECH compatibility.
- DNS tampering, connection timeouts, transport failures and recovery.
- Research on automated circumvention and adaptive routing.
- Current security advisories, interoperability problems, and new implementation capabilities.

Use published sources and public APIs in accordance with their policies and rate limits.

For every new idea, record the source, evidence, compatibility requirements, license, security risks, expected benefit, test plan, and conclusion.

The research agent must be allowed to suggest new techniques and prototype new methods. It must not be allowed to bypass the validation and deployment controls in this mission.

### C. Verified profile and update service

Design a mechanism for distributing approved connection profiles and policy/model updates.

Requirements:

- Signed manifests and authenticated distribution.
- Versioning and expiry.
- Compatibility checks.
- Server and protocol identity validation.
- Integrity checks.
- Safe rollback.
- Revocation of compromised profiles.
- Clear separation between test and production profiles.
- No private credentials embedded in public manifests.
- No changes to active configurations merely because an Internet source has published a new configuration.

An update must be verifiably authentic before use. A valid signature establishes integrity and publisher authenticity; it does not automatically establish that a profile is safe or effective.

## 2. Design a useful learning system

Collect only the minimum observations required to improve connectivity.

Potential inputs include:

- Whether the network route is reachable.
- Whether DNS resolution succeeds.
- Whether the selected transport completes its handshake.
- Whether the tunnel actually forwards traffic.
- Connection establishment time.
- Latency, packet loss and throughput.
- Reconnection success.
- Relevant server and protocol compatibility.
- Coarse, user-approved network context.
- Whether the failure was DNS-related, transport-related, authentication-related, or an ordinary service outage.

Do not use user browsing history or unrelated content as training data. Do not send raw packet captures, credentials, subscription links, DNS query histories, or destination histories to an external AI model.

### Learning behavior

The engine should learn which approved strategy is most likely to work under the current observed conditions.

Use a controlled contextual-bandit model or another interpretable approach to estimate the success and cost of candidate strategies.

Include:

- Confidence estimates.
- Exploration limits.
- Conservative fallback.
- Minimum sample requirements.
- Protection against misleading observations.
- Decaying or segmented observations so old network conditions do not dominate new evidence.
- A mechanism to reset corrupted or outdated learning state.
- Explicit separation of model predictions from verified results.

A failed connection is not automatically evidence of DPI. Consider DNS failure, server outage, account expiry, routing problems, packet loss and incorrect configuration before attributing a failure to censorship.

When evidence is inconclusive, preserve the current safe configuration and perform only bounded, reversible attempts.

## 3. Implement adaptive connection management

Integrate the intelligence engine with the real NetPulse connection manager.

The engine may recommend switching between supported and verified options in the existing architecture, including appropriate VPN transports, DNS settings, servers, or authorized relay strategies.

It must not assume every transport works on every client or network.

Implement:

- A registry of compatible strategies.
- A health-check interface.
- A connection state machine.
- Bounded retries and backoff.
- Connection timeouts.
- Successful-tunnel verification.
- A recovery and fallback policy.
- Configuration compatibility checks.
- Credential and subscription validation.
- Safe handling of network changes.
- Diagnostic reason codes.
- A conservative mode when all tested options fail.

Test transport selection independently from actual tunnel operation.

Do not report a connection as successful until the intended traffic path has been verified. Do not silently switch to a direct, unprotected route if the user expects the VPN to protect all traffic.

## 4. Build a safe Internet research and configuration discovery workflow

The research agent may search public technical sources, official protocol documentation, maintained GitHub repositories, and approved public configuration services.

It must distinguish between:

1. Documentation and source code.
2. Configuration examples.
3. Public relay or bridge metadata from its legitimate publisher.
4. Provider-issued subscription profiles.
5. Arbitrary user-submitted configurations.
6. Unknown or potentially malicious endpoints.

Never blindly import and activate arbitrary configurations copied from websites, code comments, paste services, or untrusted repositories.

A configuration candidate must pass appropriate checks, including:

- Source provenance.
- Publisher authenticity where available.
- Protocol and client compatibility.
- TLS certificate and hostname handling.
- Endpoint and credential validation.
- License and usage requirements.
- Malware or suspicious configuration review.
- A controlled connection test.
- A check that traffic is sent only through the intended route.
- A check that credentials and subscription state are preserved.
- A rollback path.

Do not scrape leaked VPN credentials, stolen subscription URLs, private keys, or private provider configurations.

Do not use arbitrary third-party hostnames as SNI or relay endpoints without authorization and correct service compatibility. A hostname that resolves does not prove it supports the desired transport.

New configuration discovery must never bypass user subscription entitlements or expose an account's credentials to a third party.

## 5. Research and experiment on new connectivity methods

Maintain a backlog of hypotheses drawn from the research corpus.

For each proposed technique:

1. Identify an observed failure.
2. Locate relevant source material and prior art.
3. State the hypothesis and its assumptions.
4. Establish a baseline.
5. Implement an isolated prototype.
6. Run the same controlled test conditions against baseline and candidate.
7. Measure real traffic success, establishment time, stability, resource cost, and failure modes.
8. Investigate security and privacy implications.
9. Repeat promising measurements.
10. Accept, reject, or defer the technique with documented reasons.

Use owned servers, authorized staging infrastructure, controlled network emulation, and approved test endpoints.

Do not test by attacking censorship equipment, probing unrelated public infrastructure, or creating uncontrolled traffic.

Use real-world measurements only where authorized access is available. Clearly distinguish lab results from observations on actual Iranian access networks.

## 6. Use evidence-driven sources

Integrate the research registry and living DPI documentation created by the existing research missions.

Start with:

- PattNG: https://github.com/patterniha/PattNG
- V2RayNG: https://github.com/2dust/v2rayNG
- Xray-core: https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core
- OONI measurements: https://explorer.ooni.org/
- OONI measurement interpretation: https://ooni.org/support/interpreting-ooni-data/
- Tor circumvention and pluggable transports: https://support.torproject.org/tor-browser/circumvention/unblocking-tor/
- Current research on adaptive network path optimization and automated censorship-circumvention discovery.

Read source material and implementation details, not just search results or repository descriptions.

Do not assume every technique is relevant to NetPulse. Evaluate compatibility with the actual client, server, platform, and user's threat model.

## 7. Design the update process

The adaptive engine can learn locally from connectivity outcomes. Improved policies and experimental strategies may be developed separately by the research agent.

Define two separate update paths:

**Local adaptation:** Update bounded local success estimates and strategy preferences without downloading executable code or changing trust roots.

**Reviewed research updates:** Propose a new strategy or policy, test it in an isolated environment, obtain the required technical review, sign the release, stage it, and deploy only after acceptance tests pass.

The model must not gain unrestricted command execution, root access, unrestricted shell access, or the ability to deploy arbitrary code because it learned a new strategy.

Do not allow an AI-generated configuration, program, or policy to enter production merely because an LLM predicts that it will work.

## 8. Integrate privacy and security protections

- Store learning data locally where practical.
- Minimize network telemetry.
- Do not collect browsing contents.
- Avoid detailed persistent mappings between user identities and destinations.
- Protect client and server credentials.
- Never expose VPN private keys or subscription URLs in model prompts.
- Provide an option to clear local learning data.
- Document what observations leave the device.
- Make external model use optional.
- Restrict profile and model updates to authenticated, integrity-checked releases.
- Preserve the selected security and leak-protection settings during recovery.

## 9. Define the evaluation plan

Compare the adaptive engine against the existing non-adaptive implementation.

Measure:

- Initial connection success.
- Success after recovery attempts.
- Time to a genuinely working tunnel.
- Time spent retrying ineffective options.
- Median and p95 connection establishment time.
- Reconnection success.
- False positive connection states.
- DNS failure and leak-test outcomes.
- Resource consumption.
- Additional network traffic used for probing.
- Performance when no external AI service is available.
- The model's ability to avoid repeating known ineffective strategies.

Use repeatable, authorized test conditions and adequate sample sizes. Explain uncertainty and avoid overstating results.

The adaptive engine must be capable of outperforming the baseline without causing unacceptable resource consumption, privacy risks, security regressions or connection loops.

## 10. Implement the feature in the actual NetPulse project

Inspect the codebase first. Identify the true client platform, VPN core, connection manager, network APIs, supported configuration formats, build system, and testing framework.

Create a modular implementation suitable for the existing stack.

Add:

- A documented policy interface.
- A compatible strategy registry.
- Local learning state.
- Bounded adaptation rules.
- Research candidate schemas.
- Signed update validation.
- Automated tests.
- Simulated network failure tests.
- Integration tests.
- A small UI section explaining connection recovery and diagnostics.
- Metrics sufficient to evaluate performance without collecting unnecessary personal data.

Preserve existing user changes and keep the project buildable.

Do not claim the feature is integrated until the actual application calls it, the policy affects real connection decisions, and the end-to-end tests pass.

## 11. Autonomous execution

Use the supported Hermes persistence mechanism to continue working through implementation, testing, and integration.

Maintain a durable backlog and research journal.

When one dependency is unavailable, continue independent tasks instead of stopping the mission.

Do not claim that execution continues after the runtime has actually terminated.

Do not create unlimited retries, unbounded test loops, or uncontrolled network traffic.

Deploy through the established release process. Keep experimental behavior disabled by default until it passes its acceptance tests.

## 12. Acceptance criteria

The feature is complete only when:

- The actual NetPulse client uses the adaptive engine.
- The engine can select among multiple compatible, approved strategies.
- It uses observed outcomes to improve future decisions.
- It can function without an external LLM service.
- Failed connections are classified without automatically assuming DPI.
- A genuinely working tunnel is distinguished from a completed handshake.
- DNS and routing behavior are tested.
- Untrusted Internet configurations cannot activate automatically.
- Updates are authenticated, versioned and reversible.
- Subscription and credential controls remain intact.
- Privacy and resource consumption are measured.
- The adaptive policy beats or meaningfully improves upon the baseline under specified test conditions.
- The final report contains test evidence, limitations and deployment status.

Use `PASS`, `FAIL`, `BLOCKED` and `NOT TESTED` accurately. Do not equate a completed build with verified connectivity.

### Start now

Inspect the actual project and research documents. Build a baseline, define the interfaces, implement the smallest useful adaptive engine, and connect it to the real VPN manager. Continue iteratively toward verified functionality rather than stopping at a proposal.

The target is a fast, compact, privacy-preserving intelligence system that learns from experience, selects reliable strategies, discovers promising improvements, and improves NetPulse without sacrificing security or silently routing traffic outside the intended protection.

const ITERATIONS = (() => {

  const buckets: string[] = [];
  for (const dnsFailing of [false, true]) {
    for (const tlsFailing of [false, true]) {
      for (const relayWorked of [false, true]) {
        for (const ipv6 of [false, true]) {

function observation(at: number, context: string, strategyId: string, ok: boolean): AdaptiveObservation {

    ok,

/** Drive the state to the policy's cap with realistic, decayed evidence. */
function fillState(now: number): AdaptiveState {

      for (let k = 0; k < 6; k += 1) {

function percentile(sorted: readonly number[], p: number): number {
  if (sorted.length === 0) return 0;
  const index = Math.min(sorted.length - 1, Math.max(0, Math.ceil((p / 100) * sorted.length) - 1));
  return sorted[index]!;
}

function summarize(samples: number[]): { p50Us: number; p95Us: number; maxUs: number; meanUs: number } {
  const sorted = [...samples].sort((a, b) => a - b);

    p50Us: Number(percentile(sorted, 50).toFixed(2)),
    p95Us: Number(percentile(sorted, 95).toFixed(2)),
    maxUs: Number(sorted[sorted.length - 1]?.toFixed(2) ?? 0),

## 1. The question

The reconciler documents an asymmetric failure policy — a failed pull keeps the
last known-good identity set, a malformed payload is a hard error, an empty but
well-formed set is applied, and `expiresAt` is enforced on every pass. Until now
that was code plus prose. Acceptance step 18 asks whether reconciliation
*restores the correct state after a simulated temporary provisioning failure*,
so the policy needs to be falsifiable: what exactly happens to the server config
and to the cache when the Worker returns 500, disappears, or answers garbage —
and what happens on the pass after that?

## 2. Method

The real reconciler, unmodified apart from the §4 fix, run in a sandbox with
`NETPULSE_*` p [… 2,417 characters omitted] ast-run.json` says `no state, pull failed`, and **no empty set is cached** (so a later outage still cannot wipe anyone) |
| Live guard | both live configs byte-identical after the whole run |

The generated config in the host apply run was accepted by the real
`xray -test`, so the file this proof wrote is a file xray itself considers valid.

## 4. Defect found by this proof, and fixed

In apply mode the last-known-good cache was written **before** the xray
validation gate:

```
summary = {...}
if fresh is not None and not dry_run:
    write_atomic(STATE_FILE, ...)      # <-- before validation
...
if not xray_config_is_valid(xray_text):
    return 2                            # config rejected, cache already advanced
```

Consequence: a config the host refused to apply still became the state it would
fall back to during a Worker outage — a set the server had never received. The
harness failed the claim `apply: the refusal wrote neither config nor state
cache (fail-closed)` on the first run; the cache write now happens only after
validation passes, immediately before the files are rewritten.

pub fn native(args: &Args) -> Command {
  let native_binary = match args.native_driver.as_deref() {
    Some(custom) => {
      if custom.exists() {
        custom.to_owned()
      } else {
        eprintln!(
          "can not find the supplied binary path {}. This is currently required.",
          custom.display()
        );
        match current_dir() {
          Ok(cwd) => eprintln!("current working directory: {}", cwd.display()),
          Err(error) => eprintln!("can not find current working directory: {error}"),
        }
        std::process::exit(1);
      }
    }
    None => match which::which(DRIVER_BINARY) {
      Ok(binary) => binary,
      Err(error) => {
        eprintln!(
          "can not find binary {DRIVER_BINARY} in the PATH. This is currently required.\
          You can also pass a custom path with --native-driver"
        );
        eprintln!("{error:?}");
        std::process::exit(1);
      }
    },
  };

  let mut cmd = Command::new(native_binary);
  cmd.env("TAURI_AUTOMATION", "true"); // 1.x
  cmd.env("TAURI_WEBVIEW_AUTOMATION", "true"); // 2.x
  cmd.arg(format!("--port={}", args.native_port));
  cmd.arg(format!("--host={}", args.native_host));

  // Don't inherit stdout from parent to prevent native WebDriver binary/HTTP protocol data
  // from corrupting tauri-driver's stdout (which gets captured by the test framework).
  // Keep stderr inherited so WebDriver logs/errors are still visible.
  cmd.stdout(Stdio::null());

  cmd

**The defect.** `tauri.conf.json` declares two bundle resources — `backend/` and `WebView2Loader.dll` — and `.gitignore` keeps both out of the repository (`.gitignore:6` and `:9`; the comment even says node.exe alone is ~92 MB). Your machine has both; `actions/checkout` gives the job neither. The Tauri build script refuses a declared resource whose path is missing and names them one at a time, which is why this hid so well:

```
resource path `backend` doesn't exist                     BUILD_EXIT=101
resource path `WebView2Loader.dll` doesn't exist           BUILD_EXIT=101
```

      - name: Satisfy the build's resource paths
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path src-tauri/backend | Out-Null
          New-Item -ItemType File -Force -Path src-tauri/WebView2Loader.dll | Out-Null
```

Placeholders are the honest shape, not a dodge: the build script checks existence only, a **debug** binary loads its document from the dev server rather than the embedded bundle, and WebView2 comes from the installed runtime (the app logs `WebView2Loader.dll next to exe: false` and runs). // The record channel: evidence for a test, never a journal.
//
// `NETPULSE_HANDOFF_RECORD` (see `HandoffSource` / `record_handoff`) exists so
// `tests/navigation_webview.rs` can read each handoff as DATA instead of

// profile and PRE-CREATE that directory: a fallback that invented a path would
// then succeed rather than fail on a missing parent, which is what lets
// "still empty" be an assertion rather than a hope.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------

/// The file's bytes, or `None` when it does not exist. Compared as BYTES in the
/// negatives below, so an append, a rewrite, or a truncation all fail the same
/// assertion a missing row would.
fn record_file(path: &Path) -> Option<Vec<u8>> {
    std::fs::read(path).ok()
}

/// An empty scratch directory named for this process and case.
fn scratch(tag: &str) -> PathBuf {
    let dir = std::env::temp_dir().join(format!("np-record-{}-{tag}", std::process::id()));
    let _ = std::fs::remove_dir_all(&dir);
    std::fs::create_dir_all(&dir).expect("scratch dir");
    dir
}

/// A scratch profile whose data dir EXISTS and is empty, as it is on a machine
/// that has run the app once.
fn scratch_profile(tag: &str) -> (PathBuf, PathBuf) {
    let profile = scratch(tag);
    let data_dir = profile.join(crate::paths::APP_IDENTIFIER);
    std::fs::create_dir_all(&data_dir).expect("scratch data dir");
    (profile, data_dir)
}

/// Every entry name in `dir`, sorted — the "did anything appear here" reading.
fn entries(dir: &Path) -> Vec<String> {
    let mut names: Vec<String> = std::fs::read_dir(dir)
        .unwrap_or_else(|e| panic!("read {}: {e}", dir.display()))
        .filter_map(|e| e.ok().map(|e| e.file_name().to_string_lossy().to_string()))
        .collect();
    names.sort();
    names
}

**Mission ID:** `NETPULSE_PAYMENT_AND_FINAL_ACCEPTANCE`

## Context

The latest full-stack acceptance investigation established the following:

- NetPulse Cloudflare Worker and D1 control plane exist.
- Abystral is the Telegram commerce authority.
- Abystral has a working double-entry ledger and idempotency mechanisms.
- The Worker mirrors subscription entitlements.
- The VPS pulls VPN identities through authenticated outbound reconciliation.
- The deployed reconciler has been fixed and verified.
- Multiple VPN protocols have been tested with real traffic.
- Credential revocation and reconciliation failure/recovery have evidence.
- Worker tests: 126/126 passing.
- Reconciler failure/recovery verification: 47/47 on the live host.
- WHITEDNS remains partially verified.
- **Neither the Worker nor Abystral currently implements a real payment provider.**

Do not rebuild components that already work. Use the existing evidence and acceptance report as the baseline. First read `FULL_STACK_ACCEPTANCE_2026-10-27.md`, `RECONCILER_FAILURE_PROOF_2026-10-27.md`, `MISSION_JOURNAL.md`, the saved transcripts, and the current source code.

Preserve all existing changes and verified production behavior.

## Phase 1 — Select the appropriate payment architecture

Investigate Telegram Stars as the first candidate because NetPulse sells digital access through a Telegram bot.

Read the current official documentation:

- https://core.telegram.org/bots/payments-stars
- https://core.telegram.org/bots/api#payments
- https://telegram.org/tos/bot-developers

Confirm the currently applicable payment requirements before implementation.

For a Telegram bot checkout selling digital VPN subscriptions, investigate and implement the documented `XTR` payment flow rather than inventing a third-party-provider flow that the platform does not permit.

Before enabling live payments, investigate and report:

- Whether Stars purchase is practically available to the intended customers, including the target Iranian user base.
- Whether the bot owner can receive, withdraw, and redeem proceeds under the owner's actual account and regional circumstances.
- Applicable Telegram terms and restrictions.
- Price denomination and conversion policy.
- Refund handling.
- Support and dispute procedures.
- Whether recurring Stars subscriptions are supported by the current API and suitable for this product.

Do not assume that successful sandbox payment tests prove real-world customer availability or payout eligibility.

If Stars is unsuitable, research compatible alternatives for checkout outside Telegram and explain the platform-policy and customer-experience implications before enabling an alternative inside the bot.

## Phase 2 — Implement the real Stars payment lifecycle in Abystral

Inspect the existing commerce implementation, 66 migrations, double-entry ledger, wallet logic, subscription records, and Telegram handlers before changing the schema.

Reuse the existing ledger and stable transaction IDs. Do not create duplicate accounting authorities.

Implement or complete the real payment lifecycle:

1. A user selects a valid NetPulse subscription plan.
2. Abystral creates a unique order linked to the Telegram user and the correct NetPulse account.
3. The bot generates a Stars invoice using currency `XTR`.
4. The invoice amount is fixed to the recorded order price.
5. The bot processes `pre_checkout_query` within Telegram's deadline and validates the order, amount, currency, user, and current purchasability.
6. The bot activates no entitlements at pre-checkout.
7. Only a verified `successful_payment` event confirms payment.
8. The payment is recorded once in the existing ledger.
9. Duplicate or replayed events are rejected or treated idempotently.
10. The subscription is activated or extended exactly once.
11. Provisioning is queued through the existing durable mechanism.
12. The user receives a receipt and accurate subscription status.

Store and reconcile Telegram's payment identifiers, including `telegram_payment_charge_id`, as appropriate for the existing schema and refund process.

Use the current official Bot API definitions rather than relying on remembered field names or old examples.

### Important accounting requirements

- Store Stars amounts as integer quantities.
- Record the `XTR` denomination unambiguously.
- Do not treat Stars as fiat currency or silently mix them with wallet balances denominated in another currency.
- Keep order, payment, ledger, subscription, and provisioning state consistent.
- Make transaction processing idempotent.
- Handle concurrent checkouts safely.
- Do not allow duplicate callbacks to double-credit a wallet or extend a subscription twice.
- Preserve an audit trail.
- Do not mark a purchase paid merely because the user returns to a successful-looking screen.
- Never grant VPN access solely on a `pre_checkout_query`.

Use the dedicated Telegram payment test environment for development. Add tests for success, cancellation, invalid amount, wrong user, duplicate events, malformed events, concurrent orders, provisioning failure, retry, expiry, and refunds where supported.

## Phase 3 — Integrate payment confirmation with the existing NetPulse control plane

After a verified payment, use the existing Abystral and NetPulse entitlement contract.

Trace the actual event format and the sign/verification logic. Do not invent a second webhook contract if one already exists.

Verify that:

- The confirmed payment activates exactly the expected plan.
- The Worker accepts only authenticated, authorized, valid events.
- Duplicate signed events cannot duplicate entitlements.
- A failed provisioning attempt does not erase a valid paid order.
- A retry cannot activate the subscription twice.
- A cancellation, expiration, or refund follows the actual business rules.
- The VPS reconciler receives only valid entitlements.
- The user's account identity maps consistently across Telegram, Abystral, NetPulse, and the VPN configuration.
- WHITEDNS access matches the plan.
- Unauthorized users cannot retrieve another account's invoice, VPN configuration, or subscription status.

Keep payment truth in the commerce authority and entitlement enforcement in the existing NetPulse architecture.

Do not place private payment credentials or VPN secrets in public D1 records, payment events, or routine logs.

## Phase 4 — Verify the complete paid-customer workflow

Build a reproducible staging or test-environment run using a dedicated test account.

Demonstrate the following sequence with saved, sanitized evidence:

1. The test user opens the Telegram bot.
2. The user views a valid subscription plan and Stars price.
3. The bot creates the correct invoice.
4. The payment test environment confirms a successful payment.
5. Abystral records exactly one payment and correct ledger effects.
6. The subscription is activated exactly once.
7. The NetPulse Worker accepts the appropriate entitlement event.
8. The VPS provisioner receives the authorized entitlement.
9. The expected VPN credentials are provisioned.
10. WHITEDNS entitlement is applied if the plan includes it.
11. The real supported client receives a valid configuration.
12. The client establishes a tunnel to the deployed VPN server.
13. External test traffic passes through the intended VPN route.
14. DNS behavior and the actual egress address are checked.
15. A repeated payment event does not create additional access.
16. An injected temporary provisioning failure recovers without losing the paid order or duplicating its entitlements.
17. Expiration and revocation remove the expected access.

Do not mark a step `PASS` merely because a mock call returned success. Label mocked tests distinctly from tests that exercised the real Telegram payment test environment, Worker, provisioner, and VPN.

## Phase 5 — Finish the remaining acceptance gaps

Address the partial WHITEDNS verification from the previous report:

- Prove that plan selection creates the correct DNS entitlement.
- Prove that the signed or authenticated event reaches the Worker.
- Prove that the VPS/client DNS configuration matches the entitlement.
- Prove the intended resolver works through an active VPN tunnel.
- Prove that expiry or revocation removes the DNS entitlement.
- Confirm that failures cannot silently route DNS outside the intended policy.

Keep the already-verified VPN reconciler and production service behavior intact. Do not run unnecessary live service restarts, destructive tests, or uncontrolled load tests.

Re-run the existing test suites after integration and update the acceptance matrix with fresh results.

## Phase 6 — Production readiness decision

Do not enable production payments solely because sandbox tests pass.

Prepare a clear go/no-go report that distinguishes:

- Code complete.
- Sandbox integration passed.
- Customer-side payment availability verified or unverified.
- Merchant payout/redemption verified or unverified.
- Production configuration complete.
- Production payment actually tested or not tested.
- Full VPN entitlement flow verified or not verified.

Use `PASS`, `FAIL`, `BLOCKED`, and `NOT TESTED` honestly.

If live merchant eligibility, payout availability, legal requirements, or a production credential requires owner action, finish every independent task and identify the exact remaining dependency. Do not invent credentials or claim that the dependency has been satisfied.

Keep production checkout disabled until the required business and payment setup is genuinely ready.

## Execution directive

Start with the existing acceptance report and source code, then implement the Stars integration in the commerce authority, connect it to the existing entitlement system, run test-environment transactions, and execute the full provisioning and VPN verification.

Do not rebuild working infrastructure. Do not fake a payment provider. Do not stop at a plan. Deliver tested implementation, durable evidence, and a clear production-readiness decision.

The payment leg is implemented, tested, and filed. Here's the complete picture.

## What was built (Abystral, the commerce authority)

Telegram Stars (`XTR`) is the only platform-permitted checkout for digital goods sold inside a Telegram bot (Bot Developer Terms §6.2), so that's what the code implements, against the current official API: `pre_checkout_query` answered within its 10-second deadline, delivery only on `successful_payment`, `telegram_payment_charge_id` stored for `refundStarPayment`, plus `/paysupport` and `/terms`.

- `workers/src/telegram/migrations/0067_xtr_payments.sql` — `xtr_orders` (integer XTR, `CHECK currency='XTR'`, order-time USD price + rate snapshot) and `xtr_refunds`, with a partial UNIQUE index on the payment charge id so a replayed event cannot be booked twice.
- `src/services/stars.ts` + `src/db/xtr-repository.ts` — order → invoice → validated pre-checkout (re-reads the order; grants nothing) → guarded claim → **one** ledger journal (cash / deferred revenue, no wallet line) → subscription (`pending_retry` → `active`) → provisioning → `subscription.activated` in the same NetPulse outbox the wallet path uses. Refunds reverse the journal, revoke access and emit `subscription.refunded`; a panel failure keeps the paid order for the retry worker.
- `src/bot.ts`, `src/handlers/buy.ts`, `src/lib/keyboard.ts`, i18n (EN+FA), and `XTR_ENABLED` which is **fail-closed** — unset means the button is hidden and pre-checkout refuses.

## Checks actually run

- `npx vitest run tests/xtr-payments.test.ts` → **21/21 pass** over the real `worker.fetch` → grammY → services → repositories → real SQLite with the full migration chain (migrations, guards and ledger triggers are real; the Bot API transport and the panel are stubbed). They prove: nothing is granted at checkout, one subscription and one balanced journal per order, replay is a no-op, wrong user/amount/payload/currency/expired/cancelled are refused with zero writes, two orders are two purchases, a late payment on an expired order is honoured once, and refunds call the provider exactly once.
- Abystral full suite: 3398 passed / 28 failed in 6 files — all pre-existing SPA/broadcast failures in files changed before this cycle. Typecheck clean. NetPulse worker suite re-run: **126/126**.
- The tests caught four real defects, now fixed: the Stars handlers were unreachable (registered after grammY's generic message fallback, so `successful_payment` was swallowed — the old stub could never have fired); `createSubscription` returns the table's `DEFAULT 'active'` row, so the "already provisioned" check would have activated orders with no panel client; activation/refund events were fire-and-forget; and one silent `.catch(() => null)`.

## Decision: NO-GO for live payments, `XTR_ENABLED` stays unset

Code complete: **YES**. Test-double integration: **PASS**. Real test-environment checkout: **NOT TESTED**. Customer-side Stars availability in Iran and owner payout/redemption: **UNVERIFIED** — Telegram itself documents a regional `stars_purchase_blocked` flag, and no official source confirms an Iran-resident owner can redeem via Fragment (0.013 USD/Star, up-to-21-day hold). Local-law exposure (VPN sale/use criminalised in Iran per third-party UK Home Office reporting) is recorded, not resolved. The remaining dependencies are exactly: owner confirms purchase availability + payout eligibility, one real test-environment checkout, and the deployed Worker accepting a signed `subscription.activated` (`NP_SERVICE_SECRET_FILE=…`) driving a provisioned credential and working tunnel.

export async function proxyProbeMany(
  nodes: readonly PublicNode[],
  deps: Pick<ProbeDeps, 'testEndpoints' | 'proxyEnginePreference'>,
  opts: {
    secretFor: (nodeId: string) => string | null;
    onGroupStart?: (indexes: readonly number[]) => void;
    onResult?: (index: number, result: NodeTestResult) => void;
    shouldStop?: () => boolean;
  },
): Promise<Array<NodeTestResult | null>> {
  const testEndpoint = await resolveTestEndpoint(deps.testEndpoints ?? null);
  const start = Date.now();

  const engineResults = await proxyProbeManyWithEngine(
    nodes.map((node) => ({ config: probeConfigOf(node), secret: opts.secretFor(node.id) })),
    {
      testUrl: testEndpoint.url,
      preferred: deps.proxyEnginePreference ? deps.proxyEnginePreference() : 'auto',
      onGroupStart: opts.onGroupStart,
      onResult: opts.onResult
        ? (index, result) => opts.onResult!(index, nodeResultFromEngineProbe(nodes[index]!, start, result, testEndpoint.url))
        : undefined,
      shouldStop: opts.shouldStop,
    },
  );

  return engineResults.map((result, index) =>
    result ? nodeResultFromEngineProbe(nodes[index]!, start, result, testEndpoint.url) : null,
  );
}

  // ---- one bounded retry for transient stalls ----
  // The ISP stalls a single port intermittently (RAW_PATH_IR_ISP: :443 answered
  // at 13:07Z and gave no answer at 13:15Z while :2053/:2087/:8443 answered), so
  // a probe that timed out once must not be recorded as a dead node. Only

  // pre-flight refusal cannot change inside one run — retrying those would only
  // double the scan. The retry pass opens NO rows (onGroupStart is omitted):
  // the caller already opened one per node on the first pass.
  const retryIndexes = engineResults
    .map((result, index) => (result && isTransientProbeFailure(result.failureKind) ? index : -1))
    .filter((index) => index >= 0);

  if (retryIndexes.length > 0 && !opts.shouldStop?.()) {
    const retried = await proxyProbeManyWithEngine(
      retryIndexes.map((index) => ({ config: probeConfigOf(nodes[index]!), secret: opts.secretFor(nodes[index]!.id) })),
      {
        testUrl: testEndpoint.url,
        preferred: deps.proxyEnginePreference ? deps.proxyEnginePreference() : 'auto',
        shouldStop: opts.shouldStop,
      },
    );
    // An upgrade only: if the retry also failed, the FIRST failure stands (it
    // describes the node rather than whatever the retry pass ran into).
    retryIndexes.forEach((index, attempt) => {
      const result = retried[attempt];
      if (result && result.status === 'done') engineResults[index] = result;
    });
  }

## Phase 1 — Select the appropriate payment architecture

Investigate Telegram Stars as the first candidate because NetPulse sells digital access through a Telegram bot.

Read the current official documentation:

- https://core.telegram.org/bots/payments-stars
- https://core.telegram.org/bots/api#payments
- https://telegram.org/tos/bot-developers

Confirm the currently applicable payment requirements before implementation.

For a Telegram bot checkout selling digital VPN subscriptions, investigate and implement the documented `XTR` payment flow rather than inventing a third-party-provider flow that the platform does not permit.

Before enabling live payments, investigate and report:

- Whether Stars purchase is practically available to the intended customers, including the target Iranian user base.
- Whether the bot owner can receive, withdraw, and redeem proceeds under the owner's actual account and regional circumstances.
- Applicable Telegram terms and restrictions.
- Price denomination and conversion policy.
- Refund handling.
- Support and dispute procedures.
- Whether recurring Stars subscriptions are supported by the current API and suitable for this product.

Do not assume that successful sandbox payment tests prove real-world customer availability or payout eligibility.

If Stars is unsuitable, research compatible alternatives for checkout outside Telegram and explain the platform-policy and customer-experience implications before enabling an alternative inside the bot.

## Phase 2 — Implement the real Stars payment lifecycle in Abystral

Inspect the existing commerce implementation, 66 migrations, double-entry ledger, wallet logic, subscription records, and Telegram handlers before changing the schema.

Reuse the existing ledger and stable transaction IDs. Do not create duplicate accounting authorities.

Implement or complete the real payment lifecycle:

1. A user selects a valid NetPulse subscription plan.
2. Abystral creates a unique order linked to the Telegram user and the correct NetPulse account.
3. The bot generates a Stars invoice using currency `XTR`.
4. The invoice amount is fixed to the recorded order price.
5. The bot processes `pre_checkout_query` within Telegram's deadline and validates the order, amount, currency, user, and current purchasability.
6. The bot activates no entitlements at pre-checkout.
7. Only a verified `successful_payment` event confirms payment.
8. The payment is recorded once in the existing ledger.
9. Duplicate or replayed events are rejected or treated idempotently.
10. The subscription is activated or extended exactly once.
11. Provisioning is queued through the existing durable mechanism.
12. The user receives a receipt and accurate subscription status.

Store and reconcile Telegram's payment identifiers, including `telegram_payment_charge_id`, as appropriate for the existing schema and refund process.

Use the current official Bot API definitions rather than relying on remembered field names or old examples.

### Important accounting requirements

- Store Stars amounts as integer quantities.
- Record the `XTR` denomination unambiguously.
- Do not treat Stars as fiat currency or silently mix them with wallet balances denominated in another currency.
- Keep order, payment, ledger, subscription, and provisioning state consistent.
- Make transaction processing idempotent.
- Handle concurrent checkouts safely.
- Do not allow duplicate callbacks to double-credit a wallet or extend a subscription twice.
- Preserve an audit trail.
- Do not mark a purchase paid merely because the user returns to a successful-looking screen.
- Never grant VPN access solely on a `pre_checkout_query`.

Use the dedicated Telegram payment test environment for development. Add tests for success, cancellation, invalid amount, wrong user, duplicate events, malformed events, concurrent orders, provisioning failure, retry, expiry, and refunds where supported.

## Phase 3 — Integrate payment confirmation with the existing NetPulse control plane

After a verified payment, use the existing Abystral and NetPulse entitlement contract.

Trace the actual event format and the sign/verification logic. Do not invent a second webhook contract if one already exists.

Verify that:

- The confirmed payment activates exactly the expected plan.
- The Worker accepts only authenticated, authorized, valid events.
- Duplicate signed events cannot duplicate entitlements.
- A failed provisioning attempt does not erase a valid paid order.
- A retry cannot activate the subscription twice.
- A cancellation, expiration, or refund follows the actual business rules.
- The VPS reconciler receives only valid entitlements.
- The user's account identity maps consistently across Telegram, Abystral, NetPulse, and the VPN configuration.
- WHITEDNS access matches the plan.
- Unauthorized users cannot retrieve another account's invoice, VPN configuration, or subscription status.

Keep payment truth in the commerce authority and entitlement enforcement in the existing NetPulse architecture.

Do not place private payment credentials or VPN secrets in public D1 records, payment events, or routine logs.

Do not enable production payments solely because sandbox tests pass.

Prepare a clear go/no-go report that distinguishes:

- Code complete.
- Sandbox integration passed.

--- migration ---
-- Migration 0067: Telegram Stars (XTR) payments.
--
-- WHY: the bot sells digital goods (VPN subscriptions) INSIDE Telegram, so the
-- Bot Platform Developer Terms (§6.2) require those sales to be carried out
-- exclusively in Telegram Stars (currency tag `XTR`). Before this migration
-- there was no Stars order, no invoice/`pre_checkout_query` validation, and no
-- way to record a `successful_payment` — the only payment paths were wallet
-- deposits (TON / card / c2c), which are OUT-OF-BAND transfers, not in-app
-- purchases.
--
-- The design keeps Stars OUT of the USD wallet ledger on purpose:
--   * Stars are an integer quantity (`amount_xtr`), never fiat; the denomination
--     is pinned by a CHECK constraint so a row can never be silently relabelled.
--   * An order is a distinct business object with its OWN price snapshot
--     (`usd_cents` + `xtr_usd_rate`) taken when the order was created — the
--     invoice amount is fixed to the recorded order, never recomputed at
--     payment time.
--   * `telegram_payment_charge_id` is the exactly-once key: a partial UNIQUE
--     index makes a replayed `successful_payment` unable to create a second
--     record, and the paid-claim UPDATE is guarded on it being NULL.
--
-- Money movement is booked once, in the existing double-entry ledger, as a
-- direct sale (Dr cash / Cr deferred revenue) with the raw XTR amount and the
-- exact rate in `rate_snapshot`. Nothing here credits a wallet balance.

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS xtr_orders (
  id                          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  -- Opaque order id. Carried as the invoice payload, so it is the ONLY handle
  -- the Bot API gives back to us on pre_checkout/successful_payment.
  order_ref                   TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  user_id                     INTEGER NOT NULL,          -- users.id (bot customer)
  telegram_id                 INTEGER NOT NULL,          -- buyer Telegram id (checked at pre-checkout)
  plan_code                   TEXT NOT NULL,
  plan_name                   TEXT NOT NULL,             -- snapshot for receipts/history
  amount_xtr                  INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (amount_xtr > 0),
  currency                    TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'XTR' CHECK (currency = 'XTR'),
  usd_cents                   INTEGER NOT NULL,          -- plan price (USD cents) at order time
  xtr_usd_rate                REAL NOT NULL,             -- USD value of one Star, recorded verbatim
  status                      TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'created'
    CHECK (status IN ('created','invoiced','paid','refunded','cancelled','expired')),
  invoice_message_id          INTEGER,
  subscription_id             INTEGER,                   -- subscriptions.id once provisioned
  panel_email                 TEXT,                      -- panel identity of the provisioned client
  telegram_payment_charge_id  TEXT,                      -- Telegram's charge id (refund handle)
  provider_payment_charge_id  TEXT,                      -- kept for parity with the Bot API object
  netpulse_account_id         TEXT,                      -- linked NetPulse account at order time (nullable)
  created_at                  TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now')),
  updated_at                  TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now')),
  invoiced_at                 TEXT,
  paid_at                     TEXT,
  refunded_at                 TEXT,
  expires_at                  TEXT NOT NULL              -- unpaid orders stop being payable
);

-- Exactly-once at the database level: one charge id can belong to one order.
-- A replayed `successful_payment` (Telegram redelivers until it gets a 200)
-- therefore cannot be recorded twice even if application guards were bypassed.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_xtr_orders_charge
  ON xtr_orders(telegram_payment_charge_id)
  WHERE telegram_payment_charge_id IS NOT NULL;

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_xtr_orders_user   ON xtr_orders(user_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_xtr_orders_status ON xtr_orders(status, expires_at);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_xtr_orders_sub    ON xtr_orders(subscription_id);

-- Refund audit trail. refundStarPayment is all-or-nothing (no partial refunds),
-- so the row records the full Stars amount plus WHO issued it.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS xtr_refunds (
  id                         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  order_ref                  TEXT NOT NULL,
  telegram_payment_charge_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  amount_xtr                 INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (amount_xtr > 0),
  currency                   TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'XTR' CHECK (currency = 'XTR'),
  actor                      TEXT NOT NULL,              -- admin telegram id / 'system'
  status                     TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'refunded'
    CHECK (status IN ('refunded','failed')),
  created_at                 TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (datetime('now'))
);

-- A charge is refunded at most once.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_xtr_refunds_charge ON xtr_refunds(telegram_payment_charge_id);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_xtr_refunds_order ON xtr_refunds(order_ref);
