## Bottom line

**Stars can be a workable way to accept payment inside a Telegram bot, but it is not safe to assume that Iranian users can always top up, or that a bot owner in Iran can always redeem earnings.** Telegram’s published terms do not give a clear Iran-specific allow/deny rule. They do explicitly allow for purchase, service, and Fragment restrictions in some regions or for some users—and say Telegram may provide no compensation if those restrictions prevent use or payout.

The key distinction is:

- **A customer’s personal Stars balance is for spending inside Telegram.** Purchased Stars cannot be sold or withdrawn.
- **Stars earned by a bot or creator may qualify for rewards** through Fragment, subject to the waiting period, account access, Fragment availability, and applicable rules. The Bot API itself has no cash-out method.

So: accepting Stars and redeeming them are separate practical questions. For an Iranian operator, I would treat redemption as **unconfirmed until tested with the actual Telegram account that owns the bot and the intended Fragment/wallet setup**.

## Iran: what is documented, and what is not

### Documented Telegram rules

- Telegram says users can obtain Stars via Apple/Google in-app purchases and, depending on client, via @PremiumBot, Telegram Web, and Desktop. It also reserves the right to apply restrictions in particular jurisdictions or to subsets of users, including restrictions that prevent buying or using Stars already purchased. [Stars Terms](https://telegram.org/tos/stars)
- For bots and Mini Apps, digital goods and services inside Telegram must be paid for exclusively in Stars (`XTR`); the official payments guide says no third-party processor or other currency for those in-app digital sales. [Bot Payments guide](https://core.telegram.org/bots/payments-stars.md) · [Developer Terms, §6.2](https://telegram.org/tos/bot-developers#6-2-digital-goods-and-services)
- Telegram’s Developer Terms say Fragment may be unable to issue rewards to certain users or in certain countries for regulatory or other reasons. They also warn that governments, ISPs, or other authorities may prevent access to Telegram, Stars, or Fragment. Telegram disclaims liability and does not promise an alternative reward or compensation if this happens. [Developer Terms, §6.2.4.1](https://telegram.org/tos/bot-developers#6-2-4-1-receiving-rewards)
- Fragment’s own terms say it may limit countries or particular services, and that it facilitates Star rewards subject to its own discretion and applicable regulatory conditions. [Fragment Terms](https://fragment.com/terms)

**I did not find a published official country list or a rule saying that all Iranian residents, Iranian-number accounts, or accounts in a named neighboring country are categorically eligible or ineligible for Star rewards.** Nor did I find an official rule saying that changing an account’s apparent region, using a different phone number, or being able to access Telegram guarantees Fragment payout. The terms leave room for user-, country-, and service-specific restrictions.

### Reports and anecdotal evidence—not policy

Telegram’s public bug-tracking site contains a user report about restrictions affecting Iranian-number accounts. Another user-authored report asserts that purchasing Premium through Fragment was straightforward for Iranians. Those reports are **not a published Telegram eligibility policy**, and Premium purchase is not the same transaction as withdrawing bot-earned Stars. [Iranian-account report](https://bugs.telegram.org/c/44987)

There are also user reports of difficulty buying Stars, but the public issue tracker is not evidence of an Iran-wide payment rule. For example, the issue titled “I can’t buy stars” records an individual problem, not a Telegram statement that Iranian accounts are barred. [Stars purchase report](https://bugs.telegram.org/c/62421)

**Practical read:** Iranian buyers may be able to use a bot and may have Stars already, but topping up through an app store or other supported purchase rail could be the limiting step. Current access to Telegram from inside Iran is also distinct from Telegram’s own payment eligibility; I did not verify present-day on-the-ground network access from a current authoritative source. Telegram’s terms themselves warn that governments or ISPs can block access.

## Can an Iranian bot owner withdraw earned Stars?

The documented reward path is **Telegram bot balance → Fragment → cryptocurrency reward to a connected wallet**, not a payout to a bank account through the Bot API.

- Telegram’s Developer Terms say bot-earned Stars are displayed in a balance accessible from the Telegram account that owns the bot. The Stars are not the developer’s property in the ordinary sense; the allowed uses include Telegram Ads and accepting rewards.
- Telegram sets the reward value at **$0.013 per Star** under the current Developer Terms. That is a reward valuation, not the price customers paid to acquire Stars, and Telegram reserves the right to change it.
- Stars may take **up to 21 days** after receipt to become available for rewards or advertising. Earned Stars expire after **three years** if not used for ads or accepted as rewards. [Developer Terms, §§6.2.2–6.2.4 and 6.2.7](https://telegram.org/tos/bot-developers)
- Fragment’s terms say bot developers and creators who received Stars may use the platform to obtain cryptocurrency based on their Star balance. Fragment determines the cryptocurrency issued and may remove access to Star rewards for regulatory or other reasons. It requires connecting a Telegram account and a TON wallet. [Fragment Terms, §6](https://fragment.com/terms)
- Neither the Bot API nor the Terms promise a fixed fiat payout, a bank transfer, or a specific cryptocurrency for all users. An older Telegram launch announcement described withdrawals in Toncoin via Fragment, but Fragment’s current terms give it discretion over the reward currency. [Telegram’s 2024 Stars announcement](https://telegram.org/blog/telegram-stars) · [Fragment Terms](https://fragment.com/terms)

**Iran-specific conclusion:** I cannot verify that an owner who resides in Iran, or whose bot-owning account is Iranian, can reliably withdraw Star rewards through Fragment. Telegram’s terms expressly permit country/user restrictions, but I found no official public list resolving Iran or nearby countries. Access to Fragment, eligibility of the Telegram account, wallet setup, local law, and the actual withdrawal option shown to the owner all matter. A neighboring-country account or wallet should not be treated as a documented workaround or guarantee.

As a secondary, non-official reference, one current third-party guide reports a **1,000-Star minimum withdrawal** and a maximum of 25 million Stars. I did **not** verify those thresholds in the official public Bot API or Terms pages I fetched; verify the amount shown in Telegram/Fragment for the owner account before relying on it. [Independent guide—threshold claim, not official policy](https://adminhub.tools/blog/withdraw-telegram-stars/)

## Current Bot API facts

### Native Stars test environment

Telegram documents a dedicated test environment for bot payments and says Stars payments can be tested there. The test environment is separate from production; you need a separate test account and bot. The official test Bot API request format is:

```text
https://api.telegram.org/bot<TOKEN>/test/METHOD_NAME
```

Telegram’s test-environment instructions give the in-app route to log into a test account and say to create a new bot with @BotFather in that environment. Since the environment is separate, do not treat a successful test payment as production revenue or assume it can be redeemed. [Telegram test-environment instructions](https://core.telegram.org/bug-bounty#test-environment) · [Stars payment testing instructions](https://core.telegram.org/bots/payments-stars.md)

### One-time digital invoices versus recurring subscriptions

For a **one-time digital sale**, use `sendInvoice` or `createInvoiceLink` with:

- `currency: "XTR"`
- an empty `provider_token`
- exactly one `prices` item for a Stars invoice
- no `subscription_period`

`sendInvoice` sends the invoice; `createInvoiceLink` creates an invoice link. Telegram’s rules require Stars for digital goods and services sold inside Telegram apps. [sendInvoice](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api/methods/sendinvoice.md) · [createInvoiceLink](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api/methods/createinvoicelink.md) · [Bot Payments guide](https://core.telegram.org/bots/payments-stars.md)

A **recurring bot subscription** is different: the current `createInvoiceLink` docs allow `subscription_period`, but it must be `2592000` seconds (30 days), use `XTR`, and the subscription price must not exceed 10,000 Stars. Omitting `subscription_period` makes it a one-time invoice rather than a recurring subscription. The subscription documentation describes automatic monthly debits from the user’s Star balance. [createInvoiceLink](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api/methods/createinvoicelink.md) · [Star subscriptions](https://core.telegram.org/api/subscriptions)

The Bot API also documents `editUserStarSubscription` for the bot to cancel or re-enable extension of a user’s Stars subscription, and `BotSubscriptionUpdated` updates for subscription state changes. [editUserStarSubscription](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api/methods/edituserstarsubscription.md) · [BotSubscriptionUpdated](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api/types/botsubscriptionupdated.md)

### Checkout, delivery, and refunds

The normal payment flow is: send invoice → receive `pre_checkout_query` → answer it → wait for `successful_payment` → deliver the product. Telegram requires an answer to pre-checkout within **10 seconds**; a successful pre-checkout answer alone does not prove payment succeeded. Save the payment’s `telegram_payment_charge_id` for support and possible refunds. [answerPreCheckoutQuery](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api/methods/answerprecheckoutquery.md) · [Bot Payments guide](https://core.telegram.org/bots/payments-stars.md)

A bot refunds a Stars payment with `refundStarPayment`, using the buyer’s `user_id` and the `telegram_payment_charge_id`. Telegram’s guide says bots should handle `/paysupport` requests; the Developer Terms make the seller responsible for resolving legitimate disputes. This is different from refunding a customer’s original purchase of Stars from Apple, Google, or another payment rail, which Telegram’s Stars Terms generally treat as final. [refundStarPayment](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api/methods/refundstarpayment.md) · [Stars Terms](https://telegram.org/tos/stars) · [Developer Terms](https://telegram.org/tos/bot-developers)

### Payout and balance API

The Bot API provides `getMyStarBalance` and `getStarTransactions` to inspect the bot’s Stars balance and transaction history. It provides **no Bot API withdrawal or payout method**. Withdrawal/reward acceptance happens through Fragment, subject to its terms and availability. [getMyStarBalance](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api/methods/getmystarbalance.md) · [getStarTransactions](https://core.telegram.org/bots/api/methods/getstartransactions.md) · [Fragment Terms](https://fragment.com/terms)

## Practical recommendation

Before building a business model around cashing out from Iran, verify the complete path with the **actual Telegram account that owns the bot**: can it see the earned-Star reward/withdraw option, can it authenticate with Fragment, can it connect the intended wallet, and can it complete the reward flow under the owner’s real location and applicable rules? Do not rely on test Stars, a user’s ability to buy Premium, or an anecdotal report as proof of payout eligibility. Telegram assigns local-law compliance responsibility to the developer; this is not a legal determination about Iranian sanctions or crypto rules.

Use the existing DPI research documents first. Update them as new evidence is gathered.

Priority research sources include:

- [PattNG](https://github.com/patterniha/PattNG)
- [V2RayNG](https://github.com/2dust/v2rayNG)
- [IRBlock — USENIX Security 2025](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity25/presentation/tai)
- [I(ra)nconsistencies — FOCI 2025](https://www.petsymposium.org/foci/2025/foci-2025-0002.php)
- [FOCI research on automated DNS censorship circumvention](https://www.petsymposium.org/)
- [OONI Explorer](https://explorer.ooni.org/)
- [OONI measurement interpretation](https://ooni.org/support/interpreting-ooni-data/)
- [Xray-core](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core)
- [sing-box](https://github.com/SagerNet/sing-box)
- [AmneziaVPN](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amnezia-client)
- [AmneziaWG](https://github.com/amnezia-vpn/amneziawg)
- [Psiphon Tunnel Core](https://github.com/Psiphon-Inc/psiphon-tunnel-core)
- [Tor anti-censorship projects](https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/anti-censorship/)

Search for at least 30 distinct, credible technical sources overall. Include relevant Iranian censorship research and actively maintained implementations. Record the search methodology and the actual sources examined.

Do not force irrelevant sources into a numerical quota. If a target category does not have sufficient credible sources, explain the gap and supplement it with directly relevant technical reports and general-purpose protocol research.

For each significant source, collect:

- Canonical URL.
- Title and publisher.
- Publication date or examined commit.
- Relevant sections or files.
- What the source actually supports.
- Limitations.
- License.
- Possible application to NetPulse.
- Confidence and evidence status.

## Research questions

Investigate documented filtering and connectivity problems involving:

- DNS manipulation and response inconsistency.
- TLS handshake behavior and client compatibility.
- SNI and ECH support and limitations.
- Protocol identification and transport disruption.
- TCP and UDP connectivity.
- QUIC and HTTP/3 availability.
- Server-side configuration and certificate errors.
- DNS bootstrap and resolver failure.
- VPN client and server version mismatches.
- CDN and reverse-proxy deployment compatibility.
- Network-specific differences.
- Client-side reconnection and adaptive selection.
- WHITEDNS behavior under difficult network conditions.
- Established circumvention tools and operational failure modes.

Do not assume an unusual SNI or TLS fingerprint is inherently better. Verify actual client/server compatibility, legitimate endpoint use, certificate behavior, and measured outcomes.

Use published observations and authorized test environments to characterize filtering. Do not attack, disrupt, or stress unrelated public systems.

Update the research corpus continuously, and turn promising findings into reproducible engineering experiments.

---

# 6. DISCOVER, TEST, AND CONNECT THROUGH REAL METHODS

This section is central to the mission.

Do not merely search for possible VPN methods and list them. Determine which methods are implementable and then connect through the best verified candidate using the real NetPulse client and an authorized server.

## Build the candidate registry

For each candidate, record:

- Protocol or method.
- Source and implementation.
- Required client support.
- Required server support.
- Endpoint ownership or authorization.
- Configuration requirements.
- Credential requirements.
- Security and privacy properties.
- Current compatibility.
- Test status.
- Previous success and failure results.
- Deployment complexity.
- Subscription requirements.
- Rollback procedure.

Only approved, compatible methods may become active strategies.

## Find, validate, and deploy candidates

For each promising candidate:

1. Read the original documentation and relevant implementation.
2. Verify the license and security history.
3. Establish which client and server versions support it.
4. Determine whether it can be deployed through the authorized NetPulse infrastructure.
5. Establish a baseline.
6. Configure or implement the candidate in an isolated environment.
7. Validate certificates, endpoint identity, configuration schema, and routing.
8. Run a controlled connection test.
9. Verify real traffic through the intended path.
10. Measure connection time, stability, throughput, DNS behavior, and recovery.
11. Compare the result against the baseline.
12. Record the decision and evidence.

Where a promising technique requires a new server profile, deploy it to the authorized test infrastructure using a reversible, restricted provisioning method.

Do not activate arbitrary Internet configurations merely because they were discovered in search results.

Do not use stolen subscription links, leaked keys, unknown private credentials, or unrelated third-party endpoints without authorization.

If a public project offers legitimate, documented connection capabilities, evaluate them according to the project's terms and actual compatibility.

If a candidate cannot be used safely or legitimately, explain why and continue with the next one.

## Actual connection requirement

For the strongest viable candidate, use a real supported NetPulse client and an authorized VPN endpoint to establish a connection.

Prove that:

- The client accepts the intended configuration.
- The connection genuinely establishes.
- The tunnel forwards external traffic.
- The observed egress path matches expectations.
- DNS follows the intended policy.
- Leak tests have been performed.
- Traffic counters change appropriately.
- Disconnect/reconnect works.
- The client remains protected during connection failure, according to its configured policy.
- Credential and subscription enforcement remain intact.

Record a sanitized connection trace and test report.

If you discover multiple viable methods, test and rank them using the same methodology. Connect through the highest-ranked method that is actually available and verified.

If no candidate works, diagnose the evidence and document the precise failure rather than fabricating a successful connection.

---

# 7. BUILD AND INTEGRATE THE ADAPTIVE AI

Implement a real lightweight AI component in the NetPulse system.

Begin with an interpretable strategy-selection policy and a small statistical learning mechanism. Introduce a more complex model only if it demonstrably improves performance.

The local intelligence engine must remain useful when external AI services are unavailable.

It should learn from relevant observations, including:

- Connection success and failure.
- Verified traffic forwarding.
- Connection-establishment latency.
- Packet loss and throughput.
- DNS resolution outcomes.
- Transport and server health.
- Compatibility.
- Reconnection success.
- Failure classification.

Use privacy-preserving local observations wherever practical.

The AI should:

- Select among verified compatible strategies.
- Explain its decisions.
- Maintain confidence estimates.
- Avoid repeated known failures.
- Adapt to changing conditions.
- Use bounded retries and backoff.
- Distinguish a tunnel failure from DNS, authentication, subscription, or server problems.
- Fall back safely when evidence is weak.
- Preserve user privacy.
- Keep active configuration versions traceable.

A separate research agent can propose improvements and test new candidates. A reviewed update process must determine whether a new strategy is safe and effective.

Never permit the model to execute arbitrary generated shell commands, disable security controls, change access permissions, expose secrets, or apply unverified Internet configurations.

The production AI may choose among approved strategies; it may not override payment, authentication, entitlement, or revocation rules.

# 8. VPN, WHITEDNS, AND VPS INTEGRATION

Inspect the existing live implementation before writing a replacement.

Verify the actual VPS, active services, deployed VPN software, server configuration, DNS integration, credential management, and reconciliation behavior.

Use existing authorized deployment access and configured secrets.

Implement any missing functions needed for:

- Provisioning VPN identities.
- Delivering valid client configurations.
- Verifying connection status.
- Routing traffic through the actual tunnel.
- Integrating the intended DNS configuration.
- Rotating credentials where supported.
- Revoking access.
- Enforcing expiration.
- Reconciling desired and actual server state.
- Recovering from temporary Worker or VPS communication failures.
- Reporting safe diagnostic information.

Reuse the existing working implementation whenever practical.

Keep the VPS management interface restricted. Use authenticated, structured provisioning jobs rather than an unrestricted remote-shell endpoint.

## WHITEDNS validation

Inspect the actual WHITEDNS repository and intended functionality.

Verify:

- DNS configuration generation.
- Resolver reachability.
- DNS behavior through the VPN.
- IPv4 and IPv6 behavior.
- DNS leakage.
- Resolver failure and fallback.
- Plan-specific DNS entitlements.
- Provisioning and revocation.
- Client configuration consistency.
- Reconciliation after service failure.

Treat WHITEDNS as part of the complete VPN architecture rather than a disconnected service.

# 9. SUBSCRIPTIONS, ACCOUNTING, AND TELEGRAM

Use the previously reported architecture as the baseline, but verify the current code and actual records.

The reported design uses Abystral for Telegram commerce and accounting, with NetPulse mirroring subscription entitlements and the VPS pulling authorized VPN identities.

Investigate the current payment-provider status. Previous reports said that no actual payment provider had been integrated and that Telegram Stars required further implementation and validation.

Complete all code-side and testable work.

The full paid-customer lifecycle should include:

1. User opens the Telegram bot.
2. User selects an existing plan.
3. The correct price and currency are displayed.
4. A unique order is created.
5. The configured payment provider or supported Telegram payment flow is used.
6. The payment is authoritatively verified.
7. The ledger is updated exactly once.
8. The subscription is activated exactly once.
9. The entitlement reaches NetPulse.
10. The VPS provisions the correct VPN access.
11. WHITEDNS access matches the plan.
12. The client receives a valid configuration.
13. The VPN connection is verified.
14. Expiry or revocation removes the proper entitlements.

Use sandbox payment tests for automated workflows.

Do not invent a provider, fake a successful payment, or treat a UI redirect as payment confirmation. If merchant eligibility, live credentials, payout access, or owner action is missing, finish everything else and mark that dependency `BLOCKED`.

Never expose payment secrets, private keys, or other users' configurations.

# 10. AGGRESSIVE, CONTROLLED CONNECTIVITY AND SECURITY TESTING

Use owned infrastructure, authorized VPS systems, staging, supported client builds, synthetic network conditions, and approved test endpoints.

Investigate difficult conditions such as:

- DNS timeout or inconsistency.
- TCP connection failure.
- UDP or QUIC unavailability.
- High latency and packet loss.
- Server restart.
- Temporary DNS resolver outage.
- API unavailability.
- Client disconnect/reconnect.
- Incorrect configuration.
- Invalid credentials.
- Expired entitlement.
- Duplicate provisioning events.
- Partial payment-to-provisioning failure.
- Unsupported transport profiles.

Run bounded load and resilience tests. Set explicit limits for duration, concurrency, resource use, request volume, and failure rates. Stop tests if they degrade unrelated workloads or exceed configured resource thresholds.

Do not perform unbounded public-network probing, brute-force login attempts, destructive production tests, or unauthorized attacks against censorship infrastructure.

A failed connection does not automatically establish that DPI caused the failure. Identify competing explanations and explain confidence.

# 11. PROFESSIONAL VISUAL DESIGN AND ANIMATIONS

The mission-control interface must be genuinely useful and visually impressive.

Create a premium engineering dashboard with smooth animations that make the system understandable at a glance.

Include:

- Animated mission progress timeline.
- Real agent and workstream status.
- Research discoveries and source links.
- A visual network path from client to VPN server and external test destination.
- Protocol comparison charts.
- DNS health and leak-test results.
- Connection latency and throughput charts.
- Success/failure timelines.
- Provisioning and subscription state transitions.
- Test-run details and logs.
- A final report browser.
- Clear error and blocker panels.
- Copyable sanitized diagnostics.
- Responsive layouts.
- Persian RTL support where appropriate.
- Reduced-motion support.

Animate real state transitions, not fake progress. Do not display false values just to make the dashboard look active.

The user should be able to select a completed test and inspect the actual evidence behind its result.

If the dashboard has buttons for retrying a test, inspecting a source, or running a validation, wire them to real, authorized operations. Do not add inert decorative controls or unrestricted server-management actions.

# 12. MULTI-AGENT EXECUTION AND PERSISTENCE

Use supported Hermes subagents to work concurrently when available.

Recommended workstreams:

1. Research and source investigation.
2. VPN and connection-method evaluation.
3. Adaptive AI implementation.
4. VPS and WHITEDNS integration.
5. Telegram, accounting, and subscription testing.
6. Dashboard and report generation.
7. Integration, security review, and final verification.

A lead agent must coordinate architecture and integration. Assign file or component ownership to reduce conflicts.

Use a shared task ledger with dependencies, owners, test evidence, and completion state.

Preserve user changes and use isolated branches or worktrees where practical. Do not let two agents blindly overwrite shared files or modify production simultaneously.

At every major milestone, integrate the changes and run the combined tests.

If the runtime supports persistent missions, scheduled execution, or automatic continuation, use those features to resume incomplete work. If execution terminates, save state and resume through the supported mechanism. Do not claim that the agent will run indefinitely after the platform stops it.

---

# 13. PRODUCTION DEPLOYMENT POLICY

Deploy working, tested changes through the established release process.

Before deployment:

- Verify current environment and deployment target.
- Inspect the changed-file diff.
- Run relevant tests and builds.
- Confirm required secrets are configured without revealing them.
- Verify migration safety.
- Prepare appropriate backups and rollback.
- Test in staging where practical.

After deployment:

- Verify the expected revision is actually running.
- Run health and smoke tests.
- Verify the real VPN connection path.
- Check sanitized logs.
- Confirm reconciliation and subscription enforcement.
- Revert a release if it causes an unacceptable critical regression.

Do not make destructive database changes, remove customer records, overwrite critical DNS/firewall settings, or interrupt unrelated services without a reviewed recovery plan.

The goal is to make the product operational, not to maximize the number of deployments.

# 14. FINAL REPORT: A COMPLETE INVESTIGATION RECORD

Generate a detailed final report with a human-readable executive summary and a technical appendix.

Save the report in the existing project report structure, adapting to established naming conventions.

Provide Markdown and, where feasible, a polished HTML report that can be opened locally or viewed in Mission Control. A machine-readable JSON summary should be available for automation.

Include the following sections.

## A. Executive summary

Explain:

- What was inspected.
- What was discovered.
- What was implemented.
- What was successfully tested.
- Which method or methods worked.
- Whether an actual VPN connection succeeded.
- How the application performed.
- Which blockers remain.
- What should happen next.

## B. System inventory

List every relevant repository, service, deployment, database, and subsystem inspected.

Clearly distinguish current verified state from historical claims.

## C. Research bibliography

For every significant source, include:

- Title.
- Canonical URL.
- Date or version examined.
- Relevant technical findings.
- Evidence and limitations.
- Implementation relevance.
- License considerations where applicable.

Include links to the actual source code, paper, experiment, or measurement.

## D. Candidate methods

For every candidate evaluated, provide:

- Method and supported implementation.
- Source.
- Client/server compatibility.
- Endpoint authorization status.
- Configuration requirements.
- Test environment.
- Test timestamp.
- Result.
- Failure reason, if applicable.
- Performance measurements.
- Security and privacy limitations.
- Recommendation.

Do not omit failed tests. Failed attempts are valuable evidence.

## E. Real connectivity evidence

Document:

- Which client was used.
- Which server and protocol were used.
- Where the test was performed.
- Whether the tunnel was established.
- Whether external traffic actually passed through it.
- Observed egress verification.
- DNS and leak-test outcomes.
- Connection latency and throughput.
- Reconnection behavior.
- Subscription and credential enforcement.
- Relevant sanitized logs.

Distinguish laboratory or VPS results from results obtained on an actual Iranian ISP. Never claim a method works on an Iranian network unless that environment was actually tested.

## F. Implementation details

List:

- Files changed.
- Features implemented.
- Database migrations.
- New services or integrations.
- AI selection logic.
- Changes to the connection manager.
- WHITEDNS integration.
- Dashboard and animation work.
- API contract changes.
- Deployment revisions.
- Test commands and results.

## G. Security and operational assessment

Document:

- Known vulnerabilities and mitigations.
- Secret handling.
- Authentication and authorization.
- Routing and DNS leak observations.
- Update authenticity.
- Third-party dependency risks.
- Failure recovery.
- Rollback instructions.
- Known operational risks.

## H. Final acceptance matrix

For every objective, use exactly one status:

- `PASS` — demonstrated with appropriate evidence.
- `FAIL` — tested and unsuccessful.
- `BLOCKED` — an explicit external dependency or permission is missing.
- `NOT TESTED` — no valid test evidence exists.

Attach evidence links to all critical `PASS` claims.

## I. Unfinished tasks and next actions

Rank remaining tasks by:

- Severity.
- User impact.
- Expected improvement.
- Confidence.
- Engineering effort.
- External dependency.
- Deployment risk.

Do not hide blockers behind vague language such as “almost complete.”

{"kind":"tool","id":"g2XWcOYHpKg","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":"apps/web/src/features/vpn/QuickConnectActivity.tsx","instructions":"Show authentic per-run adaptive VPN connection events as a live animated timeline.","content":"import { Activity, Check, Circle, Loader2, Radio, ShieldCheck, X } from 'lucide-react';
import { useEffect, useMemo, useState } from 'react';

import { subscribeTest } from '@/lib/ws';

interface ActivityEvent {
  type: string;
  stage?: string;
  message?: string;
  at?: number;
  engine?: string;
  node?: string;
  profile?: string;
  done?: number;
  total?: number;
  latencyMs?: number;
  exitIp?: string | null;
  dnsPolicy?: string;
  error?: string | null;
  ok?: boolean;
}

const STAGE_META: Record<string, { label: string; tone: string }> = {
  accepted: { label: 'REQUEST', tone: 'text-muted' },
  preparing: { label: 'INIT', tone: 'text-muted' },
  handoff: { label: 'HANDOFF', tone: 'text-warn' },
  'memory-check': { label: 'MEMORY', tone: 'text-cyan-300' },
  'adaptive-plan': { label: 'POLICY', tone: 'text-violet-300' },
  'adaptive-choice': { label: 'DECISION', tone: 'text-violet-300' },
  'discovery-start': { label: 'SCAN', tone: 'text-cyan-300' },
  'dns-probe': { label: 'PROBE', tone: 'text-cyan-300' },
  'core-start': { label: 'CORE', tone: 'text-sky-300' },
  'core-ready': { label: 'CORE READY', tone: 'text-sky-300' },
  'core-failed': { label: 'CORE FAILED', tone: 'text-red-300' },
  'dns-policy-active': { label: 'DNS POLICY', tone: 'text-cyan-300' },
  'relay-check': { label: 'TUNNEL TEST', tone: 'text-amber-300' },
  'dns-response': { label: 'DNS RESPONSE', tone: 'text-cyan-300' },
  'verification-failed': { label: 'VERIFY FAILED', tone: 'text-red-300' },
  'attempt-failed': { label: 'RETRY', tone: 'text-amber-300' },
  connected: { label: 'VERIFIED', tone: 'text-emerald-300' },
  'route-active': { label: 'ROUTE ACTIVE', tone: 'text-emerald-300' },
  complete: { label: 'COMPLETE', tone: 'text-emerald-300' },
};

function IconForStage({ stage }: { stage: string }) {
  if (stage === 'complete' || stage === 'connected' || stage === 'route-active' || stage === 'core-ready') return <Check size={12} />;
  if (stage.includes('failed') || stage === 'attempt-failed') return <X size={12} />;
  if (stage === 'relay-check' || stage === 'dns-probe' || stage === 'core-start' || stage === 'dns-policy-active') return <Loader2 size={12} className="animate-spin" />;
  return <Circle size={9} />;
}

export function QuickConnectActivity({ activityId, busy }: { activityId: string | null; busy: boolean }) {
  const [events, setEvents] = useState<ActivityEvent[]>([]);
  const [connected, setConnected] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => {
    setEvents([]);
    setConnected(false);
    if (!activityId) return;
    return subscribeTest(`quick-connect:${activityId}`, (msg) => {
      const event = msg as ActivityEvent;
      if (event.type !== 'quick-connect:activity' || !event.stage) return;
      setEvents((previous) => {
        const next = [...previous, event];
        return next.slice(-48);
      });
      if (event.stage === 'complete' || event.stage === 'connected') setConnected(Boolean(event.ok ?? event.stage === 'connected'));
    });
  }, [activityId]);

  const latestProbe = useMemo(() => [...events].reverse().find((event) => event.stage === 'dns-probe'), [events]);
  if (!activityId && events.length === 0) return null;

  const active = busy && !events.some((event) => event.stage === 'complete');
  const latest = events[events.length - 1];
  const title = active ? 'Adaptive agent is working' : connected ? 'Route verified' : events.length ? 'Agent run finished' : 'Connecting to agent stream…';

  return (
    <section aria-live="polite" aria-label="Adaptive connection activity" className="relative overflow-hidden rounded-xl border border-cyan-400/20 bg-[#07121b] shadow-[0_0_34px_rgba(34,211,238,0.07)]">
      {active && <div className="pointer-events-none absolute inset-x-0 top-0 h-px animate-[pulse_1.8s_ease-in-out_infinite] bg-gradient-to-r from-transparent via-cyan-300/80 to-transparent" />}
      <div className="flex items-center justify-between gap-3 border-b border-white/5 px-4 py-3">
        <div className="flex min-w-0 items-center gap-3">
          <div className={`relative grid h-9 w-9 shrink-0 place-items-center rounded-lg border border-cyan-300/20 bg-cyan-300/10 text-cyan-200 ${active ? 'animate-pulse' : ''}`}>
            <Activity size={17} />
            {active && <span className="absolute -right-1 -top-1 h-2.5 w-2.5 rounded-full bg-emerald-400 ring-2 ring-[#07121b]" />}
          </div>
          <div className="min-w-0">
            <h3 className="truncate text-sm font-semibold text-text">{title}</h3>
            <p className="truncate text-[11px] text-faint">{latest?.message ?? 'Waiting for server-side progress events'}</p>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div className="flex shrink-0 items-center gap-1.5 text-[10px] font-medium uppercase tracking-[0.16em] text-cyan-200/80">
          <Radio size={12} className={active ? 'animate-pulse' : ''} />{active ? 'Live' : 'Trace'}
        </div>
      </div>

      <div className="grid gap-3 p-3 sm:grid-cols-[minmax(0,1fr)_160px]">
        <div className="relative max-h-56 space-y-0.5 overflow-y-auto pr-1">
          <div className="absolute bottom-3 left-[5px] top-3 w-px bg-gradient-to-b from-cyan-300/50 via-violet-300/20 to-transparent" />
          {events.map((event, index) => {
            const meta = STAGE_META[event.stage ?? ''] ?? { label: event.stage?.toUpperCase() ?? 'EVENT', tone: 'text-muted' };
            const failed = event.stage?.includes('failed') || event.stage === 'attempt-failed';
            const done = event.stage === 'complete' || event.stage === 'connected' || event.stage === 'route-active' || event.stage === 'core-ready';
            return (
              <div key={`${event.at ?? index}-${index}`} className="relative flex animate-[fade-up_220ms_ease-out_both] gap-2.5 py-1.5" style={{ animationDelay: `${Math.min(index * 22, 180)}ms` }}>
                <span className={`relative z-[1] mt-0.5 grid h-3 w-3 shrink-0 place-items-center rounded-full ${failed ? 'bg-red-400/20 text-red-300' : done ? 'bg-emerald-400/15 text-emerald-300' : 'bg-[#07121b] text-cyan-200'}`}><IconForStage stage={event.stage ?? ''} /></span>
                <span className="min-w-0 flex-1">
                  <span className="flex flex-wrap items-baseline gap-x-2 gap-y-0.5">
                    <span className={`font-mono text-[9px] font-semibold tracking-[0.14em] ${meta.tone}`}>{meta.label}</span>
                    {event.engine && <span className="font-mono text-[10px] text-violet-200/80">{event.engine}</span>}
                    {event.node && <span className="truncate text-[10px] text-faint">{event.node}</span>}
                    {event.at && <time className="ml-auto font-mono text-[9px] text-faint/70">{new Date(event.at).toLocaleTimeString()}</time>}
                  </span>
                  <p className={`break-words text-[11px] leading-relaxed ${failed ? 'text-red-200/90' : 'text-muted'}`}>{event.message}</p>
                  {event.error && <p className="break-words font-mono text-[10px] text-red-200/70">{event.error}</p>}
                </span>
              </div>
            );
          })}
          {active && <div className="relative flex items-center gap-2.5 py-1.5 text-[10px] text-faint"><span className="relative z-[1] h-2.5 w-2.5 rounded-full border border-cyan-300/40 bg-[#07121b]" /><Loader2 size={11} className="animate-spin text-cyan-200/70" /> awaiting next measured milestone</div>}
          {!events.length && <p className="py-5 text-center text-xs text-faint">Connecting to the secure activity stream…</p>}
        </div>

        <aside className="flex flex-col justify-between gap-3 rounded-lg border border-white/5 bg-black/20 p-3">
          <div>
            <p className="mb-2 flex items-center gap-1.5 text-[9px] font-semibold uppercase tracking-[0.16em] text-faint"><ShieldCheck size={11} className="text-cyan-200" /> Route telemetry</p>
            <div className="space-y-2">
              {[
                ['Discovery', latestProbe ? `${latestProbe.done ?? 0}/${latestProbe.total ?? 0} checked` : 'pending'],
                ['Probe depth', latestProbe?.depth ?? 'pending'],
                ['Measured probe', latestProbe?.latencyMs != null ? `${Math.round(latestProbe.latencyMs)} ms` : 'not measured'],
                ['DNS policy', latest?.dnsPolicy === 'tunnel-configured' ? 'core configured' : latest?.dnsPolicy === 'core-default' ? 'core default' : 'pending'],
                ['Verified egress', latest?.exitIp ?? 'not yet observed'],
              ].map(([label, value]) => <div key={label} className="flex items-baseline justify-between gap-2 text-[10px]"><span className="text-faint">{label}</span><span className="max-w-[92px] truncate text-right font-mono text-muted" title={value}>{value}</span></div>)}
            </div>
          </div>
          <p className="border-t border-white/5 pt-2 text-[9px] leading-relaxed text-faint">A green DNS event means the trace hostname resolved during a real tunneled HTTPS request. It does not independently identify the resolver.</p>
        </aside>
      </div>
    </section>
  );
}
"}}

# NETPULSE — PAYMENT COMPLETION & END-TO-END PRODUCTION READINESS

**Mission ID:** `NETPULSE_PAYMENT_AND_FINAL_ACCEPTANCE`

## Context

The latest full-stack acceptance investigation established the following:

- NetPulse Cloudflare Worker and D1 control plane exist.
- Abystral is the Telegram commerce authority.
- Abystral has a working double-entry ledger and idempotency mechanisms.
- The Worker mirrors subscription entitlements.
- The VPS pulls VPN identities through authenticated outbound reconciliation.
- The deployed reconciler has been fixed and verified.
- Multiple VPN protocols have been tested with real traffic.
- Credential revocation and reconciliation failure/recovery have evidence.
- Worker tests: 126/126 passing.
- Reconciler failure/recovery verification: 47/47 on the live host.
- WHITEDNS remains partially verified.
- **Neither the Worker nor Abystral currently implements a real payment provider.**

Do not rebuild components that already work. Use the existing evidence and acceptance report as the baseline. First read `FULL_STACK_ACCEPTANCE_2026-10-27.md`, `RECONCILER_FAILURE_PROOF_2026-10-27.md`, `MISSION_JOURNAL.md`, the saved transcripts, and the current source code.

Preserve all existing changes and verified production behavior.

## Phase 1 — Select the appropriate payment architecture

Investigate Telegram Stars as the first candidate because NetPulse sells digital access through a Telegram bot.

Read the current official documentation:

- https://core.telegram.org/bots/payments-stars
- https://core.telegram.org/bots/api#payments
- https://telegram.org/tos/bot-developers

Confirm the currently applicable payment requirements before implementation.

For a Telegram bot checkout selling digital VPN subscriptions, investigate and implement the documented `XTR` payment flow rather than inventing a third-party-provider flow that the platform does not permit.

Before enabling live payments, investigate and report:

- Whether Stars purchase is practically available to the intended customers, including the target Iranian user base.
- Whether the bot owner can receive, withdraw, and redeem proceeds under the owner's actual account and regional circumstances.
- Applicable Telegram terms and restrictions.
- Price denomination and conversion policy.
- Refund handling.
- Support and dispute procedures.
- Whether recurring Stars subscriptions are supported by the current API and suitable for this product.

Do not assume that successful sandbox payment tests prove real-world customer availability or payout eligibility.

If Stars is unsuitable, research compatible alternatives for checkout outside Telegram and explain the platform-policy and customer-experience implications before enabling an alternative inside the bot.

## Phase 2 — Implement the real Stars payment lifecycle in Abystral

Inspect the existing commerce implementation, 66 migrations, double-entry ledger, wallet logic, subscription records, and Telegram handlers before changing the schema.

Reuse the existing ledger and stable transaction IDs. Do not create duplicate accounting authorities.

Implement or complete the real payment lifecycle:

1. A user selects a valid NetPulse subscription plan.
2. Abystral creates a unique order linked to the Telegram user and the correct NetPulse account.
3. The bot generates a Stars invoice using currency `XTR`.
4. The invoice amount is fixed to the recorded order price.
5. The bot processes `pre_checkout_query` within Telegram's deadline and validates the order, amount, currency, user, and current purchasability.
6. The bot activates no entitlements at pre-checkout.
7. Only a verified `successful_payment` event confirms payment.
8. The payment is recorded once in the existing ledger.
9. Duplicate or replayed events are rejected or treated idempotently.
10. The subscription is activated or extended exactly once.
11. Provisioning is queued through the existing durable mechanism.
12. The user receives a receipt and accurate subscription status.

Store and reconcile Telegram's payment identifiers, including `telegram_payment_charge_id`, as appropriate for the existing schema and refund process.

Use the current official Bot API definitions rather than relying on remembered field names or old examples.

### Important accounting requirements

- Store Stars amounts as integer quantities.
- Record the `XTR` denomination unambiguously.
- Do not treat Stars as fiat currency or silently mix them with wallet balances denominated in another currency.
- Keep order, payment, ledger, subscription, and provisioning state consistent.
- Make transaction processing idempotent.
- Handle concurrent checkouts safely.
- Do not allow duplicate callbacks to double-credit a wallet or extend a subscription twice.
- Preserve an audit trail.
- Do not mark a purchase paid merely because the user returns to a successful-looking screen.
- Never grant VPN access solely on a `pre_checkout_query`.

Use the dedicated Telegram payment test environment for development. Add tests for success, cancellation, invalid amount, wrong user, duplicate events, malformed events, concurrent orders, provisioning failure, retry, expiry, and refunds where supported.

## Phase 3 — Integrate payment confirmation with the existing NetPulse control plane

After a verified payment, use the existing Abystral and NetPulse entitlement contract.

Trace the actual event format and the sign/verification logic. Do not invent a second webhook contract if one already exists.

Verify that:

- The confirmed payment activates exactly the expected plan.
- The Worker accepts only authenticated, authorized, valid events.
- Duplicate signed events cannot duplicate entitlements.
- A failed provisioning attempt does not erase a valid paid order.
- A retry cannot activate the subscription twice.
- A cancellation, expiration, or refund follows the actual business rules.
- The VPS reconciler receives only valid entitlements.
- The user's account identity maps consistently across Telegram, Abystral, NetPulse, and the VPN configuration.
- WHITEDNS access matches the plan.
- Unauthorized users cannot retrieve another account's invoice, VPN configuration, or subscription status.

Keep payment truth in the commerce authority and entitlement enforcement in the existing NetPulse architecture.

Do not place private payment credentials or VPN secrets in public D1 records, payment events, or routine logs.

## Phase 4 — Verify the complete paid-customer workflow

Build a reproducible staging or test-environment run using a dedicated test account.

Demonstrate the following sequence with saved, sanitized evidence:

1. The test user opens the Telegram bot.
2. The user views a valid subscription plan and Stars price.
3. The bot creates the correct invoice.
4. The payment test environment confirms a successful payment.
5. Abystral records exactly one payment and correct ledger effects.
6. The subscription is activated exactly once.
7. The NetPulse Worker accepts the appropriate entitlement event.
8. The VPS provisioner receives the authorized entitlement.
9. The expected VPN credentials are provisioned.
10. WHITEDNS entitlement is applied if the plan includes it.
11. The real supported client receives a valid configuration.
12. The client establishes a tunnel to the deployed VPN server.
13. External test traffic passes through the intended VPN route.
14. DNS behavior and the actual egress address are checked.
15. A repeated payment event does not create additional access.
16. An injected temporary provisioning failure recovers without losing the paid order or duplicating its entitlements.
17. Expiration and revocation remove the expected access.

Do not mark a step `PASS` merely because a mock call returned success. Label mocked tests distinctly from tests that exercised the real Telegram payment test environment, Worker, provisioner, and VPN.

## Phase 5 — Finish the remaining acceptance gaps

Address the partial WHITEDNS verification from the previous report:

- Prove that plan selection creates the correct DNS entitlement.
- Prove that the signed or authenticated event reaches the Worker.
- Prove that the VPS/client DNS configuration matches the entitlement.
- Prove the intended resolver works through an active VPN tunnel.
- Prove that expiry or revocation removes the DNS entitlement.
- Confirm that failures cannot silently route DNS outside the intended policy.

Keep the already-verified VPN reconciler and production service behavior intact. Do not run unnecessary live service restarts, destructive tests, or uncontrolled load tests.

Re-run the existing test suites after integration and update the acceptance matrix with fresh results.

## Phase 6 — Production readiness decision

Do not enable production payments solely because sandbox tests pass.

Prepare a clear go/no-go report that distinguishes:

- Code complete.
- Sandbox integration passed.
- Customer-side payment availability verified or unverified.
- Merchant payout/redemption verified or unverified.
- Production configuration complete.
- Production payment actually tested or not tested.
- Full VPN entitlement flow verified or not verified.

Use `PASS`, `FAIL`, `BLOCKED`, and `NOT TESTED` honestly.

If live merchant eligibility, payout availability, legal requirements, or a production credential requires owner action, finish every independent task and identify the exact remaining dependency. Do not invent credentials or claim that the dependency has been satisfied.

Keep production checkout disabled until the required business and payment setup is genuinely ready.

## Execution directive

Start with the existing acceptance report and source code, then implement the Stars integration in the commerce authority, connect it to the existing entitlement system, run test-environment transactions, and execute the full provisioning and VPN verification.

Do not rebuild working infrastructure. Do not fake a payment provider. Do not stop at a plan. Deliver tested implementation, durable evidence, and a clear production-readiness decision.

import { transport, initTransport } from '@/lib/transport';
import { api } from '@/lib/api';

export interface WsTestMessage {
  type: string;
  testId?: string;
  task?: string;
  pct?: number;
  message?: string;
  result?: unknown;
  error?: unknown;
  observation?: unknown;
  targetId?: string;
  observationId?: string;
  sweepId?: string;
  /** discovery progress frames (`discovery` topic): real per-candidate counts */
  done?: number;
  total?: number;
  profile?: string;
  stage?: string;
  at?: number;
  engine?: string;
  node?: string;
  depth?: string;
  latencyMs?: number | null;
  exitIp?: string | null;
  dnsPolicy?: string;
  ok?: boolean;
}

/**
 * Subscribe to live progress for a running test. Returns an unsubscribe fn.
 *
 * The socket URL comes from the transport layer: desktop mode connects to the
 * loopback sidecar. The WS upgrade authenticates with a single-use 30 s
 * ticket minted via the authenticated REST surface (see below) — progress
 * frames carry no privileged data, but the endpoint is still ticket-gated.
 */
export function subscribeTest(
  testId: string,
  onMessage: (msg: WsTestMessage) => void,
): () => void {
  let ws: WebSocket | null = null;
  let closed = false;
  let cancelled = false;

  void (async () => {
    await initTransport();
    if (cancelled) return;
    const t = transport();
    try {
      // The WS route requires a single-use ticket (the session cookie is
      // SameSite=strict and browsers cannot attach Authorization headers to
      // WebSocket handshakes). Mint one via the authenticated API first.
      const { ticket } = await api.post<{ ticket: string; expiresInMs: number }>('/ws/ticket');
      ws = new WebSocket(`${t.wsBase}/api/v1/ws?ticket=${encodeURIComponent(ticket)}`);
    } catch {
      return;
    }

    ws.onopen = () => {
      ws?.send(JSON.stringify({ type: 'subscribe', testId }));
    };
    ws.onmessage = (event) => {
      try {
        onMessage(JSON.parse(event.data as string) as WsTestMessage);
      } catch {
        // ignore malformed frames
      }
    };
    ws.onerror = () => {
      // progress is best-effort; the POST response carries the final result
    };
  })();

  return () => {
    if (closed) return;
    closed = true;
    cancelled = true;
    try {
      ws?.close();
    } catch {
      // already closed
    }
  };
}

import { useEffect } from 'react';

/** React hook: subscribe to live progress for a test while testId is set. */
export function useWsTestProgress(
  testId: string | null,
  onMessage: (msg: WsTestMessage) => void,
): void {
  useEffect(() => {
    if (!testId) return;
    // The test republishes its full result on completion, so resubscribing only
    // when testId changes is sufficient for correctness of the final result.
    const unsub = subscribeTest(testId, onMessage);
    return unsub;
  }, [testId, onMessage]);
}

/**
 * Quick-connect picker logic.
 *
 * Pure, React-free rules for the keyboard overlay, so the overlay itself only
 * renders: which nodes a query matches, how the active row moves, and which
 * text a row shows. Keeping them here means the keyboard behaviour is testable
 * without a DOM, and the candidate shape is documented in one place.
 */

/**
 * The subset of a node DTO the picker needs.
 *
 * No host/port: the server never sends a node's dial endpoint to the browser,
 * and the overlay only ever posts the id back.
 */
export interface QuickNode {
  id: string;
  /** Server-built display name; always non-empty. */
  label: string;
  protocol: string;
  country: string | null;
  city: string | null;
  remark: string | null;
  medianProxyMs: number | null;
  status: string;
}

/** Everything a token may match, lower-cased and joined once. */
export function quickNodeHaystack(node: QuickNode): string {
  return [node.label, node.protocol, node.country, node.city, node.remark]
    .filter((v): v is string => typeof v === 'string' && v.length > 0)
    .join(' ')
    .toLowerCase();
}

/**
 * Filter by every whitespace-separated token, in the order the server returned
 * (already fastest-tested first).
 *
 * The whole query as one substring would make "japan tokyo" match nothing even
 * though both words are on screen; token AND is what a user typing two words
 * expects. An empty query keeps the list — opening the overlay should show
 * candidates, not a blank panel.
 */
export function filterQuickNodes(nodes: readonly QuickNode[], query: string): QuickNode[] {
  const tokens = query.trim().toLowerCase().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
  if (tokens.length === 0) return [...nodes];
  return nodes.filter((node) => {
    const haystack = quickNodeHaystack(node);
    return tokens.every((token) => haystack.includes(token));
  });
}

/**
 * Move the active row by `delta`, wrapping at both ends.
 *
 * Wrapping matters here because the overlay opens with the first row selected:
 * ArrowUp from the top should reach the last candidate (the slowest one, still
 * possibly the right choice), not stall.
 */
export function stepActive(index: number, length: number, delta: number): number {
  if (length <= 0) return 0;
  // Double modulo, not a `< 0` branch: `-1 % 1` is `-0` in JavaScript, which
  // passes `< 0` and would put `-0` into state (0 that logs and prints as -0).
  return ((index + delta) % length + length) % length;
}

function anchor(href: string, text = 'link'): HTMLAnchorElement {
  const a = document.createElement('a');
  a.href = href;

/** A drag payload: jsdom has no DataTransfer, so model the two methods we use. */
function dragEvent(type: string, data: Record<string, string>): Event {
  const event = new Event(type, { bubbles: true, cancelable: true });
  Object.defineProperty(event, 'dataTransfer', {
    value: {
      types: Object.keys(data),
      getData: (kind: string) => data[kind] ?? '',
    },
  });
  return event;
}

export type AgentHopState = 'pending' | 'active' | 'ok' | 'failed';

  id: AgentHopId;

  for (let i = events.length - 1; i >= 0; i -= 1) {
    if (events[i]?.stage === 'attempt-start') return events.slice(i);

function lastOf(events: readonly AgentPathEvent[], stages: readonly string[]): AgentPathEvent | null {
  for (let i = events.length - 1; i >= 0; i -= 1) {

# The two host reconciler verifiers (`scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-removal.py`

#   success -> comment the recovery and close that issue

# purpose: the issue is the durable record, and a site without the secret still
# gets a real alert rather than a skipped step.

{"kind":"tool","id":"g8YlVIv2hqg","toolName":"write_file","input":{"path":".github/workflows/reconciler-verifiers.yml","instructions":"Add the scheduled workflow that runs both host reconciler verifiers and alerts on failure.","content":"# The two host reconciler verifiers, on a schedule, with an alert on failure.
#
# What they prove and why it needs a schedule:
#
#   scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-removal.py
#     A rotated secret, a revoked identity and an expired identity must be gone
#     from the server config the reconciler would write, an unchanged set must
#     not churn it, and the retired shared-secret inbound must be left alone.
#
#   scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-failure.py
#     A failed pull keeps the last known-good set, a malformed payload applies
#     nothing, an empty set applies deny-all, `expiresAt` is still enforced while
#     the Worker is unreachable, recovery converges, and an unusable `xray`
#     binary fails closed.
#
# Both run the REAL `scripts/vps-sync-vpn-users.py` in `--print` mode against a
# sandboxed copy of the server config and a loopback stand-in for the Worker, so
# this needs no VPN host, no SSH key and no production credential. That is why
# they can be scheduled at all.
#
# The failure they guard against is silent: nothing crashes, the reconciler just
# stops removing what it should, or starts wiping on a transient error. A red
# check on a scheduled run has no audience, so `alert` turns the result into a
# GitHub issue that stays open until a run passes (and an optional
# `OPS_ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL` push, when that secret is configured).

name: Reconciler verifiers

on:
  schedule:
    # Daily. Cron is UTC; 02:17 rather than 02:00 so it does not pile onto the
    # top-of-hour runs every other repository schedules.
    - cron: '17 2 * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      - scripts/vps-sync-vpn-users.py
      - scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-removal.py
      - scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-failure.py
      - scripts/alert-reconciler-regression.sh
      - .github/workflows/reconciler-verifiers.yml
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - scripts/vps-sync-vpn-users.py
      - scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-removal.py
      - scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-failure.py
      - scripts/alert-reconciler-regression.sh
      - .github/workflows/reconciler-verifiers.yml

concurrency:
  group: reconciler-verifiers-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  verify:
    name: ${{ matrix.verifier }} verifier
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    strategy:
      # Both verifiers must report: a removal regression must not hide a
      # failure-handling regression behind a cancelled matrix leg.
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - verifier: entitlement-removal
            script: scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-removal.py
          - verifier: failure-handling
            script: scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-failure.py

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # The reconciler reads YAML server configs; PyYAML is the one dependency
      # neither the harness nor the runner guarantees.
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'

      - name: Install PyYAML
        run: python -m pip install --disable-pip-version-check pyyaml

      - name: Run the ${{ matrix.verifier }} verifier
        shell: bash
        run: |
          set -o pipefail
          python "${{ matrix.script }}" 2>&1 | tee "reconciler-${{ matrix.verifier }}.log"

      # The log is the evidence for the alert and for anyone reading the run
      # later; keep it even (especially) when the verifier failed.
      - name: Upload verifier log
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: reconciler-${{ matrix.verifier }}-log
          path: reconciler-${{ matrix.verifier }}.log
          if-no-files-found: warn
          retention-days: 30

  alert:
    name: alert on regression
    needs: verify
    # Runs even when (especially when) the verifiers failed. Skipped on pull
    # requests: a fork's token is read-only, and the red check is the alert there.
    if: always() && github.event_name != 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    permissions:
      contents: read
      issues: write

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Record the result
        shell: bash
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
          RESULT: ${{ needs.verify.result }}
          RUN_URL: ${{ github.server_url }}/${{ github.repository }}/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }}
          EVENT: ${{ github.event_name }}
          WEBHOOK: ${{ secrets.OPS_ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL }}
        run: bash scripts/alert-reconciler-regression.sh
"}}

## What runs, when

New workflow [reconciler-verifiers.yml](.github/workflows/reconciler-verifiers.yml):

- **Schedule:** daily at `02:17 UTC` (`17 2 * * *`), plus `workflow_dispatch` for an on-demand run.
- **Also on change:** `push` to `main` and every `pull_request` that touches the reconciler, either verifier, the alert script, or the workflow itself — so a regression is caught at review time, not only the next morning.
- **Matrix, `fail-fast: false`:** `verify-vps-reconciler-removal.py` and `verify-vps-reconciler-failure.py` run as separate legs, so a removal regression cannot hide a failure-handling one. Each installs PyYAML (the reconciler's only real dependency), runs the verifier with `set -o pipefail`, and uploads its log as a 30-day artifact even when it fails.

These are credential-free by design: both harnesses drive the real `scripts/vps-sync-vpn-users.py` in `--print` mode against a sandboxed config and a loopback stand-in Worker, so a GitHub runner can execute them with no VPS, SSH key, or production secret.

## How a failure becomes an alert

New [alert-reconciler-regression.sh](scripts/alert-reconciler-regression.sh), run by an `alert` job that fires with `if: always()` and `issues: write`:

- **Failure** → opens an issue labelled `reconciler-regression` naming which trigger and run failed and what each verifier guards; if one is already open it comments instead of opening a duplicate.
- **Recovery (a later pass)** → comments the passing run and closes the issue with `completed`.
- **`cancelled` / `skipped`** → no state change. Concurrency cancels superseded runs routinely, and minting a regression issue for each one would train you to ignore the label.
- **Optional push:** if `OPS_ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL` is set as a repository secret, it also POSTs `{"text": ...}` to it (Slack/Discord/Teams-compatible). Without the secret the issue is still the alert, so the job never silently no-ops.

+#
+#   scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-failure.py

+#     nothing, an empty set applies deny-all, `expiresAt` is still enforced while
+#     the Worker is unreachable, recovery converges, and an unusable `xray`
+#     binary fails closed.
+#
+# Both run the REAL `scripts/vps-sync-vpn-users.py` in `--print` mode against a
+# sandboxed copy of the server config and a loopback stand-in for the Worker, so
+# this needs no VPN host, no SSH key and no production credential. That is why
+# they can be scheduled at all.
+#
+# The failure they guard against is silent: nothing crashes, the reconciler just
+# stops removing what it should, or starts wiping on a transient error. A red
+# check on a scheduled run has no audience, so `alert` turns the result into a
+# GitHub issue that stays open until a run passes (and an optional
+# `OPS_ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL` push, when that secret is configured).

+name: Reconciler verifiers
+
+on:
+  schedule:

+      - scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-removal.py
+      - scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-failure.py
+      - scripts/alert-reconciler-regression.sh

+      - scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-removal.py

+      - scripts/alert-reconciler-regression.sh
+      - .github/workflows/reconciler-verifiers.yml

+  cancel-in-progress: true
+
+permissions:

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+# Surface a reconciler-verifier regression without anyone watching the Actions tab.
+#
+# The two host reconciler verifiers (`scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-removal.py`
+# and `scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-failure.py`) prove that a revoked or
+# expired identity disappears from the server config, and that a Worker outage
+# cannot wipe or resurrect one. They run on a schedule because the failure they
+# guard against is silent: the reconciler keeps working, just on stale input.
+#
+# A red check on a scheduled run is not an alert — nobody is looking. This
+# script turns the run result into state that persists until someone acts:
+#
+#   failed  -> open (or comment on) a GitHub issue labelled `reconciler-regression`
+#   success -> comment the recovery and close that issue
+#
+# It also POSTs a short message to `OPS_ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL` when that secret is
+# configured, so the owner can be reached on a phone. The webhook is optional on
+# purpose: the issue is the durable record, and a site without the secret still
+# gets a real alert rather than a skipped step.
+#
+# Every gh call names `--repo` explicitly: a scheduled run's checkout can be
+# detached, and gh would otherwise have to infer the repository.
+#
+# Inputs (all from the workflow):
+#   REPO      owner/name
+#   RESULT    needs.<job>.result — success | failure | cancelled | skipped
+#   RUN_URL   link to the run
+#   EVENT     github.event_name (for the issue text)
+#   WEBHOOK   optional secret; empty means "no push notification"
+#
+# Exit status is 0 once the alert state is recorded, even for a failed verifier
+# — the verifier job is what must go red. A failure of the alerting itself exits
+# non-zero so a broken alert path cannot masquerade as "nothing to report".
+
+set -euo pipefail
+
+REPO="${REPO:?REPO is required}"
+RESULT="${RESULT:-unknown}"
+RUN_URL="${RUN_URL:-}"
+EVENT="${EVENT:-unknown}"
+WEBHOOK="${WEBHOOK:-}"
+
+LABEL="reconciler-regression"
+TITLE="Reconciler verifier regression (entitlement removal / failure handling)"
+
+if [ -z "${GH_TOKEN:-}" ] && [ -z "${GITHUB_TOKEN:-}" ]; then
+  echo "alert: no GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN in the environment" >&2
+  exit 2
+fi
+
+open_issue() {
+  gh issue list --repo "$REPO" --label "$LABEL" --state open --json number --jq '.[0].number // empty'
+}
+
+ensure_label() {
+  gh label create "$LABEL" --repo "$REPO" \
+    --color B60205 \
+    --description "A scheduled reconciler verifier failed" \
+    --force >/dev/null
+}
+
+body_for_failure() {
+  cat <<EOF
+The scheduled host-reconciler verifiers failed.
+
+- **Result:** \`${RESULT}\`
+- **Trigger:** \`${EVENT}\`
+- **Run:** ${RUN_URL}
+
+What is guarded:
+
+- \`scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-removal.py\` — a rotated secret, a revoked
+  identity and an expired identity must not survive the next reconciler pass,
+  and an unchanged set must not churn the config.
+- \`scripts/verify-vps-reconciler-failure.py\` — a failed pull keeps the last
+  known-good set, a malformed payload applies nothing, an empty set applies
+  deny-all, expiry is still enforced while the Worker is down, and an invalid
+  \`xray\` binary fails closed.
+
+This issue stays open until a run passes, at which point it is commented and
+closed automatically. Do not close it by hand to silence the alert.
+EOF
+}
+
+body_for_recovery() {
+  cat <<EOF
+Recovered: the scheduled reconciler verifiers passed again.
+
+- **Run:** ${RUN_URL}
+
+Closing automatically. Reopen by re-running the workflow if this was a flake.
+EOF
+}
+
+# A cancelled or skipped run proved nothing — concurrency cancels a superseded
+# run routinely, and opening a regression issue for it would train the owner to
+# ignore the label. Only a real pass may close an alert, and only a real failure
+# may open one.
+if [ "$RESULT" = "cancelled" ] || [ "$RESULT" = "skipped" ]; then
+  echo "alert: verifiers did not run (${RESULT}); alert state left untouched"
+  exit 0
+fi
+
+ensure_label
+existing="$(open_issue)"
+
+if [ "$RESULT" = "success" ]; then
+  if [ -n "$existing" ]; then
+    gh issue comment "$existing" --repo "$REPO" --body "$(body_for_recovery)" >/dev/null
+    gh issue close "$existing" --repo "$REPO" --reason completed >/dev/null
+    echo "alert: recovery recorded on issue #$existing"
+  else
+    echo "alert: verifiers passed and no regression issue is open"
+  fi
+  exit 0
+fi
+
+body="$(body_for_failure)"
+if [ -n "$existing" ]; then
+  gh issue comment "$existing" --repo "$REPO" --body "$body" >/dev/null
+  echo "alert: commented on open issue #$existing"
+else
+  url="$(gh issue create --repo "$REPO" --title "$TITLE" --body "$body" --label "$LABEL")"
+  echo "alert: opened $url"
+fi
+
+if [ -n "$WEBHOOK" ]; then
+  payload="$(python3 - "$TITLE" "$RUN_URL" "$RESULT" <<'PY'
+import json, sys
+title, run_url, result = sys.argv[1:4]
+print(json.dumps({"text": f"{title}: {result}. {run_url}"}))
+PY
+)"
+  # `--fail` so a rejected webhook is visible in the job log, but the issue above
+  # is already the durable alert — do not re-fail the workflow over transport.
+  curl -sS --fail -X POST -H 'content-type: application/json' \
+    --data "$payload" "$WEBHOOK" >/dev/null || echo "alert: webhook delivery failed" >&2
+fi

Measured on this host with a tunnel live, and filed in the evidence report.

## What was actually running

A real tunnel was already up: an xray TUN on interface `happ-xray` (ifIndex 18) holding the default route, with egress `83.229.87.141` (DE, colo FRA) — confirmed by Cloudflare's trace, not assumed. That TUN was **not** started by this workspace, and it is not NetPulse's own tunnel: both local app databases have empty `public_nodes` tables and no VPS client credential exists in the tree, so the product's tunnel could not be brought up.

## Method

New read-only harness [measure-dns-leak.ps1](scripts/measure-dns-leak.ps1) — no elevation, no route/resolver/tunnel change:

1. Identifies the tunnel interface from the address the OS actually egresses as, plus the route to it.
2. For every **configured** resolver, asks `Find-NetRoute` which interface a datagram to it would use — the same decision the DNS client makes.
3. Queries each resolver for `whoami.akamai.net` (an A-record echo that names the resolver's egress) and records whether it answered.
4. Classifies: answered *and* routed off-tunnel = leak; answered *and* routed through the tunnel = no leak; off-tunnel but silent = unreachable, not a leak.
5. Records the **fail-open surface**: public resolvers left on physical adapters, which are harmless while the tunnel owns the route and become raw-path queries the moment it stops.

TXT echo was the first choice and was dropped for a measured reason: every plaintext TXT answer came back empty on this path — even `cloudflare.com TXT` via `1.1.1.1` and via the tunnel resolver `172.19.0.2` — while the same name over DoH through the tunnel returned a valid record. That is itself a path characteristic worth knowing, but it makes TXT useless as a leak witness here.

## Result: NO LEAK OBSERVED

| resolver | configured on | route interface | answered | resolver echo | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1.0.0.1 | physical adapters | happ-xray | yes | 172.71.140.37 | tunneled path |
| 1.1.1.1 | physical adapters | happ-xray | yes | 172.71.140.37 | tunneled path |
| 172.19.0.2 | happ-xray | happ-xray | yes | 172.71.140.37 | tunneled path |
| 192.168.1.1 | Ethernet | Ethernet | no (timeout) | — | off-tunnel, unreachable |

System resolution of `example.com` succeeded through the same path, so DNS was working rather than merely failing closed. Every resolver that answered routes through the tunnel; the one configured off-tunnel resolver (the LAN router) never answered. Two independent runs agreed.

## What this does not prove

- **No packet capture** — the classification is the routing decision, not an observed packet (capture needs administrator rights this run did not take). This TUN owns the default route, so route membership is the right test for it; a rule-capturing tunnel would not be visible this way.
- **Fail-open risk is measured, not hypothetical.** `1.1.1.1`, `1.0.0.1` and `192.168.1.1` are configured on physical adapters. While the tunnel route exists they are tunneled; if it disappears those same resolvers become raw-path queries. Fail-closed behaviour on tunnel drop was **not tested** — dropping the tunnel would have cut your live connectivity, which this measurement was not authorised to do.
- One network, one moment, one external client — it says nothing about NetPulse's own tunnel or its TUN gateway ([tunGatewayHandle.ts](apps/api/src/services/tunGatewayHandle.ts)), which was not brought up here.
